# EPISTLE

->The greatest Glory of the HOUSE OF ANHALT<-

As I considered whether, in these most wretched Times of ours—in which almost nothing is usually safe from the most insolent slanders of an envious Tongue—I should release into the light this, my **CHEMICAL ROYALTY** <term>Basilica Chymica</term><note>The title translates to "Royal Chemical Pharmacy." This work was one of the most influential texts of iatrochemistry, a branch of medicine that sought chemical solutions to diseases, heavily influenced by the teachings of Paracelsus.</note>, which was gathered through various and lengthy travels, tireless labors and night-watches, at no small expense, and finally by long observation and meditative study, and written several years ago; and whether I should venture upon the perilous sea of public opinion: various obstacles met me as I hesitated at the crossroads of this uncertain judgment. For those who, with right reason, devote themselves entirely in this most unhappy age of ours to the studies of true Wisdom...

<summary>In this opening of his dedicatory epistle, Oswald Croll expresses his hesitation to publish his long-researched medical work due to the harsh criticism and envy prevalent in his time. He emphasizes the immense personal effort, travel, and expense he invested in compiling the "Basilica Chymica."</summary>

<header>PREFACE</header>

<margin>Victor. God's gifts grow and increase by being shared.</margin>
Rightly we are bound to imitate Him, whose children we ought to be; and those most of all, whom His gracious mercy has led out from the dark labyrinth and maze of Labors and Errors to the manifest path and center of Rest and Truth. Therefore, it did not seem right to me to bury the talent entrusted to me by the <term>Father of Lights</term> <note>original: "Patre Luminum" — a biblical title for God (James 1:17), frequently used by alchemists to emphasize that true scientific insight is a gift from the Divine</note> in a shroud through some impious silence, or to hide it any longer with inhumane envy. Indeed, it is a kind duty, full of humanity, to readily show the way to a wandering neighbor, or to keep one who is not wandering on the right path. For this reason, friend reader—to the praise and glory of Divine Majesty and Liberality (of whose many mercies and granted benefits I desire and hope to be, in this publication, at least the instrument and pen, however far inferior)—and also for

### ADMONITORY REMARKS

...to learn, nor could I receive it by hearing, nor understand it from the monuments of the ancients. It has always been foreign to my nature to burden the reader with trifles and lies, of which our age—the <note>original: "fax & amurca mundi" — literally the dregs and dross of the world</note> **scum and dregs of the world**—is quite fertile. <margin>
The more numerous the virtues, the fewer [the recipes].
</margin>

I see medical students already being overwhelmed and so entangled by these patchwork compositions <note>original: "centonibus" — a "cento" was a poem or work made of scraps from other authors</note> that they almost collapse and die under such a heavy weight of Recipes. However, for nearly twenty years, during my hardships and various laborious travels of fortune through France, Italy, Germany, Hungary, Poland, and Bohemia, I have sought something else.

<margin>
It is a kind act, as Pliny testifies in his Epistle to Vespasian, and full of noble shame to confess through whom we have made progress.
</margin>

From <term>Chymiatrists</term> <note>Physicians who utilized alchemical and chemical methods to prepare medicines, as opposed to traditional herbalists</note>, especially from men of great experience and learning, I have obtained knowledge—partly through prayers, partly through price and exchange (not to mention my own findings discovered through my own study by the will of God in medical practice, and those not few). Through tireless diligence and curious exploration, preferring the common good to private utility, and further moved by Christian charity for the misery and necessity of the sick, I have acted according to my fidelity toward the **Medical Republic**. These remedies have been already most thoroughly proven by the <term>benefit of Vulcan</term> <note>original: "Vulcani beneficio" — Vulcan was the god of fire; in alchemy, this refers to the use of the furnace and laboratory testing</note>. # ADMONITION

<margin>

</margin>

These preparations require a craftsman of such character—having nothing in common with the common rabble of Alchemists <note>original: "Alchymistarum uulgo" — a frequent dismissal by "true" chemists of those they considered fraudulent or unlearned "puffers."</note>—lest the errors of the craftsman be attributed to the art <note>original Greek: "τὰ τοῦ τεχνίτου σφάλματα, τῇ τέχνῃ ἐπινομίζηται" (ta tou technitou sphalmata, tē technē epinomizētai). In those practical <note>original Greek: "ἐγχειρητικοῖς" (encheirētikois) — referring to manual or experimental operations.</note> arts, I say, there will be no doubt that the other powers obtained by the most expert Chemical-Physicians <term>Chymiatri: doctors who utilized chemical and mineral remedies, often inspired by Paracelsian theories, rather than relying solely on traditional herbalism.</term> through long experience, proven by many experiments, and now published by a singular effort, will undoubtedly fulfill the desired effect and satisfy both the vow and the eager expectation of the seeker.

What in such a great number of detractors who gnaw at even the best things in the worst way...

By this rash daring, for several years without harm to his health, he made a living here and there in the city, etc.

<note>original: "Admonitoria," meaning Admonitory Remarks or Warnings.</note>

Nor ought we be so devoted to any man's authority that we do not prefer **Truth** itself, for without Truth, all authority is harmful and should be considered of no weight by the wise. One should attend not to **who** speaks, but to **what** is said; and no one should be so bound by the judgment of others...*

...so addicted [to his own opinion] that he is utterly stripped of any personal judgment.

The true method consists in the knowledge of the Disease and its Cure—namely, that which expels the illness and introduces health through a proper regimen of diet and suitable Medicines. For this reason, **Wimpenaeus** <note>original: "VVimpenæus." Referring to Johann Wimpina, a physician who wrote in defense of Paracelsian "Spagyric" medicine.</note> learnedly discusses how the most serious diseases are healed today by the **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of Paracelsus who used chemical processes to create medicine.</note> for three reasons.

<margin>Every limb <note>original: "membrum." In early modern medicine, this often refers to specific internal organs as well as external limbs.</note> has its own digestion and separation within itself, as well as its own emunctory and excrement.</margin>
**FIRST**, because diseases are understood more perfectly. For in the past, when all diseases were attributed to the **four humors** <note>The traditional medical theory that health was governed by the balance of blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, those illnesses could not be cured whose cause was **Tartar** <note>term: **Tartar** (original: "Tartarus"). In Paracelsian medicine, this refers to stony or calcified deposits—like kidney stones, gouty crystals, or dental plaque—formed when the body's "internal alchemist" fails to process waste.</note> adhering to some limb, which cannot be attributed to any of those four humors. Since we have happened upon the subject of Tartar here, a more abundant mention of it must be made in this convenient place.

# PREFACE

*Seek the way of understanding the dead letter of* **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541).</note> *and the* **Philosophers**. *His writings, published for the public good through the promotion and at the expense of the most Serene and Reverend* **ERNEST, Prince Elector of Cologne** <note>Ernest of Bavaria (1554–1612), a high-ranking church official and prince who was a great patron of the sciences and alchemy.</note>, *have given opponents an opportunity to claim that they are entangled in the most evident contradictions. He was moved by a just indignation toward certain most unjust and inhuman* **Physicians** *and* **Pharmacists** *of his time, who often lay in wait for him with poison, seeking to shorten his life. If he had written more clearly, then those traveling peddlers and common Alchemists would have surpassed all physicians and would have prostituted the art to the great injury of Nature. He hid his* **mysteries** *under common and various names; therefore, metaphors must not be mistaken for the truth itself. For few understand the* **Secrets** <note>original: "Arcana." Therefore, readers have need of a* **Delian swimmer** <note>An ancient Greek proverb referring to a diver who can reach the depths of a difficult text without drowning in its complexity.</note> *and a most sharp wit; they also require a* **magical Intellect**—*namely, a purified eye of the mind that can investigate their meanings and hidden mysteries. By* **Magic**, *I always mean that which is True and lawful (not the infamous and profane* **sorcery** <note>original: "goeteian" (Greek: γοητεία), referring to deceptive or demonic magic.</note> *worthy of* **Vulcan** <note>The Roman god of fire; here implying crude, purely material chemical work or "black" magic.</note>, *which I deplore...*

# ADMONISHMENTS

For this work depends not on the **power of the one who wills**, but on the **will of a merciful God** <note>original: "non in Posse volentis, sed in Velle miserentis DEI." This is an alchemical application of Romans 9:16.</note>, who knows that it is not beneficial for the salvation of all people to possess **Honors** and **Riches** alongside **Health**. And although the key to the **Philosophical Garden** might by chance fall to someone (just as He knows it has happened to certain people), nevertheless, because of the bolted Door—namely, the denial and resistance of Divine Grace and Blessing—they were never able to open it, much less enter and pluck the desired fruits of the <term>Hermetic Tree</term> <note>A symbolic representation of the alchemical process, where the "fruits" represent the successful transformation of matter or the attainment of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, or take possession of the sweetest kernels of this mystery.

Thus, in our century, certain impostors acquired the very true <term>Philosophical Ferment</term> <note>The substance used to "ripen" or transform base metals; often another name for the Philosopher's Stone in its active form.</note>—which had been prepared by others—by illicit means, through right and wrong. However, because of their ignorance of the first principles, they were unable to multiply it further. Indeed, this most holy science never admits such ignorant **braggarts** <note>original: "Thrasones." A reference to Thraso, a boastful soldier from Roman comedy; used here to describe arrogant pseudo-alchemists.</note> into its inner chambers. 

This is that work, hidden under the garment of the <term>Philosophical Virgin</term> <note>A symbolic term for the pure, uncorrupted "First Matter" or the elusive secret of the alchemical process.</note>, which not even a brother wished to teach to a brother. (Therefore, it is a vain effort to wish to incite an **Adept Philosopher** to communicate his knowledge through deserved benefits, goodwill, or any kind of service that can be devised.) This is that **Secret**, placed and buried in the most hidden Treasures of the Mind and Memory, over which the genuine Philosophers—those of a hidden and sagacious subtlety of genius—carry the laws...

# PREFACE

in all the limbs: When the blood is pure, the **vital spirit of the Heart** <note>original: "spiritus Cordis vitalis". Therefore, so that the consumption and dissipation of said spirit may be avoided (as far as Nature allows), this Natural spirit and heat existing in Human bodies, thus diminished or hindered, must be increased and strengthened, so that it may perform its duty more strongly and better.

<margin>

<margin>**a** This book is titled *The Royal Chemistry* <note>original: "Basilica Chymica." A famous work by Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609) that combined Paracelsian medicine with spiritual alchemy.</note>, just as in a royal or principal court there is a magnificent and most precious display of all kinds of things, so too here there are only the most select of medicines. <margin>**d** Remedies ought to be similar to the **balsam** <note>The body's internal healing power or "life-force."</note>; this is the highest axiom of physicians, introduced into sound therapeutics by the "Dictator" Hippocrates in Book 2 of *On Winds* and Aphorism 22 of Section 2: **Contraries are remedies for contraries** <note>original: "Contrariorum contraria sunt remedia." The traditional Galenic view that a "hot" disease requires a "cold" medicine.</note>. Opposed to this seems to be the saying of the Hermeticists <note>Followers of Hermes Trismegistus/Paracelsus who favored "chemical" medicine.</note>: **Likes are cured by likes** <note>original: "Similia similibus curantur."</note>. But there is no real contradiction; rather, both must be understood correctly: remedies must indeed be similar to nature—or to the balsam and innate heat—which they must assist in overcoming the disease, but they must be contrary to the disease itself.</margin>

## UNIVERSAL DIGESTIVE
->or ripener.<-

*In diseases which consist of mobile and superficial impurities, which have not struck fixed roots nor are destined for difficult coagulations—which is detected from the signs of pain and from the inconstant and swelling eruptions of symptoms, such as most* **fevers**, *catarrhs, coughs, hoarseness, and similar conditions—in these there is no need for a* **Digestive** <note>In ancient and early modern medicine, a "digestive" or "maturative" was a medicine used to "cook" or prepare "peccant humors" (harmful fluids) so they could be more easily expelled from the body.</note>; *they are safely and suddenly removed by the help of Purgatives and Purifiers.* *However, feverish and inflammatory impurities—which have more difficult tinctures* <note>original: "Tincturas." In alchemy and medicine, this refers to the deep-seated coloring or essential quality of a substance; here, it refers to how deeply the disease has "stained" or taken hold of the body's tissues.</note> *because they allow for fixed resolutions and coagulations of vapors that are difficult to dissolve (such as those perpetually received in suspected parts and related mines* <note>original: "mineris." A term used by Galen for a treatment that gradually tempers or evacuates humors rather than doing so all at once.</note> *(which are clearly equivalent curative indications). For they do not obey the raw powers of common purgative medicines, which [deal] with bodily and raw spi[rits]*...

## II.
# EMETIC [VOMITIVE].

In provoking this [vomiting], the properties of Antimony, Vitriol, and Hellebore <gloss>a</gloss> are powerful; they leave nothing harmful in the stomach but pull out all <gloss>b</gloss> impurity by the roots <gloss>c</gloss>.

*A Hellebore Emetic is found in the work of Conradinus, a most experienced physician, in his booklet on Hungarian Fever <note>Hungarian Fever: historically identified as typhus, which affected armies in 16th-century Hungary</note>: here we will treat Vitriol; preparations of Antimony will follow shortly after.*

a. Of white hellebore.
b. i.e., All humors <note>humors: the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which pre-modern medicine sought to keep in balance</note>.

### CONRADINUS’S EMETIC.

c. The process for Conradinus’s Emetic is as follows: though it is found in a mutilated <note>mutilatus: likely meaning the original text was damaged, incomplete, or corrupted</note> state in the aforementioned book. Roots of bryony <term>bryony: a climbing plant used as a powerful purgative</term> and sowbread <term>cyclaminis: the root of the cyclamen plant, used to purge the bowels and induce vomiting</term>, 2 drams <term>dram: an apothecary weight, approximately 3.9 grams</term> of each. White hellebore, 1 dram. Once these roots have been properly cleaned, washed, and dried in the shade, grind them into a powder; pour over it spirit of wine <term>spirit of wine: high-proof alcohol or ethanol used as a solvent</term> to a height of two or three fingers above the solids. Let them stand in a water bath <term>B.: abbreviation for Balneum Mariae, a warm water bath used for gentle heating</term> for several days, then slowly distill through an alembic <term>alembic: a traditional distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</term>. Remove and grind the dregs <note>original: "fæces"</note>. Pour back the previously distilled spirit of wine and leave it for some time in a warm, well-sealed vessel. Afterwards, filter it, and you will have a true emetic. Usage: The outermost feathers of a quill, which [are chosen] over the others... <meta>catchword: quis</meta>

## GILLA OF THEOPHRASTUS<sup>a</sup>
### or Salt of Vitriol.

Crystals of Vitriol <term>vitriol: a sulfate of certain metals; in this context, usually iron or copper sulfate used as a powerful emetic</term>, prepared from Venus <term>Venus: the alchemical name for copper</term> or Mars <term>Mars: the alchemical name for iron</term> (as will be described shortly in the section on the Specific for the Stomach), should be dissolved in acid phlegm <note>acid phlegm: the first watery, acidic distillate collected during the heating of vitriol</note>, which is the first thing that comes out during the distillation of common Vitriol; let these be circulated <term>circulated: a chemical process where a liquid is heated in a closed vessel so its vapors condense and return to the base, "refining" the substance over time</term> together for eight days. Of this circulated liquor, give a dose from 1 scruple to 1.5 drams, or 2 scruples.

This liquor will work far more effectively and conveniently than the Salt extracted from the *caput mortuum* <term>caput mortuum: literally "dead head"; the useless residue or dregs left over after distillation or sublimation</term> of common Vitriol, or the white vitriol of Goslar <note>Goslar: a German town in the Harz Mountains famous for its historical lead and zinc mines, a major source of vitriol</note>, however it is extracted.

<margin>a. It is called "Gilla" by Paracelsus in his book *On Natural Things*, chapter 8, where he discusses the properties of crude Vitriol and *colchothar* <term>colchothar: the red iron oxide residue remaining after the distillation of vitriol</term> (otherwise also called "the red Heinz" <note>original: "der rothe Heinze"; a traditional German nickname for the red residue of vitriol</note>). It seems that the name Vitriol received was "Grilla" rather than "Gilla," and that secretly. However, in chapters 3 and 4 of book 2 of *On the Powers of Internal Diseases*, he calls the liquor of Vitriol an *arcanum* <term>arcanum: a "secret" or concentrated essence believed to have powerful healing properties</term> extracted from Gilla, used for those great afflictions of the brain: vertigo, frenzy, mania, and the falling sickness <note>falling sickness: a historical term for epilepsy</note>. Whether it is called by that name or this, it will be the same thing. Furthermore, Paracelsus undoubtedly meant crude Vitriol in the former passage, and therefore a different species from the artificial kind made from Mars and Venus. The dose...</margin>

In the sixth book of his works, Paracelsus <note>Paracelsus (1493–1541) was a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of minerals and chemicals in medicine.</note> teaches to take only 3 drops, which perhaps equals 1.5 grains <note>original: "1.ß. gr." — 'ß' is the medical abbreviation for 'semis,' meaning half; a grain was a very small unit of weight based on a grain of wheat.</note>; he says this dose should be repeated in turn if, by chance, the first vomitings do not occur. ### ACID PHLEGM OF VITRIOL.

**b** Acid and aromatic Phlegm <term>phlegm: in alchemy, the watery, tasteless, or acidic liquid that comes off first during distillation</term> of Vitriol: prepared in the following manner, it is to be preferred. Distill the phlegm from ashes <note>distill from ashes: using a sand or ash bath to provide even, indirect heat during distillation</note> through an alembic, ensuring that no spirits <term>spirits: the volatile, potent vapors of a substance</term> come out at the same time. That water acquires such a sweet odor, especially if, after the final distillation, it is circulated <term>circulated: heated in a closed vessel so the vapors condense and fall back, refining the liquid</term> for some time in moderate heat. It is otherwise a secret remedy <term>arcanum: a "profound secret" or a powerful medicine believed to have transformative healing properties</term> for headache and epilepsy, if half a spoonful is taken by itself in the morning and evening; it also gently moves the bowels. With this Phlegm, the Gilla of Paracelsus and emetic Vitriol can be more correctly administered. **NB.** <note>NB: abbreviation for 'Nota Bene,' meaning 'Note Well'</note> In the administration of vitriolated emetics, one must be careful of asthma and other chest afflictions. Those who use crude vitriol to achieve a low voice <note>original: "bassam vocem" — likely a reference to singers or orators using mineral salts to clear the throat or deepen the tone</note> eventually fall into serious illnesses.

# BASILICA

* Not by reason of the medicine itself, but because of the diversity of the subject <note>In medical terms of this era, the "subject" refers to the patient’s individual constitution or temperament.</note>.

### BLESSED WATER.

*Martin Ruland* the Elder, in his hundreds of empirical "centuries" of cures, very frequently used his "Blessed Water"—as he called it—for its emetic <note>original: "vomitoria"; a substance used to induce vomiting</note> and purgative <note>original: "ruptoria"</note> properties. In Century 5, Cure 95, he states that it is composed of Saffron of Metals <term>crocus metallorum: a reddish-yellow preparation made from antimony, often used as a powerful emetic</term> in the quantity of a pea, macerated in water, wine, beer, or mead. Of this infusion, once it has been boiled and strained, he prescribes a dose from half an ounce to two ounces.
<margin>What Saffron of Metals is.</margin>
What this "Saffron of Metals" actually is, and from what it is made, is something many have anxiously desired to know for a long time. Consequently, many commentaries have arisen from various authors, each drifting into different opinions. On this matter, see *Joseph Quercetanus* <note>Joseph Duchesne (1544–1609), a prominent French physician and chemist</note> in his *Pharmacopoeia*, chapter 7, at the end of the section on waters; also in his *Alexicacus* <note>A work titled "The Warder-off of Evil"</note>. See also the *Chemical Primer* <term>Tyrocinium Chymicum: one of the first chemistry textbooks, written by Jean Beguin in 1610</term>, chapter 12, book 2, published with my own notes which I shared with *Dr. Beguin*. See also *Libavius* <note>Andreas Libavius, a famous German chemist known for his systematic textbooks</note> in both of his collections, and others. It is certain that it is prepared from *Antimony* or *stibium* (which *Quercetanus* calls "Saturnine Magnesia"), but not everyone agrees on the method of preparation. *Libavius*, in his second collection, brings forth a "Saffron of Metals" described by the hand of *Ruland*, but it is a flawed version and useless for making "Blessed Water." Therefore, it was hardly put into use by *Libavius* himself—that "great practical chemist," if it pleases the gods <note>original: "si Diis placet"; a sarcastic remark suggesting the author does not hold Libavius's practical skills in high regard</note>—but was instead stealthily snatched by Ruland the Younger from the seventh academic dispute held under my presidency, and sold to *Libavius* as if it were his father’s own invention. Out of all these many formulas or methods of operation, the one that follows is the most exquisite of all; it has been proven by use many times,

### SAFFRON OF METALS
->*The Preparation.*<-

Take one pound or two pounds of pure, well-purified nitre <note>original: "nitri puri, bene defaecati"; also known as saltpeter</note>, and the same amount of antimony. Let the nitre melt in a pan <note>original: "fartagine"; a shallow metal vessel used for heating</note> over a very slow fire, without the vessel itself becoming violently hot. Remove the vessel from the fire and add the antimony, which must be thoroughly and finely powdered. If the two substances allow themselves to be mixed together without catching fire or detonating <term>detonatio: a rapid chemical reaction accompanied by a loud report and a flash, common in early chemistry</term>, it is well. If they do not, wait a while until the nitre has cooled sufficiently so that it can completely endure and retain the antimony powder—mixing it little by little at the start, and then more heavily later. Everything, however, should be stirred continuously with an iron spatula. When all parts have been thoroughly mixed, ignite the whole mixture with a live coal, or better yet, with a glowing iron rod. Once they have detonated, the Saffron of Metals <term>crocus metallorum: a liver-colored or reddish-orange preparation of antimony</term> is ready. Then, indeed, the antimony prepared in this way is left behind looking not unlike saffron.

### THE USES OF SAFFRON OF METALS.

The general use and dose is 6 or 12 grains <note>a grain (gr.) was a very small unit of weight, approximately 65 milligrams</note>. These should be macerated—and if the necessity is urgent, boiled—in water, wine, beer, mead, or any other liquid, provided it is suitable for the specific disease. Of this strained liquid, from half an ounce to two ounces is drunk, either cold or hot. It is called "Blessed Water." Indeed, this is administered with the greatest benefit to the sick, even in incurable diseases, either by itself or mixed with other liquids, as the demonstration of Ruland <note>Martin Ruland the Elder (1532–1602), a physician known for his chemical remedies</note> himself—

<header>BASILICA III. <note>The Third Book of the "Royal" Medical Treatise</note></header>

# RESOLVING, cleansing, 
## and washing CATHARTIC. <note>original: *CATHARTICVM RESOLV-tiuum, mundificatiuum, abluens*</note>

->*It is powerful with the strengths of Scammony and Colocynth ᵃ.*<-
<note>Scammony is a resin from a vine root, and Colocynth is the "bitter apple"; both were famous in early modern medicine as "drastic" or very strong purgatives.</note>

### Observations.

1. *Every Laxative <term>Laxatiuum; a medicine that loosens the bowels</term> consists of three Energies, according to Paracelsus ᵇ, so that it may loosen Nature when it is tired from Evacuation, and may strengthen and mitigate that which is weakened.*
<note>Paracelsus (1493–1541) was a Swiss physician who argued that medicines should not just strip the body of waste, but also contain "energies" to protect and repair the patient's vital forces during the process.</note>

2. *Purges which bring about symptoms of poisonous ᶜ properties still remaining, and which cause a loss of strength, are to be perpetually avoided.*

### PRECIPITATION OF MERCURY
->excellent.<-

First, let *aqua fortis* <term>aqua fortis: literally "strong water," a corrosive mineral acid, primarily nitric acid, used to dissolve metals</term> be made from 2 pounds of nitre <note>potassium nitrate or saltpeter</note>, 1 pound of vitriol <note>iron or copper sulfate</note>, 6 drams of uncalcined <note>raw or unheated</note> alum, and 6 drams of common salt. Mix these, distill them, and let the "water" be made in the usual way, as the *Tyrocinium* teaches in Book 3, Chapter 2. Take as much purified mercury as you wish and dissolve it with the "water," as much as you wish to dissolve. (Note: You must dissolve as much mercury as the water is capable of holding, otherwise the precipitation will not happen readily.) When the mercury is thus dissolved, pour in 2 or 3 ounces of cold spring water and leave it for some time in a quiet place, away from the fire for several hours, so that the mercury may precipitate to the bottom of its own accord. If the mercury has indeed precipitated, pour on plenty of cold water and leave it to settle; pour off the top layer of water and pour on fresh water. Repeat this process of pouring off and replacing the water until no acrimony <note>original: *acrimonia*; the sharp, stinging acidity of the leftover acid</note> can be detected in the precipitated mercury. Remove the mercury and digest it in a small matrass <note>a round-bottomed glass flask</note> or a wide-mouthed bottle without a still-head <note>original: *sine alembico*</note> over a very gentle fire until it is dry. # MERCURY PRECIPITATE
## Solar <note>In alchemy, "Solar" refers to Gold, the metal associated with the Sun.</note>

Take (℞) half a dram <note>ʒß</note> of pure and highly purified gold. It must then be heated and slowly calcined under the cover once more.

## THE GOLD OF LIFE

Take (℞) 4 ounces <note>℥ iiij</note> of *aqua fortis* <term>aqua fortis: "strong water," or nitric acid</term> made from equal parts of vitriol, nitre, and alum. In 2 ounces of this, dissolve half a dram <note>ʒ ß</note> of the finest gold, and keep the solution warm. 

Next, in 1 pound <note>℔ j</note> of common *aqua fortis*, dissolve 6 ounces <note>℥ vj</note> of well-purified crude mercury. Then mix both solutions—the gold and the mercury—together, and immediately everything will appear completely black. Distill this in a sand bath with an alembic over a slow fire, gradually increasing the heat until the substances at the bottom turn red and it appears the "spirits" <note>acidic vapors</note> have evaporated. 

Finally, increase the heat until the cucurbit <term>cucurbit: the gourd-shaped base of a still</term> glows red-hot for some time. Remove it and, in a small dish under a hood, calcine <term>calcine: to heat a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder</term> the powder, stirring it occasionally with an iron rod until the spirits have been thoroughly separated from the *aqua fortis*. Lastly, wash away all saltiness with fresh water, and after corrected spirit of wine <term>spirit of wine: high-proof distilled alcohol</term> has been repeatedly distilled over it through cohobation <term>cohobation: the process of pouring a distilled liquid back onto its residue and re-distilling it to increase potency</term>, store this powder of the "Gold of Life." Its use is excellent in the plague and many other diseases.

On a **porphyry stone** <term>Porphyry: A very hard igneous rock; here, a flat slab of it is used to allow a substance to 'deliquesce'—meaning it absorbs moisture from the air and turns into a liquid oil</term> in a cold, damp place, dissolve this stone into an oil. After discarding the dregs, coagulate it again, and repeat this coagulation a third time. This is the **highest elixir of life** <note>original: "summum elixir vitæ"</note> and a **mercurial laudanum** <note>original: "laudanum mercuriale"</note> that must be carefully kept in glass. Its dose is 1 grain <note>original: "gr. j."; a tiny amount, about 65 milligrams</note> mixed with an extract of **theriac** <term>Theriac: A famous historical polypharmaceutical "cure-all" paste</term> and a sufficient quantity of **licorice powder** <note>original: "puluere liquiritiæ"</note> to be formed into a pill. It should be drunk with a draught of wine for any disease, repeating the doses if necessity demands. **Note Well.** <note>original: "NB"</note> The white body of gold remaining at the bottom of the vial, which is usually called **fixed Moon** <term>Luna fixa: In alchemical terminology, "Moon" is silver; "fixed" silver or "white body of gold" refers to a metallic substance that has been chemically altered to resist heat or change color</term>, recovers its original color if it is melted by means of **antimony**. See Paracelsus' *Great Surgery* <note>original: "chirurgiam magnam"; refers to the *Die grosse Wundarzney* by Paracelsus, a foundational medical text</note>.

### MINERAL LAUDANUM
#### Of Dr. Hartmann <note>Johann Hartmann (1568–1631), the first professor of Chymiatry (chemical medicine) at the University of Marburg</note>.

From the **coralline secret** <note>original: "arcano corallino"; a red chemical preparation of mercury</note>, another and indeed quite excellent **alexipharmic** <term>Alexipharmic: A medicinal remedy intended to ward off poison, infection, or "contagious air"</term> can subsequently be made. Extract it with distilled vinegar over gentle heat until the vinegar turns a yellow color; afterwards, draw off the vinegar, and from the remaining extract, pull out the redness with **spirit of wine** <term>Spirit of wine: High-proof alcohol or ethanol</term>. Once that is removed, a red powder remains; preserve this. Two grains of it, administered in the evening in a suitable liquid even in desperate illnesses, loosen the bowels and finally induce sweat and sleep. I call it **Mineral Laudanum**.

...our [author] <note>The text begins mid-word, likely "investigator" or "author" (investigator/auctor noster)</note> reviews, but does not explain, which are worthy of being known and practiced; while he was writing these things, they were most secret. ## THE MANNER OF PRECIPITATING
### *Mercury by itself.* <note>original: "Mercurium per se"</note>

Let there be made in the glass-making shops flattened and wide vials, scarcely a **cubit** <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger (about 18 inches)</note> high inside and with a very narrow opening that barely admits a needle. Into the wide base, let raw mercury (thoroughly and completely purified) be poured so that it finally covers the bottom, and at least some part of the glass remains empty beneath the upper covering. Therefore, place it very precisely in sand at an equilibrium <note>meaning perfectly level</note>, so that the quantity of mercury is nowhere higher or lower due to an uneven position. Cook it first with a slow fire, and afterwards with a stronger fire, until of its own accord it turns into a very red powder like **cinnabar** <term>Cinnabar: Historically, the bright red mineral form of mercury sulfide; here, the author is describing the creation of red mercuric oxide through heat</term>. This should be carefully **sweetened** <term>Edulcoration: The process of washing a chemical precipitate with water or alcohol to remove any leftover acidic or salty impurities</term> with cordial waters or **spirit of wine** <note>distilled alcohol</note>. It is administered in doses of 4 to 6 grains. It strongly induces sweating, and if administered six or seven times, it completely eradicates and eliminates the **venereal plague** <note>original: "luem veneream"; syphilis</note>, provided that other things necessary for this cure are also at hand. Furthermore, it plainly removes all fevers, both continuous and intermittent.

-># SWEET MERCURY,<-
->## *The All-Humor-Driver of Quercetanus.*<- <note>original: "Panchymagogon Quercetani"</note>

**Sweet Mercury** is also called the **Tamed Dragon** <term>Draco mitigatus: A poetic alchemical name for mercury that has had its corrosive, "biting" qualities neutralized</term> by the author of the *Chemical Starter* <note>Jean Beguin (c. 1550–1620), whose "Tyrocinium Chymicum" was a standard chemistry textbook of the 17th century</note>, Beguinus, in book 2, chapter 18. It is made from mercury sublimate <term>Mercurius sublimatus: Corrosive sublimate or mercuric chloride, which is highly toxic and acidic</term> and raw mercury combined in specific weights and sublimed again. In this way, the corrosive spirits in the sublimate are removed through a "homogeneous artifice"—that is, they are "killed" or neutralized by the addition of more living mercury. The entire compound is then made **tasteless** <note>original Greek: "ἄποιον" (apoion); meaning without any sharp, biting, or medicinal quality</note>, or rather, it tends toward a certain sweetness. Regarding this substance, one should read **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French Paracelsian physician and diplomat</note> in his *Treatise on the Four Grave Affections of the Head*. The *Starter* adds **Colcothar** <term>Colcothar: Also known as "crocus martis," this is the red iron oxide residue left over from the distillation of vitriol</term> to its preparation in the cited passage, but this is not necessary. On their own, without the addition of any foreign substance, the two forms of mercury easily unite through the process of sublimation.

The method is as follows: Take 8 ounces <note>The symbol ℥ represents an apothecaries' ounce</note> of pure and genuine mercury sublimate (as I taught in the notes to the aforementioned chapter of the *Starter* published by **Gluckradius**) <note>Gluckradius was a pseudonym for Johann Hartmann, the editor of this text and the first professor of chemistry at Marburg</note>, and 6 ounces of well-purified mercury. Mix them together in a stone mortar, adding them bit by bit and grinding them until the living mercury is entirely consumed into the sublimate. Next, sublime the mixture in a vial filled only halfway, placed in a sand bath, until the entire mass has risen to the upper part of the vial; this usually occurs within 8 or 10 hours. After breaking the glass, carefully remove the raw mercury that comes out during this first distillation. Sublime the remainder again in the same manner, and repeat this a third or fourth time without adding any external substance. It will emerge as transparent as crystal, which suddenly [lays aside] <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "depo-" suggests "deponat," meaning to lay aside or drop</note> all its sharpness...

...deposited. Indeed, the vitriolic spirits <term>Spiritus vitriolati: Acidic residues derived from sulfuric acid (vitriol) used during the initial creation of corrosive sublimate</term> remaining and active in the mercury sublimate are rectified by a "homogeneous artifice," as the author calls it—that is, by the addition of raw, running mercury. It is not, as **Libavius** <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), a German physician and chemist who wrote the first systematic chemistry textbook</note> believes, that those spirits simply depart through the mutual action and passion of mixing and grinding, leaving the powder as if dead. Rather, they are completely "extinguished" <note>original: "emoriuntur"</note>, just as these or other sharp spirits are typically neutralized by others. Once the sublimations are finished, the denser mass is reduced to a fine powder, which should be washed several times with rose water. 

<margin>Dose.</margin> Its dose: 15 to 20 grains, or 30 for robust individuals, given with some purging extract, such as 4 or 5 grains of **extract of Alhandal troches** <term>Trochiscorum alhandal: Lozenges made from colocynth or "bitter apple," a potent and very bitter purgative</term>, formed into small pills. It purges all harmful humors without any great disturbance to the body.

<margin>Usage.</margin> It is administered for all types of ailments and is most conveniently given after midnight. Its operation is more evident if 16 grains of this substance are mixed with 2 grains of **flowers of butter of antimony** <term>Butyrum antimonij: Antimony trichloride, a potent chemical used here to boost the mercury's effects</term>, also known as **mercury of life** <term>Mercurius vitæ: Despite the name, this is an antimony compound (antimony oxichloride), not mercury</term>. These must first be thoroughly ground together for a long time with a pestle that is neither metal nor wood, as the substance would certainly stick to those materials. Afterward, form the doses into pills. (They should be ground for three hours; they work better the more they are ground, as extensive grinding increases their effectiveness without inducing excessive vomiting.) The dose could be repeated on the second day. If no sickness <note>original: "vitij"; literally "vice" or "fault" in the humors</note> is present, the medicine expels nothing. One should rest after taking it. Some people have used this medicine every single month.

**N.B.** <margin>Caution.</margin> It must not be administered in any vehicle such as a liquid, but only in the form of pills. ### ANOTHER SWEET MERCURY. <note>original: "MERCURIUS DULCIS ALIUS"</note>

Take raw Mercury, and **Regulus of Antimony** <term>Regulus antimonij: The pure metallic form of antimony, separated from its ore</term>, made with **mercury sublimate** <term>Mercurio sublimato: Corrosive sublimate or Mercury(II) chloride, a highly toxic compound</term> to draw out the **butter** <term>Butyrum: Antimony trichloride, a thick, oily substance resembling butter</term>, half a pound [℔ ß]. Afterward, place the mercury powder into a fresh vial and sublime in hot sand for a full hour or even longer: in this way it becomes exceptionally white. It perfectly cures a recent case of the **French Disease** <term>Morbus Gallicus: A common historical term for Syphilis</term>. Administer 6 to 15 grains [gr. vj to xv] every eight or ten days in the pulp of a roasted apple, while observing the rules of a suitable diet.

The dose is from 6 to 12 grains.

->ANTIMONIAL PILLS<-

## THE MOST CONVENIENT WAY OF PREPARING
### *the Flowers of Antimony.*

Take 9 ounces of **Antimony**. Put it into a glass vessel (called a cucurbit), and once the other instruments are attached and lying at an angle, apply heat. The antimony emerges as "flowers" <note>Fine, powdery sublimates that form when a mineral is heated until it vaporizes and then condenses.</note> which are partly red and partly purple, rising into the attached instrument—specifically the cap—without leaving behind any **dead head** <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>The worthless dregs or solid residue remaining after a substance has been distilled or sublimated.</note>, except for some crystals of the raw antimony itself that may have been lifted to the upper part of the retort. 

All these flowers are to be carefully collected after the operation is finished. The dose is 2 or 3 grains. These flowers are indeed emetic <note>They induce vomiting.</note> (the red ones are more violent), but if they are calcined <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to oxidize it or change its chemical state.</note> or circulated <term>circulation</term> <note>A process where a liquid is continuously distilled and then allowed to flow back into the same vessel to be refined further.</note> with the **spirit of wine** <note>High-proof alcohol.</note> and the spirit of honey, they lose all their violence and retain only the power to purge the bowels. This violence is clearly due to their "rawness," which becomes mild through the "taming" and "cooking" action of noble solvents <term>menstruums</term> <note>The alchemical term for a solvent used to extract the medicinal virtues of a substance.</note>.

At the end, increase the fire so that the spirit of honey also passes over and is joined with the spirit of wine. # THE ROYAL DISPENSARY <note>original: "BASILICA"; referring to Oswald Croll’s *Basilica Chymica*, a foundational text of 17th-century chemical medicine.</note>

<margin>Glass of antimony.</margin>
<margin>The time for smelting glass of antimony.</margin>
*a* It is called the **Electuary of antimony** <note>An electuary is a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup to make them palatable.</note> because the glass of antimony, when correctly prepared and refined several times, and then joined with other medicinal ingredients <note>original: "speciebus theriacalibus"; referring to ingredients used in "Theriac," a famous ancient cure-all.</note>, presents as a medicine in the form of an electuary, which has many uses. This **Glass of antimony** is so named because it turns into a transparent, glass-like form. It is more commendable for this recipe if it is made from the powder of raw antimony alone, calcined <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile impurities and reduce it to a powder.</note> for a long time over a gentle fire until it reaches an ash-gray color. According to the author’s intent, it should be melted by itself in the month of January or February. This method is superior to the common way using borax and raw antimony. It is, without a doubt, purer and more excellent for producing successful results due to the celestial influences of the **Sun** and **Moon** when they are in the watery signs of **Aquarius** and **Pisces**.

*b* For the **correction** <note>original: "correctionem"; in alchemy, this refers to tempering or refining a substance to remove its "venomous" or violent qualities—in this case, reducing its tendency to cause violent vomiting.</note> of the glass of antimony, our author uses strong distilled vinegar, which is not unsuitable. However, a better method—and one closer to achieving a certain "fixation" <note>The chemical process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</note>—is the correction of the same glass performed with the **oil or spirit of vitriol** <note>original: "spiritum vitrioli"; a historical name for sulfuric acid.</note>. In this way, the lighter and cruder parts of the substance, which cause such great and violent vomiting, are more strongly matured or "ripened." This makes the medicine more suitable, so that it moves the patient more easily and almost entirely through the bowels <note>acting as a purgative rather than an emetic.</note>. Therefore, it is better to proceed in the following manner:

### Another Highly Refined GLASS OF ANTIMONY

Take powder of antimony, well ground; mix it with an equal amount <note>original: "ana"; a medical shorthand meaning equal parts of each ingredient.</note> of common salt, and <term>sublime</term> <note>To heat a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, a process used to purify substances.</note> it in a luted crucible <note>A heat-resistant melting pot sealed with "lute," a protective paste of clay and sand.</note>. Grind it very well, and then let it melt in a double crucible over a gentle fire. Afterward, pour it drop by drop into a basin; it will then acquire the color of a ruby.

->CHYMICA<-

*Let everything be powdered, and reduced into a mass of the right consistency.*

☘ This description of the **Panchymagogon** <note>original: "Panchymagogi"; a universal purgative, from the Greek meaning "drawer of all humors"</note> is the invention of **Isaac Hollandus** <note>Johannes Isaac Hollandus, a famous 15th-century alchemist whose works were highly regarded in the early modern period</note>; it is found, of course, in his *Vegetable Work*, and is highly commendable. The *Tyrocinium* <note>referring to Jean Beguin’s *Tyrocinium Chymicum*, one of the most popular chemistry textbooks of the 17th century</note> recorded it among the extracts in book 2, chapter 9. It is called "Panchymagogon" because it draws out all humors.

<margin>Whether there exists an **Antimony** that purges only through the lower parts?</margin>
Regarding the wish added by the author for an **Antimony** <note>a metallic element used extensively in 17th-century medicine, though often controversial due to its toxicity</note> that possesses the power to purge only through the bowels, the judgments of dissenting opinions—which consist of experience and the testimony of so many most famous men—protest against it. Indeed, an antimony can be prepared that is endowed with the power of moving only through the bowels. For indeed, every **emetic** <note>vomit-inducing</note> property can be taken away from antimony, so that it moves neither upward nor downward but produces only **diaphoresis** <note>sweating</note>. This, however, is accomplished by art <note>meaning chemical skill or laboratory manipulation</note>. If art can therefore take away all purging power, it can also retain in the same substance only that power which leads through the bowels, while mitigating or completely removing the other. For both indeed belong to the same <unclear>operation</unclear>, whether through the bowels or through vomiting. Therefore, that which can abolish the whole can also abolish either one.

Thus, our author a little earlier corrected the **Flowers of Antimony** <note>original: "flores antimonij"; the white oxide of antimony produced by sublimation, known for being a very violent emetic</note> so that they would not move so violently upward. Similarly, in the notes on the Flowers of Antimony, we said that these same "flowers" are tamed—so that they do not move upward—by circulation through more noble **solvents** <note>original: "menstrua"; substances used to dissolve or extract chemicals</note> like **Spirit of Wine** <note>distilled alcohol</note> and **Honey**, and finally through simple digestion. Even Flowers of Antimony lose their power of vomiting through the mere grinding with common salt continued for some time.

<margin>Is there an antimony that purges only through the lower bowels?</margin>
Regarding the author’s expressed wish for a version of antimony <note>original: "antimonij"</note> powerful enough to purge only through the bowels <note>original: "per aluū"; the "lower" route, as opposed to the "upper" route of vomiting</note>, the judgments of conflicting opinions—as well as experience and the testimony of so many famous men—cry out in response. Indeed, antimony can be prepared so that it possesses only the power of moving the bowels. All emetic <note>vomit-inducing</note> power can be stripped from antimony, so that it moves neither upward nor downward, but produces only diaphoresis <term>diaphoresis: the process of inducing heavy sweating to expel toxins through the skin</term>. This is achieved through the chemist's art. If, therefore, art can take away all purging power, it can also retain in that same substance only the power which leads through the bowels, while mitigating or entirely removing the other. Either operation—purging through the bowels or through vomiting—can be isolated. Since art can abolish the whole effect, it can also abolish either one of the two. Thus, our author a little earlier corrected the "flowers of antimony" <term>flowers of antimony: the white vapor or "oxide" produced when antimony is heated; it was notoriously violent in its effects</term> so that they would not move so vehemently "upward" <note>original: "sursum"; i.e., causing vomiting</note>. Similarly, we have said in the notes to the flowers of antimony that these same flowers can be "tamed" <note>original: "cicurari"; literally to domesticate or make mild</note> by circulation through more noble solvents <note>original: "menstrua"</note> like spirit of wine <note>distilled alcohol</note> and honey, and finally by simple digestion <note>prolonged, gentle heating</note>, so they do not cause vomiting. Even the flowers of antimony lose their power to cause vomiting simply by being ground for a long time with common salt.

<meta>This page continues the pharmaceutical discussion from the previous page, moving from specific recipes for antimonial purgatives to a broader chemical debate regarding the nature of solvents. Specifically, it addresses whether alcohol (spirit of wine) is the correct medium for extracting purgative properties from plants and minerals, referencing the work of Jean Beguin.</meta>

<page-num>97</page-num>
<header>CHYMICA.</header>

<sig>G</sig>

After many others, the author of the *Tyrocinium Chymicum* <note>Jean Beguin (c. 1550–1620) was a Flemish chemist whose "Chemical Beginner's Guide" was one of the most popular laboratory manuals of the 17th century</note> discusses the nature of extracts in Book 2, Chapter 9. He believes, however, that in some cases the purgative power of a substance is weakened <note>original: "infringatur"</note> through digestion with **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine: an early name for ethanol or high-proof alcohol</term>. But he seems to commit a logical error <note>original: "elenchum"; specifically a fallacy of misinterpreting an argument</note>: for the spirit does not weaken the power, it simply fails to draw it out.

The capacity of purgatives resides in a **volatile mercurial salt**; therefore, it requires a similar medium <term>menstruum: a solvent used to dissolve or extract a substance</term>, based on the principle that "like attracts like" <note>original: "symbolum est idem cum eodem"; a core alchemical belief that substances of a similar spiritual or chemical nature will interact</note>. **Spirit of wine**, however, is sulfurous in nature and retains the qualities of sulfur. Thus, it attracts from substances that which is of its own nature—namely, sulfur—and leaves the mercurial salts untouched. Consequently, it is better suited for extracting those things whose essence consists of sulfur, such as **diaphoretics** <term>diaphoretica: medicines used to induce sweating</term>, but it is not so for purgatives.

Nor can our opinion be undermined by the views of those who try to persuade us of the contrary: namely, that no purgative power remains in the materials once spirit of wine has been poured over them. For they claim that the cathartic <term>catharticam: a strong laxative or purgative</term> power is indeed extracted by the spirit of wine, but that it cannot be easily separated from it; rather, they say that when the spirit is distilled away, it carries the power off with it.

Truly, experience dictates a different story. For firstly, how can spirit of wine attract to itself something that is not of its own nature, as was just stated? Secondly, if it were to extract the purgative power entirely, why is it that when such an extract (tainted by this solvent) is afterwards thoroughly dried and a different, suitable liquid is poured on, it brings the hidden cathartic power back into the light most effectively? And finally, the claim that the cathartic power cannot be easily separated from the spirit of wine is likewise clearly contradicted by experience. For who will deny that spirit of wine, used as a solvent in an extract of **colocynth** <term>colocynth: the "bitter apple," a desert vine known for its incredibly potent and harsh purgative properties</term>—

# BASILICA

[...used for scammo]ny, it cannot easily be separated from the purging tincture? For this reason, the purging power is not fixed in the **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine: an early name for high-proof alcohol or ethanol</term>. Indeed, the dregs <note>original: "magmata"; the solid residue left after a substance has been steeped or pressed</note> of the purgatives, which are left behind by the **spirit of wine** after the work of extraction is finished, will later yield their purging power if they are stirred by other **solvents** <term>menstrua: solvents used in alchemy to dissolve solids or extract essences</term>. This power, which would have been nothing if the alcohol had taken it, is finally released.

Therefore, for the correct preparation of extracts from purgatives—excepting **bitter apple** <term>colocynth</term>, **scammony**, and **wild cucumber juice** <term>elaterium</term>, whose harshness is corrected by the **spirit of wine**—other **solvents** are more suitable. These include **vinous mead** <term>hydromel vinosum: a fermented mixture of honey and water</term>, **Canary wine**, **milk whey**, and the waters of **fragrant apples**, **betony**, **fennel**, **anise**, **roses**, **meadowsweet** <term>ulmaria</term>, **blessed thistle**, **fumitory**, and similar plants. This is especially true when a few drops of **oil of tartar** <term>oil of tartar: a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, which acts as a strong alkaline base</term> (prepared by "deliquium" <note>a process where a salt is left in a cellar to naturally absorb moisture from the air until it turns into a liquid</note>) have always been mixed in first. In this way, those solvents more quickly attack the **mercurial salt** <note>the alchemical principle thought to carry the active medicinal "virtue" of a plant</note> and draw it to themselves.

From all of this, it is clear enough why the purging power is often weakened in extracts, such that in practice we often add certain purgatives in their raw substance. For this reason, it must be well noted and observed which **solvents** ought to be applied to this or that purgative.

Chemists have observed that the same reasoning and method is necessary for the proper and skillful preparation and correction of **Euphorbium** <note>A very caustic resin from the *Euphorbia* plant, used as a drastic purgative.</note>, which certainly should by no means be admitted into pills and other remedies being prepared from it, unless it undergoes this genuine [refinement].

<meta>This page continues the pharmaceutical instructions from page 117, specifically detailing a more efficient method for preparing a purgative medicine. # B A S I L I C A

A method discovered by me and frequently refined: Let the **spirit of Tartar** <term>spiritus Tartari</term> <note>a liquid produced by the high-heat distillation of the crusty deposits found in wine barrels</note> be distilled just as the author instructs below in the section on **Diaphoretics** <term>Diaphoreticis</term> <note>medicines used to induce sweating to expel toxins</note>, but without the addition of **spirit of wine** <term>spiritus vini</term> <note>distilled alcohol or ethanol</note>.

To one pound of this, add two pounds of spirit of wine and two ounces of rectified **spirit of vitriol** <term>spiritus vitrioli</term> <note>sulfuric acid</note>. Pour this mixture together over the **colcothar** <term>colcathar</term> <note>the red iron oxide residue left after distilling vitriol</note> of vitriol and the **dead head** <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>the chemical dregs or waste remaining after a distillation</note> of Tartar—specifically the residue from which the spirit was originally drawn and which was afterwards **calcined** <note>burned or roasted at high heat</note> to blackness. Pour these into a suitable, well-closed vessel and **digest** <note>apply gentle, steady heat to encourage chemical reaction</note> them in a **Mary's Bath** <term>Balneo Mariæ</term> <note>a water bath or bain-marie, providing gentle heat at the boiling point of water</note> for several days.

Finally, distill the mixture through a **retort** <term>retortam</term> <note>a glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note> over an open flame; but at the beginning, the heat should be very mild and slow, so that the spirits—which are very delicate—do not evaporate and vanish. At the end, increase the heat; this distillation is completed in barely three days.

From the "dead head" residue that remains after this distillation (which must first be thoroughly and strongly burned in a potter's kiln), extract the **salt** <term>sal</term> in the usual way. **Digest** this salt with the previously distilled spirit for fifteen days in a Mary's Bath. Finally, mix both into a paste with dry clay, or even with calcined pumice stone, and distill it from an earthen retort over an open fire.

In this way, the salt itself will come forth along with the spirit, having been made entirely "spirituous" <note>transformed from a solid salt into a volatile, vaporous state</note>, and it will be mixed into the resulting liquid. According to the author, you should **cohobate** <term>cohoba</term> <note>a process where the distilled liquid is poured back over the solid remains and distilled again to concentrate its "virtues"</note> this liquor repeatedly—that is, distill it several times—or at least leave it to digest in the water bath until the salts, having been driven back to the bottom, begin to appear of their own accord. These are finally ready to be used for the desired **purgation** <note>a cleansing of the body's internal systems</note>.

By this method, you will save more than half the time usually required for that more lengthy preparation. Nor does the author’s original method surpass this one in quality, since a more concise way of preparing a medicine is superior to a long and complicated series of operations. The **dosage** <term>Dosis</term> and **use** <term>vsus</term> are found in the author’s main text.

CHYMICA.

H 4

# A MASTERFUL METHOD OF SECRETS
## *and Plant-based Substances.*

From those medicinal plants <term>vegetabilibus</term> <note>original: "vegetabilibus," referring to any botanical matter used in pharmacy</note> necessary for a specific purgative, just as from all others, subtle **secrets** <term>arcana</term> <note>in alchemy, an "arcanum" is the inner, hidden essence or power of a substance, extracted and purified to its most potent state</note> can be extracted in a certain way. This method is not yet known to many, but it is nonetheless entirely *Philosophical* <note>here, "philosophical" implies a process based on the true principles of alchemy rather than crude herbalism</note>. By this means, all the virtues—the healing powers which otherwise flourish in the raw plants—are preserved intact. Furthermore, they are reduced to a liquid <term>liquorem</term> that is pleasing to the palate and the stomach, of which a very small part is as powerful as any large quantity of the whole plant. I faithfully commend this method to all my students, so that they may hold it as sacred as it was sincerely handed down to them.

From any herbs and roots, but specifically from those which our author instructs—whether they are all fresh and green or some are dried, since not all can be obtained at one and the same time—once they have been somewhat fermented and **digested** <note>kept in a steady, gentle heat to break down the material</note>, create a **spirit** and a **phlegm** <term>phlegma</term> <note>the watery, less potent part of a distillate that is separated from the "spirit" or active essence</note>. Keep the spirit partly separate, and keep the phlegm separate as well.

From the **dead head** <term>capite mortuo</term> <note>the "caput mortuum" is the chemical residue or dregs remaining in the vessel after distillation</note> which has been **calcined** <note>roasted or burned to ash</note> in the common manner, extract the salts using the phlegm so that they become **alkaline lyes** <term>lixiuia</term> <note>liquid solutions made by leaching water through the plant's ashes to retrieve its mineral salts</note>. Once these have been evaporated into a substance with the consistency of an oil, join them with their spirit that was previously reserved. Mix this with three or four times as much clay or calcined pumice-stone, and distill the mixture from a **retort** <term>retorta</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long, curved neck used for distilling liquids</note> with a fire that gradually increases in strength. 

This should be distilled into a very large receiving vessel, in the bottom of which you have already placed a moderate quantity of the plants combined (if using many) or just a single plant (if the distillation is from one species alone). The material in the receiver should not be completely dry, but somewhat soft or "flaccid," since the elementary or external moisture will have already been somewhat consumed by that point.

## COMPOUND SPIRIT OF SALT.

There is also another spirit of salt, more elegant and pure, and possessed of great virtues; however, it is a compound made from **saltpeter** <term>nitrum</term> <note>Potassium nitrate</note> and common salt. Its concise preparation is as follows:

♃ <note>Recipe symbol</note> Take equal parts of the purest saltpeter and **decrepitated common salt** <note>Salt that has been heated until it stops crackling/popping to remove moisture</note>; mix them with a triple quantity (others say quadruple) of dry clay, and from this, draw out the spirit over an open fire in the usual manner. To 1 pound of this spirit, add 4 ounces of **fused common salt** <note>Salt that has been melted into a solid mass</note>; let it digest for some time so that the added salt can be dissolved by the spirit, and immediately distill it through a **retort** <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note>. By this method, you will increase the spirit and make it stronger. You may increase it further at your pleasure by following this exact method with new fused salt, taken in the same quantity, as often and as long as you like. From that spirit, draw off the **phlegm** <term>phlegma</term> <note>The watery, weak part of the distillate</note> using a **water bath** <term>Balneum Mariae</term> <note>original: "Balneum Mariae," a gentle heating method using hot water, similar to a double boiler</note>, and then **rectify** <note>Purify by redistilling</note> the spirit from a retort. Finally, combine it with an equal part of **spirit of wine** <term>alcohol vini</term> <note>Concentrated ethanol</note>. Afterward, unite them by **circulating** <note>Repeated distillation in a closed vessel where the vapor returns to the liquid</note> and **cohobating** <term>cohobando</term> <note>Pouring the distilled liquid back over the solid remains to redistill it, concentrating the essence</note> these spirits—namely the spirit of wine and the spirit of salts—until they are inseparably joined. This spirit resists thirst so effectively that those suffering from **dropsy** <term>hydropici</term> <note>Edema or swelling caused by excess fluid; the spirit was thought to manage the patient's desperate thirst</note> do not seek water for three days.

A sweet oil can also be drawn from sea salt in this manner: Let it be dissolved in distilled rainwater, filtered, and **calcined** <note>Heated to a high temperature to reduce it to powder</note> over a moderate fire, stirring constantly so that it does not melt; let this be done 15 times or more. Afterward, let the same salt be extracted with the best spirit of wine; when the spirit is removed, the salt will turn into a stone-like substance. From these crystals, with ar- <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page</note>

It is given with 2 ounces of warm spring water, using a mixture of **spirit of wine** <note>distilled alcohol</note> and **nitre**; it induces sweating and immediately settles colic pains. See the *Practice of Chymiatry* <note>original: "Praxin chymiatricam," a reference to the author's other works on chemical medicine</note> of our edition, page 111, regarding the "colic passion."

*d* This spirit is also given as a cooling agent in fevers, delivered in suitable "vehicles" <note>liquid carriers for medicine</note> such as water of **endive**, **chicory**, or **dandelion**. To quench thirst, it is given in doses of 6 to 11 drops. It is more conveniently administered than the **Stone of Prunella** <note>original: "lapide Prunellæ"; a preparation of saltpeter fused with a small amount of sulfur, often used for throat infections</note> itself, because that stone sometimes triggers nausea.

<margin>Decoction of elecampane.</margin>
*e* Not only at the end but also at the beginning of colic, a decoction of **Elecampane** is wonderfully effective.
Take: Roots of **Elecampane** <term>Enula</term> cut into small slices, 1 ounce.
Powdered **Fennel seed**, half an ounce.
**Lemon balm water**, 2 or 3 pounds.
Cook in a **double boiler** <term>diplomate</term> <note>literally "in a diploma," referring to a water bath or bain-marie to prevent burning</note> for one and a half hours, then strain through a **Hippocratic sleeve** <term>manicam Hippocratis</term> <note>a conical fabric filter bag used by apothecaries</note>. Take the first draft of the strained liquid in the evening when going to bed, the second on an empty stomach, the third also in the evening; continue in this way if necessary, and the cure will be complete.

<header>THE ROYAL PHARMACY</header>

# V.

## THE DIAPHORETIC.
<note>A diaphoretic is a substance used to induce sweating, often used in early modern medicine to "expel" toxins from the body.</note>

<margin>Many diseases, such as Plagues and Pleurisies, seek to be cured at least through sweating and the opening of the pores <note>original: "emunctoria"; the organs or channels that eliminate waste from the body</note>.</margin>
Sweating in the Plague and the Hungarian Disease <gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: "Morbo Vngarico"; a term historically used for typhus, which was prevalent among troops in Hungary</note> is a universal evacuation of the poison of the entire body—not only in the blood but also in the very constitution <gloss>b</gloss> <note>original: "habitu"; referring to the general state or "habit" of the physical body</note> of the body, and thus sticking in all its parts. By the benefit of this sweating, the poison—which the surrounding cold had driven toward the heart—is shut out. For just as we draw in a poisonous aura <gloss>c</gloss> through the inhalation of the spirit, so too must that very thing be exterminated from all the limbs by sweat. No part of the body, however small, is without air; therefore, all parts are capable of sweating. Thus, sweating is a universal evacuation, seeing as nearly a third of all diseases that infest the human body can be cured through sweat.

### DIAPHORETIC ANTIMONY. <gloss>d</gloss>

Take 1 pound <gloss>e</gloss> <term>℔</term> of **mercury sublimated** <note>mercury(II) chloride</note> by **vitriol** <note>sulfates</note> and **salt**, then add 2 pounds <term>℔</term> of **Hungarian Antimony** <note>stibnite, or antimony trisulfide</note>. Let them be ground together and mixed, and let them all be placed in a glass retort <gloss>f</gloss> protected with a coating of clay <note>original: "luto"; used to protect glass from high heat</note>. With a closed receiver joined to it, let the distillation be done in a sand bath with the **control of the fire** <term>Ignis regimine</term> <note>the precise management of heat levels during a chemical reaction</note>, so that the drops in the neck do not—like

The remainder will stick to the bottom and also to the walls, yellowish in color, like **Earth**.*

->### CHYMICA.<-

...[dia]phoretic <note>original: "diaphoreticũ"; a medicine that induces sweating to expel toxins</note>, or that he described it in his own or others' words—as Libavius dares to frivolously assert at the end of the 18th chapter of the first part of his *Hermetic Apocalypse*—is a lie, which Libavius rightly should have refrained from. Rubeus <note>Girolamo Rossi, an Italian physician and author of "De destillatione" (1582)</note>, in his little book on distillations (besides which nothing else has been published by him), deals in the whole of Chapter 22, Section 2, with stibium or antimony and its various preparations. At the end, he mentions a medicine made from **mercury sublimate**, the **regulus of antimony** <term>regulus</term> <note>the metallic form of antimony produced by smelting</note>, and gold, dissolved separately in the **water of separations** <note>original: "aqua separationum"; usually nitric acid or Aqua Fortis, used to separate gold from silver</note>, mixed together, and distilled by **cohobations** <note>the process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto its residue and re-distilling it to increase potency</note>, and burned into a red powder. 

But how far is that removed from **diaphoretic antimony**? In our process, even if antimony is taken for the making of the **butter** <note>butter of antimony, or antimony trichloride</note>, little or nothing of its physical substance actually remains in the final product; whereas in Rubeus's process, the regulus is produced and is entirely **fixed** <note>rendered non-volatile or stable through chemical action</note>. Secondly, the mercury sublimate hardly remains red with that red powder of his, but in each distillation of *aqua fortis* <note>nitric acid</note> it eventually rises [evaporates]. Although some might remain, it all vanishes into smoke during **calcination** <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to oxidize it or remove volatile parts</note>. In our work, however, this mercury sublimate—which is the butter of antimony—is truly fixed. 

Thirdly, that red powder of Rubeus is **corrosive**; the **Mineral Bezoar**, however, is not so at all. Finally, Rubeus's powder is the same as the **Gold of Life** <note>original: "auro vitæ"; also known as *mercurius vitae*, a potent and often toxic emetic</note>; therefore, it is numbered among the mercury precipitates and is at the same time a **cathartic** <term>cathartic</term> <note>a medicine that causes purging of the bowels</note>. Our Bezoar, namely Croll’s and my own, is no such thing. 

Let Libavius therefore cease to draw his lying pen against others, unless he wishes to be spoken of very poorly in return. The man’s character and his pestilential envy are well known, and it is not the part of a wise man to either fear or praise them.

## THE TRUE PREPARATION OF THE SOLAR BEZOAR
### *preparation.*

m Experience and the following reasoning prove that this addition of gold is in no way necessary or useful. Gold, of course, returns to its original body; therefore, it can in no way act upon the powder of antimony nor make it more potent. But if gold were clearly reduced from its bodily form into a spiritual substance, its addition would certainly be very useful. If the gold is mixed into the Bezoar itself in the smallest particles <note>original: "per minima"; referring to the theory of minima naturalia, the smallest possible units of a substance</note>, it exerts its powers. $p$ The procedure <note>original Greek: Εγχειρημα (Encheirēma)</note> is as follows: Take twice as much common sulfur <term>sulfur</term> <note>a foundational substance in alchemy, here used as a purifying agent</note> compared to one part of this fixed earth—that is, the Mineral Bezoar <term>Bezoardicum minerale</term> <note>a medicinal compound of antimony, named for its supposed ability to resist poisons like a natural bezoar stone</note>. $q$ It acts neither through the upper nor the lower channels <note>meaning it does not induce vomiting or purging</note>.
$r$ In certain cases, but rarely.
$s$ Also effective without gold.
$t$ By itself, it is not particularly effective, but after the necessary preparations have been made, it is administered with other sweat-inducing medicines <term>sudoriferis</term> <note>substances that promote sweating to expel toxins</note>, primarily with peach-leaf water <term>aqua persicariae</term>.

$vv$ In water of fern or wall germander.
$x$ In water of dwarf elder.
$y$ In a decoction of common centaury or fever-fleeing water <term>aqua febrifuga</term>.

$aa$ In water of restharrow, saxifrage, strawberry, or parsley.

## DIAPHORETIC ANTIMONY,
### or *Fixed Antimony*.

There is another type of Diaphoretic Antimony <term>ANTIMONIVM DIAPHORETICVM</term> <note>a medicinal preparation intended to induce sweating (diaphoresis) to expel "ill humors"</note> which is made through glass <term>vitrum</term> <note>referring here to the "glass of antimony," a vitrified form of the mineral</note> with its own single calcination <term>calcinatione</term> <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to oxidize it or reduce it to powder</note>. From this, through this calcination repeated three times—which chemists otherwise call detonation <term>detonationem</term> <note>a rapid chemical reaction, often with a flash or sound, caused by adding nitre (saltpeter) to the heated mineral</note>—all the sulfurous and mercurial parts perish, and only the earthy part remains, which possesses the power of drying and promoting sweat. Beguinus <note>Jean Béguin (c. 1550–1620), a famous French chemist and author of one of the first chemistry textbooks</note> describes this in his *Chemical Primer* <note>original: "Tyrocinio chymico"</note>, Book 2, Chapter 12, under the title of "diaphoretic antimony," and indeed he does so correctly. 

But experience itself has taught that in the preparation of this medicine, the liquefaction <note>the process of melting</note> which Beguinus suggests there should not be "metallic," but only as much as is needed for the mixture to flow like salt when cast in. Furthermore, after each of the three calcinations with nitre <term>nitro</term> <note>potassium nitrate or saltpeter, used as an oxidizing agent</note>, it must always be washed with warm, fresh water, and the powder dried, which finally becomes white. With this operation, the *Primer* and others are satisfied. But far finer powders are produced if, after the final calcination and a slight liquefaction, all that remains is ground and boiled <meta>catchword: in water</meta>

### *SCHEUNEMANN’S BEZOARDIC.*

Another mineral Bezoardic or *Nepenthes* <note>a legendary medicine for chasing away sorrow; here used as a name for a potent remedy</note> is described by Scheunemann <note>Henning Scheunemann (c. 1570–1615), a Paracelsian physician and chemist</note> in his booklet on the fountain of Saint Anne, which he calls *Hydromantia*, page 59. To the "weaker Dragon" <term>Draconi</term> <note>alchemical code for antimony</note>, he adds "Mars" <term>martem</term> <note>iron</note> to be devoured before the "battle" <note>the chemical reaction</note>; when it has been devoured, he brings it forth to the battle—that is, to be distilled—and immediately they give off great boilings, that is, they grow violently hot. Thus the "butter" distills from it, with "appearing serenity," that is, after everything has come forth, he washes the Mars left behind after distillation: and "resuscitates it by solar heat," that is, he dissolves it in spirit of nitre, which he afterward dissolves and distills with the "Dragon"—that is, with the butter and dissolved spirit of nitre—and thus fixes it in the otherwise usual manner. See the author himself for more details.
