You will then have a greenish Lunar Bezoardic <term>Bezoardicum viridiusculum</term>, most useful for afflictions of the head, especially for Erysipelas <note>a bacterial skin infection characterized by redness and swelling</note> of the head in women, which is very common; see the *Practice of Chymiatry* <note>original: "praxin chymiatricam"</note> page 13.

2. Or, from Silver <term>Luna</term> calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> with common sulfur, extract a blue color—which others call ultramarine or azure <term>Lazurinum</term>—using spirit of urine <term>spiritu urinæ</term> <note>a solution of ammonia derived from fermented urine</note>, about which I spoke in the Microcosmic preparations <note>preparations derived from the human body</note> under the title of "urine" regarding the extraction of vitriol from metals. Dissolve this blue extract in *aqua fortis* <note>nitric acid</note> and join it with a tenfold amount of butter of antimony liquefied in *aqua fortis*. By following the rest of the prescribed labors, you will have a Lunar Bezoardic of the same, or even greater, virtue.

3. Or, dissolve fine Silver <term>Luna</term> in *aqua fortis*; precipitate it with oil of salt of Tartar <term>oleo salis Tartari</term> <note>a concentrated potassium carbonate solution</note> by deliquescence or by a solution made in common water in a large vessel. It will be precipitated to the bottom like cotton <term>gossipij</term>. Afterward, let it be sweetened <note>rinsed with water to remove salts</note> and extracted with distilled vinegar; it then acquires a blue color, though if it stands longer, it turns green. Proceed with this Tincture <term>Tincturâ</term> as with the others.

4. But the most excellent of all Lunar Bezoardics will be that where the silver <term>luna</term> is reduced into vitriol <term>vitriolum</term> <note>a crystalline metal salt</note> with spirit of nitre, and fixed into a powder with butter of antimony according to the rules of the art. By this reasoning, the "body" of the silver is rendered somewhat thinner by the spirits of nitre and is more easily mixed into minute parts with the butter of antimony, thereby becoming more effective for producing a medicinal result.

### SATURNINE BEZOARDIC

In exactly the same way, extract a tincture from **Glass of Lead** <term>vitro Saturni</term>—which is made from **minium** <note>red lead oxide</note> and flints fused together—by using rectified **butter of antimony** <note>antimony trichloride</note> several times. Fix it in the aforementioned manner with **spirit of nitre** <term>spiritu nitri</term> <note>nitric acid</note>. This is an effective remedy for all afflictions of the spleen.

### JOVIAL BEZOARDIC

Take 6 ounces of **Regulus of Antimony** <term>Reguli antimonij</term> <note>the pure metallic form of antimony</note> made without iron <term>sine marte</term>. Add to this, while melted in a crucible, 4 ounces of the purest **English Tin** <term>Iouis Anglici</term> <note>tin was associated with the planet Jupiter</note>, likewise melted, so that an amalgam is formed. Afterward, reduce it to a very fine powder on a marble slab. To this, add an equal part—that is, 10 ounces—of the best **sublimated Mercury**, and from a retort <note>a glass vessel with a long neck used for distillation</note> proceed as above. Fix the resulting butter with three distillations using spirit of nitre; afterward, calcinate <note>heat to a high temperature to drive off volatile substances</note> it. While it is glowing hot, extinguish it in **spirit of wine** <term>spiritu vini</term> <note>highly distilled alcohol</note>, dry it, and preserve it. It becomes a gray powder. The dose is from 1 to 2 grains. It most powerfully induces sweating and is a "medicine of many uses" <term>polychrestum</term> for all things, but especially for obstructions of the liver.

### MARTIAL BEZOARDIC

From **Saffron of Mars** <term>Croco Martis</term> <note>a red iron oxide</note> made by the benefit of fire alone, according to the instructions in the *Tyrocinium* <note>Jean Béguin’s *Tyrocinium Chymicum*, a famous 17th-century chemistry textbook</note> Book 2, Chapter 15, extract a deep red Tincture through digestion with rectified butter of antimony. Fix the butter, now impregnated with the tincture of antimony, with a medium of spirit of nitre in the usual way. It is a specific and most ready remedy for all flows of the belly <note>diarrhea or dysentery</note>, especially those taking their origin from the liver. Its color resembles the color of the liver itself, or **liver-colored** <term>Leberfarb</term> <note>original German: "Leberfarb"</note>. See Scheunemann in his *Paracelsian Hydromancy*, page 59, where he discusses the Martial Bezoardic.

### JOVIAL BEZOARDIC

## VENEREAL BEZOARDIC
### <note>original: BEZOARDICVM VENEREVM</note>

In exactly the same way, a **tincture** <note>an extract of the medicinal essence of a substance</note> is drawn out from **copper flakes** <term>squama æris</term> <note>Venus is the alchemical name for copper; "scales" or flakes were produced by hammering heated copper</note> using **rectified butter of antimony** <term>butyro antimonij</term> <note>antimony trichloride</note> through the process of **digestion** <note>gentle heating over a period of time</note>. It is then fixed with **spirit of nitre** <term>spiritu nitri</term> <note>nitric acid</note>, which must be poured off and added several times. Aside from its other virtues, it possesses a most certain **alexiteric** <note>protective against poison or infection</note> power in any case of **gonorrhea**.

## MERCURIAL BEZOARDIC
### <note>original: BEZOARDICVM MERCVRIALE</note>

From **glass of Mercury of Life** <term>vitro Mercurij vitæ</term> <note>"Mercury of Life" (Mercurius Vitae) was a common name for antimony oxychloride, a potent emetic; here it is processed into a "glass" or solid form</note>, the description of which has already been given, a **red tincture** is drawn out with rectified butter of antimony. When this same substance is fixed by the spirit of nitre, it passes into a **Bezoardic** that is excellent in its virtue and not inferior to those previously mentioned. (Note: If you were to join the **mercury of life** with **butter of antimony** and afterward fix it with **spirit of nitre**, what, I ask you, would be produced? Would it not be an excellent, corrected **purgative**, to be administered in a larger dose? Think on this diligently.)

In these ways, therefore, **Bezoardics** or **Diaphoretics** <term>diaphoretica</term> <note>medicines that induce sweating to expel toxins</note> can be made from all metals. In these, the virtuous parts of the metals themselves are joined with butter of antimony and fixed together by the noble **menstruum** <note>solvent</note> of **salt of nitre**, whereby they turn into noble medicines. Indeed, many other things can be fashioned and prepared from these same materials according to these same formulas—things which perhaps the previous age never even thought of. Let **Libavius** <note>Andreas Libavius (1550–1616), a famous chemist and critic of the more mystical alchemical practices; the author here is challenging Libavius's claim that there is "nothing new" in this chemistry</note> go now and stubbornly repeat that nothing new has been brought forward.

### COMPOUND APERITIVE SPIRIT OF TARTAR
### *opening the passages.*

From one pound (lb 1) of the simple spirit drawn from cream of Tartar <term>cremor Tartari</term>, as previously described, they add four ounces (oz 4) of spirit of wine <term>alcohol</term>. To this mixture, they add two pounds (lb 2) of vitriol <term>vitrioli</term> <note>likely iron or copper sulfate</note> that has been dried over a moderate fire until it turns red. They sprinkle and moisten the mixture gradually, allowing it to soak in, then digest it in a Water Bath <term>Balneo</term> for eight days. Soon after, they drive the substance through a retort <term>retortam</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long neck used for distilling</note> using all degrees of heat. Everything that comes forth is then poured over the black "dead head" <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>the solid remains or dregs left after distillation</note> of the Tartar from which the simple spirit was originally made. They let this digest for 24 hours, then separate the water—now imbued with the Tincture of Tartar—by decanting it <note>tilting the vessel to pour off the liquid while leaving the sediment</note>. They burn the remaining dregs of the Tartar <term>calcinat</term> until they reach a white ash. From these ashes, they extract the salt using the previously tinted water, leaving it in a warm place for 24 hours. Finally, they purify this water through a filter. They administer this with great success for stubborn obstructions of the internal organs, for foul complexions <note>likely referring to jaundice or skin discoloration</note>, long-lasting fevers, and dropsy <term>aquam intercutem</term>, in doses of 1 to 2 scruples <term>scrupulus</term> <note>a small unit of weight; 1 scruple is about 1.3 grams</note> in appropriate medicinal waters.

*l* In gentle distillation, salts retain a stench which comes from the combustible oil; once this oil is removed from both, they are rendered purer.

*m* This is also true in cases where the substance has been made into an essence <note>original: "essentificatus est"</note> with its own salt, but it is beneficial to take it either with wine or with cloves <term>caryophyllis</term>.

*n* Its administration <note>original: "operatio"</note> must be exact; otherwise, any substances mixed with it will make it weaker.

### PANACEA OF THE SULFUR
#### *Of Antimony.*

The true sulfur of antimony is like a panacea <note>a universal cure-all</note> when it is joined and fixed with the "Regulus" <term>regulus</term> <note>the metallic heart of the mineral</note> of antimony, melted and prepared in the transparent gold method already described. # CHEMICAL MATTERS. 169

**Salt of pearls** <term>Sal perlarum</term> <note>original: Sal perlarum</note> is so named because it closely approaches the form of a salt. This does not refer, of course, to the "third hypostatical principle" <note>In the Paracelsian system of chemistry, the "Three Principles" (Tria Prima) are Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury. "Salt" represents the principle of fixity and body.</note>, which can eventually be extracted even from this salt of pearls once the **Sulphur** <term>sulphur</term> and **Mercury** <term>Mercurius</term> have been removed. Rather, the name simply refers to the pearls being reduced into a liquid by the benefit of a **solvent** <term>menstruum</term> <note>original: menstruum. In early chemistry, a "menstruum" is a solvent capable of dissolving a solid body.</note>, and finally, after the solvent is removed, being reduced back into a certain form resembling salt.

The author praises **distilled wine vinegar** <term>acetum destillatum vini</term> as a solvent for pearls, which is certainly appropriate; however, other juices should not be looked down upon. Some facilitate the dissolution of pearls using pressed **lemon juice** and **birch sap** <term>Betulae liquorem</term> as follows:

℟ <note>The symbol for "Recipe," meaning "Take."</note> 2 pounds of pressed and purified lemon juice.
With 8 pounds of birch sap collected in the month of April, cook gently in an **unglazed pot** <note>original: olla devitreatam. This refers to a ceramic vessel without a glass-like glaze, or perhaps one treated to remove the glaze, to avoid chemical reactions with the lead often found in early glazes.</note> until reduced to 7 pounds. Then, by adding 1 pound of lemon juice, first distill it, and afterwards distill it from a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbita</term> <note>A gourd-shaped chemical flask used in distillation.</note> two or three times. Keep this solvent in a well-sealed glass vessel. Then, cast whole pearls—which have been washed in wine and dried—into it. They will dissolve into a liquid resembling a very fresh wine or **must** <note>original: musti. Unfermented grape juice.</note>. This is afterwards administered in **lemon balm water** <term>aqua melissae</term> or another **cordial** <note>A medicinal drink intended to stimulate the heart and improve the patient's spirits or "vital heat."</note> in doses ranging from 1 ounce to a half-ounce.

The most common dissolution of pearls is done with vinegar, provided the process follows the author’s instructions. Some prepare the vinegar in this way: they distill 6 pounds of the best distilled vinegar from 1 pound of the ashes of **Jointed Glasswort** <term>Herba Kali geniculati</term> <note>original: Herba Kali geniculati. Likely *Salicornia*, a plant used to produce soda ash for soap and glassmaking.</note>. (These are the ashes used to make lye and soap, and are also used by glassmakers to purify glass). Furthermore, the **magisteries** <term>magisteria</term> <note>A "magistery" is a chemical preparation where the entire substance is converted into a new, often more potent form, without separating its constituent elements.</note> of pearls and corals are made by dissolving them in **distilled vinegar** <note>original: aceto destillato</note>; regarding these, see Beguin’s *Tyrocinium Chymicum* with my notes in Book 2, Chapter 19. It is the supreme preservative against **arthritis** <note>original: arthritidis</note>.

## THE FIFTH ESSENCE OF PEARLS.

<margin>Buttery Magistery of Corals</margin>
The preparation of the **buttery magistery** <term>magistery: a concentrated essence or chemical precipitate, often having a refined or "masterful" quality.</term> of corals through **magic fire**. Take as much as you wish of **red corals** <note>original: 'Corallorum rubrorum'</note> ground into a very fine powder. Pour over it **magic fire**, which is to say, a **spagyric solvent spirit** <term>spagyric: an alchemical term for the process of separating and then recombining the essential components of a substance (the "solve et coagula").</term>; it will begin to boil immediately, as if fire had been placed beneath it. The spirit, however, will appear like a mixture of white milk foam, while the thick and dreg-filled material sinks to the bottom. Carefully remove this milky and foaming spagyric spirit from the dregs by pouring it off, and distill it in a sand bath with a stronger fire, leaving an almost impalpable powder at the bottom. Keep this powder—which should be sweetened by distilling it several times with **May dew** <note>original: 'rorem maialem'; dew collected in the month of May was highly prized by alchemists for its supposed celestial purity.</note>—and dry it in the sun. It melts in the mouth like butter. It is a **great secret** <note>original: 'Magnum arcanum'</note> for correcting irregular menstruation and for bestowing strength to the stomach in wasting diseases, such as **dysentery**, **diarrhea**, and **epilepsy**.

->BASILICA<-

In this manner: using ashes <note>The "ashes" refers to the heat-conducting medium of a furnace.</note> and bags the size of a fist filled with sand placed into the honey to be distilled, the **spirit of honey** <note>original: 'spiritus mellis'; a liquid produced by the destructive distillation of honey, used here as a solvent.</note> is produced according to the rules of the art using an **alembic** <term>alembic: a traditional distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube or "beak."</term>. This spirit, when poured over fragments of corals previously **calcined** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a brittle or powdery state.</term> with **spirit of nitre** <note>original: 'spiritu cum nitro'; likely referring to a derivative of saltpeter or nitric acid.</note>, becomes colored repeatedly. Once this colored liquid is decanted, it is slowly drawn off in a similar manner using the same spirit of honey in a **Water Bath** <note>original: 'Balneo'; refers to the *Balneum Mariae*, a gentle heating method using hot water.</note>. The residue remaining at the bottom is dissolved two or three times in distilled water; after the water is evaporated, the material coagulates, and from it a very red **Tincture** is extracted with **spirit of wine** <note>original: 'spiritu vini'; ethanol or high-proof alcohol.</note>. Finally, after the alcohol is drawn off, the substance should be reduced to a thicker consistency. In this way, the true Tincture of corals is extracted using the spirit of honey.

Many "Tinctures of Corals" are circulated which are not genuine but are merely devised for deception. This reality seems to have caused our author some doubt, as he freely confesses that he has never seen a true and genuine Tincture of corals. It is, however, proven by experience that corals do release their Tincture and deposit it into nobler **solvents** <term>menstrua: alchemical terms for solvents capable of extracting the "essence" of a solid substance.</term>, provided that everything is done correctly and all other necessities are applied in their proper order and law. We shall teach two methods proven by our own experience.

### FIRST METHOD FOR THE TINCTURE OF *corals.*

First, let the corals be dissolved in the **strongest vinegar** <note>original: 'aceto fortissimo'</note>. Afterward, as our author taught, once the solvent is removed by distillation, let their **salt** be collected. This salt should then be impregnated with distilled vinegar for as long as the salt is able to absorb that spirit. One must proceed, therefore, in this manner: To each—

# CHYMICA.

To these pounds of salt of corals, add for the first time 2 ounces of the sharpest distilled vinegar, and distill it gently; at first, only a tasteless **phlegm** <note>original: 'phlegma'; a watery, inactive liquid produced during distillation.</note> will trickle out. For the second time, add 3 ounces of the previous vinegar, and distill gently in turn; proceed in this manner, adding 1 ounce of vinegar each time, increasing the amount and then distilling, until the distilled vinegar comes out just as sharp as when it was first poured in. See the *Tyrocinium* <note>Referring to Jean Beguin’s *Tyrocinium Chymicum* (1610), a landmark chemistry textbook.</note> book 2, chapter 3, regarding the **quintessence of corals** <note>original: 'quinta corallorum Essentia'; the most purified and potent form of a substance.</note>; however, Beguin’s process is not perfect. Let this impregnated salt **putrefy** <note>In alchemy, putrefaction refers to letting a substance sit in gentle heat to break down its structure.</note> for 20 days in a warm **Water Bath** <note>original: 'Balneo'; the *Balneum Mariae*.</note>, and afterward let it be distilled from a **retort** <term>retort: a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids.</term> in a closed **reverberatory furnace** <note>original: 'reuerberio'; a furnace that reflects heat onto the vessel.</note> or a dry bath. Do this in such a way that the useless phlegm evaporates first; afterward, the emerging whitening spirits should be collected separately in a large **receiver** <note>The vessel that catches the distilled liquid.</note>. Continue in this way until all the spirits have come out along with a **red oil** that looks like blood. This spirit has a good smell and burns like **spirit of wine** <note>original: 'spiritus vini'; high-proof alcohol.</note>; it must be **rectified** <term>rectification: the process of purifying a liquid through repeated distillation.</term> once more through the retort, leaving the red oil behind. This noble **menstruum** <term>menstruum: a solvent used to extract the "essence" or medicinal properties from a substance.</term>—produced partly from the vinegar and partly from the corals themselves—extracts a very red **Tincture** from fresh corals placed within it. If this Tincture is then freed from this spirit by distillation and finally joined with spirit of wine or another appropriate **cordial water** <note>A medicinal liquid intended to invigorate the heart or spirit.</note>, or made volatile through **circulation** <note>original: 'cohobia'; the repeated redistillation of a liquid from its own residue.</note> with them, it becomes a most elegant Tincture of corals, of a very sweet taste and a most fragrant smell.

# BASILICA

Therefore, because this [previous method] is not pure, it can hardly satisfy the medical purpose. Thus, another method must be investigated by which the **Tincture of corals** can be elegantly extracted; and it is as follows: First, the corals are **calcined** <note>original: 'Calcinantur'; heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or change its state.</note>, not pulverized but whole, using a slow **reverberatory fire** <note>original: 'igne reuerberij'; a furnace that reflects or 'reverberates' the heat back onto the substance.</note> at first, so that at least a living flame touches the surface of the corals placed in vessels (earthen dishes) within the reverberatory furnace. In this way, at the first stage, the corals turn white and hide their natural color. Therefore, the body of the corals must be worked with successive degrees of fire until they are transformed from whiteness to yellowness, and from yellowness to a supreme redness, the whole body being made spongy and light, which is usually accomplished in two or three days. 

When this sign is manifest, then finally, through the benefit of the degrees of fire, the corals are made fit to deposit their own tincture into another **solvent** <term>menstruum: a solvent used to extract the medicinal or chemical essence from a substance.</term>. Thus, if the prepared corals are cast into spirit of wine [alcohol] or into the alcohol of the spirit of **May-dew** <note>original: 'roris majalis'; dew collected in May was highly prized by alchemists, who believed it contained a pure celestial or atmospheric energy.</note>, a little later they will spontaneously deposit the tincture into that same alcohol, while those dregs, lacking any power, remain at the bottom. 

Therefore, once a portion of the wine solvent is removed by distillation, this Tincture becomes deep red with a certain sweetness. It is of such great power that after its use is repeated several times, it is impossible for any impurity to remain in the blood of the entire human body. It is administered in suitable **carriers** <note>original: 'vehiculis'; the liquid medium, such as water or wine, used to deliver the drops.</note> in doses of 3 to 6, 8, and 10 drops. Truly, this Tincture of corals ought to be most highly recommended to the Physician because of its stupendous powers, as it has a great affinity with the **vital spirits** <note>original: 'spiritibus hominum'; the subtle energies thought to circulate through the body to maintain life.</note> of man.

## OIL OF CINNAMON.

*Oil of Cinnamon <gloss>a</gloss> prepared correctly can be counted among the most effective Spagyric <term>Spagyric: a branch of alchemy (from the Greek words for "separate" and "combine") focused on creating potent medicines by extracting the essential virtues of plants and minerals.</term> strengtheners.*

*And although the method of preparing it is obvious to anyone practiced in Chemistry, yet I warn here in passing that the spices to be distilled are not to be reduced to powder, as some are accustomed to do preposterously, but are only to be broken into pieces and slightly bruised; otherwise they will supply you with half as much oil, as I have experienced several times by trial.*

*In this way, a greater quantity of oil can be obtained than by common distillations.*

*You should place the choicest broken Cinnamon into a glass retort <term>retort: a bulbous glass vessel with a long, downward-sloping neck, used for heating substances so that their vapors condense and trickle into a separate receiver.</term> and distill it in a vapor bath <gloss>b</gloss> <note>original: "Balneo vaporoso"; a method of heating using steam, providing a gentler and more uniform heat than a direct flame.</note>; then the Water and oil <gloss>c</gloss> come out together. *q* Here we must expose the craftiness and deception of certain untrained practitioners <term>empirics</term> <note>A term used here for "quacks" or those practicing medicine without formal theoretical training</note>. These people have tried—and still strive—to manufacture "potable gold" (or rather, "supposable gold" <note>The author uses a Latin pun here: *potabile*, meaning drinkable, vs. *putabile*, meaning imaginary or thought-to-be</note>) using distilled aromatic oils. Any honest man should be able to distinguish such swindlers <term>stelliones</term> <note>Literally "spotted lizards," a term used in law and alchemy for deceitful people or "shifty" characters</note> from true chemical doctors and physicians. Thurneysser, and after him Huler, and many others following them, would take distilled aromatic oils—especially oils of cinnamon, cloves, thyme, and linden—along with camphor oil, and reduce what they called "gold filings" or its "calx" <note>A powder produced by heating a metal until it oxidizes</note> into a colored essence. They then sold this for a high price as "potable gold." But this is a lie. The process is as follows: first, choice camphor is dissolved in "strong water" <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>Nitric acid</note> made from equal parts saltpeter and alum. Shortly thereafter, the camphor will float on the water like a yellow oil; this must be frequently separated and kept aside. Then, have ready the oils of cloves, cinnamon, thyme, and linden, and also the finest gold powder <term>calx solis</term>.

## CHEMISTRY <note>original: *CHYMICA*</note>

...impurities. Elixirs are chemical mixtures composed of many different types of simple ingredients. One such mixture is the **Elixir of Propriety**, named so by Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician and alchemist who popularized chemical medicines</note> in the eighth book of his *Archidoxes* <note>original: *Archidoxeos*; one of Paracelsus's foundational works on the "ancient doctrines" of chemistry</note>, title 6, "Elixirs." The reason why he calls it "of propriety" [or "of property"] seems obvious. Specifically, in this elixir, one can find the natural, harmonious **Properties** <term>Proprietates: the inherent, essential qualities or medicinal virtues of a substance</term> needed to achieve its intended purpose. These healing powers are not granted to the ingredients by the process of preparation itself; rather, they are innate and essential to them. They simply reveal themselves more successfully when a proper extraction is performed, as our author correctly instructs. Paracelsus himself, it must be said, left the description of this recipe somewhat incomplete.

## STRENGTHENING BALMS <note>original: *BALSAMA CONFORTANTIA*</note>
### *a* Thickened by the benefit of wax.

Because **Aromatic Oils** in liquid form cannot be carried about conveniently or safely—due to the danger of spilling or the breaking of the glass vials—the **Iatrochemists** <term>Chymiatri: physicians who applied alchemical and chemical principles to medicine, often following Paracelsus</term> began to devise a method of thickening them. In this way, various preparations can be carried more easily in tin or silver boxes (provided they are well-gilded) and be ready at hand in case of urgent necessity.

### FENNEL BALSAM

Take: **Tincture of Fennel made from the seeds with spirit of wine** <note>spirit of wine: high-proof alcohol or brandy used as a solvent</note>, 3 ounces.
**White wax**, ½ ounce.
**Fennel oil**, 2 ounces.

Melt the wax—which has been thoroughly cleaned and thinly shaved—over a gentle heat. Once melted, add the oil, and stir it with an iron spatula away from the fire until it thickens; afterward, add the Tincture extracted with spirit of wine, and mix again. When all these things have been brought to their proper consistency and have cooled, add **Salt of Fennel** <note>a salt produced by burning the plant remains and leaching the ashes, a process central to Paracelsian chemistry</note> at a rate of ½ dram for every ounce of the total composition (which makes 2 drams in total), and so let it be kept for use.

However, because wax becomes rancid with age and thus imparts an unpleasant flavor to such compositions, and furthermore, because it is of a "sticky" <note>original: *emplasticae*; a term for substances that clog the skin</note> and thick essence that prevents perspiration—as **Galen** <note>the famous 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for over a millennium</note> notes in **Book 7 of *On the Properties of Medicines***—it may close the pores. If the pores are closed, a "sterile" or ineffective operation of the balsams must necessarily follow; and if the operation is ineffective, only an ineffective result can follow. Therefore, in the composition of these balsams, wax seems useless. 

To avoid all these issues, prudent physicians instead extract a Tincture from expressed **Oil of Nutmeg** <note>original: *Nucis Moschatae*</note> using spirit of wine, until a very white body is left as a residue. Because this residue is entirely tasteless and [has no]...

### VII.
## PAIN-RELIEVING <note>original: *Anodynum*; from the Greek meaning "without pain"</note>, MITIGATING, Sleep-inducing, and Sedating.

*There are many diseases that cannot be cured without pain-relievers. Therefore, in the treatment of all diseases, where wakefulness accompanies pain and there is a loss of strength, appropriate internal pain-relievers can be administered, so that—once the very roots of the destructive torments of the symptoms have been removed—the friendly rest of Nature may be restored.*

*For sleep is a secret remedy <note>original: *arcanum*</note> in medicine, above all gems and precious stones: And he who can [direct] the sleep-inducing secret taken from the true Essence (when indeed the enemy diseases, having been at rest, are unseasonably awakened from sleep)...*

## OBSERVATIONS ON the preparation of Laudanum.

1. *The younger, fresh, succulent, outer roots and barks of **Henbane** <note>original: *Hyoscyami*; a potent sedative plant in the nightshade family</note> (discarding the inner woody stem) should be gathered while the Sun and Moon are in either **Aries** or **Libra** before the full moon; others gather them, if possible, at the very hour when the Moon is renewed in the aforementioned signs. The pressed juice, having been skimmed and passed through a filter, is thickened in a warm place to the consistency of honey, and afterwards hardens in the sun; from this, a **tincture** <note>an alcoholic extract</note> is extracted with spirit of wine.*

2. *Let the **Opium** be purified first in a liquid of **Hyssop** <note>a purifying herb often used in medicinal preparations</note>, or in distilled water <gloss>e</gloss>, as is customary with **Aloes**; afterwards, let it also be extracted with spirit of wine <gloss>f</gloss>.*

3. *The juice of Henbane and the opium (before they are mixed with the rest) should first, through **digestion** <note>a process of gentle heating to promote chemical changes</note>, cast off their harmful **sulfurs and poisons** <note>original: *sulphura & venena*; in Paracelsian thought, "sulfur" refers to the combustible, often toxic, oily component of a substance</note> (which seek the surface like foam); for it is from these that such various and disastrous symptoms arise in those sick people who [do] not [use] Opium and Henbane [properly...]*

<margin>a</margin> Anodynes <term>original: *Anodyna*; medicines that alleviate pain</term> are commonly soothing agents <term>original: *parergorica*; palliative treatments that address symptoms rather than the root cause</term> which, while they remove pain, usually lull the extreme passions of pain and torment to sleep by a gently introduced slumber. Our author is not entirely foreign to the Laudanum of Paracelsus, nor even to that...

### A GENUINE DESCRIPTION OF OPIATED LAUDANUM
->*description.*<-

This genuine and easy composition of opiated laudanum with opium (for there is indeed also a laudanum without opium—which is nonetheless an <term>anodyne|a medicine that relieves pain</term>—derived from the "sulfur" of vitriol <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" refers to the oily, combustible principle of a substance, while vitriol is a sulfate mineral</note>, about which more a little later) used by me is this. Take of genuine **Thebaic Opium** <term>high-quality opium sourced from Thebes, Egypt</term>, firm and not withered, as much as you wish. Cut it into small and thin particles or flakes, and in a glass dish over a slow fire of sand or ashes <note>a "sand bath" or "ash bath" provided gentle, indirect heat in early laboratories</note>, dry it for a while until it can be ground into powder of its own accord and with the fingers, and until it smells good and aromatic; for at the beginning, the coarse and foul sulfur smells very badly. Once this foul sulfur is removed or evaporated—in which all the <term>narcotic|sleep-inducing</term> and stupefying power consists—extract the **corrected** <note>to "correct" a substance meant to remove its toxic or unwanted properties while preserving its medicinal power</note> opium with distilled vinegar by pouring the vinegar over it to a height of five or six fingers, and leaving it in a warm place for some time. Separate the colored vinegar from the dregs by passing it through a filter, and again pour fresh vinegar over the dregs. When that which has been tinted with a reddish color by repeated <term>digestion|the process of softening or extracting a substance using gentle heat</term> has been separated again in the previous manner, cease the extraction further. ### USES OF OPIATED LAUDANUM.

The general use of opiated laudanum is: 1. It settles all pains. 2. It induces sleep. 3. It stops every <term>fluxion|an excessive flow of bodily fluids, such as a runny nose or diarrhea</term>. 4. It consumes heat <note>fever or inflammation</note>. 5. It strengthens the nature <note>the patient's constitution</note>, etc. Its special use is in delirium, <term>phrenitis|severe inflammation of the brain or high fever</term>, fevers, pleurisy, vomiting and arthritis, lower back pain, <term>suffocation of the womb|historically called "hysteria," believed to be caused by the uterus moving within the body</term>, the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>, etc. It should not be given twice in one day unless extreme pain demands it. **Crollius** <note>Oswald Croll, a famous follower of Paracelsus</note> administers it three times: in the evening, at midnight, and in the morning. See *Chemical Practice* <note>original: *Practicam Chymiatricam*</note> pages 23, 24, 25, etc.

2. Take 1 part of the purest <term>iron filings|original: *Limaturæ Martis*; literally "filings of Mars," the alchemical name for iron</term> free from all dust, and 2 parts of blue Hungarian Vitriol, or the Vitriol of Venus <note>copper sulfate</note> (of which I speak below in the section on specific stomach remedies). Afterward, cook and coagulate the mixture over a sand bath <note>a container of sand heated from below to provide steady, even heat</note> until it is dry. At the end, increase the heat slightly so that the material turns somewhat reddish. Pour more fresh distilled vinegar over this powder to a depth of four fingers. Leave it in a warm place for several hours, and the vinegar will become tinted. Pour this off and filter it. Add more vinegar, and in the same way, remove the tinted liquid by tilting the vessel without disturbing the dregs, as before. Proceed in this manner until the vinegar is no longer tinted. 

In this collected and tinted vinegar is the "burning sulfur of vitriol." Indeed, if you wish to test it, you may evaporate the vinegar from a small portion of it and wash what remains several times with pure spring water. If you then carefully dry it on <term>filter paper|original: *charta emporetica*; a porous paper used by apothecaries for straining</term> over a slow fire, you will see that it catches fire when brought near a flame and is entirely consumed by the fire just like common sulfur. This "burning" <term>kauston|original: *καυστὸν*; Greek for burning or caustic</term> sulfur of vitriol is "fixed" <note>rendered stable or non-volatile</note> and made into an anodyne in the following way: Into the vinegar impregnated with the tincture of sulfur, add drop by drop...

**Afterward:**

Take:
*   **Powdered Red and Yellow Sandalwood**, 1 ounce of each
*   **Mace**,
*   **Galangal**,
*   **Black and Long Pepper**, 3 drams of each
*   **Aloeswood**,
*   **Greater and Lesser Cardamom**, 2 drams of each

Extract the essence of all these in the customary manner using **spirit of wine** <note>high-proof alcohol</note>. In the same way, using **chicory water**, extract:
*   **Red Myrrh**,
*   **Egyptian Mummy**, 1 ounce of each <note>original: *Mumiæ Ægyptiacæ*; in this period, actual mummified human remains were ground into powder and used as a medicine thought to have great healing powers</note>

Carefully collect the tinctures from both extractions, mix them, and pass them through a filter. Then add:
*   **Narcotic Sulfur of Vitriol**, 2 drams.

Let this mixture circulate in a closed vessel in a **Water Bath** <note>original: *Balneo*; a gentle heating method where the vessel sits in hot water</note> for five days. Afterward, remove the solvents by distillation until the mixture reaches the consistency of honey <note>original: *mellaginem*</note>. To this, add:
*   **Extract of Saffron**, half a dram
*   **Salt or Magistery of Pearls and Corals**, 1 dram of each <note>a "magistery" is a refined precipitate of a substance, intended to capture its essential virtues</note>

Reduce the mixture into a solid mass. This is truly a most excellent and great **Anodyne** <note>a medicine that kills pain</note>.

# EPILEPTIC LAUDANUM.
<note>original: *Laudanum Epilepticum*</note>

Take:
*   **Sulfur of Vitriol Laudanum**, 2 ounces. (This laudanum is made by the same preparation, rule, and measure of ingredients as in the opiate laudanum, except that in place of the essence of opium, anodyne sulfur of vitriol is used).
*   **True Oil of Camphor**, 1/2 ounce.

And the Epileptic laudanum will be ready, which most certainly cures the falling sickness <note>original: *morbum comitialem*; an old term for epilepsy, so named because meetings of the Roman assembly (comitia) were abandoned if someone had a seizure</note>. See the genuine and true description of oil of camphor in the *Chemical Practice* <note>original: *Practica chymiatrica*</note> page 44 of our Leipzig edition. Of this, 2 to 4 grains are given, either during a paroxysm <note>a sudden attack or seizure</note>, and thus it is quickly resolved, or thereafter daily for some time, especially around the new moons <note>historical medicine often linked epilepsy to the phases of the moon</note>, while observing the other things necessary for this cure: not only is the paroxysm resolved, but the disease is even completely abolished. **Note:** oil of camphor evaporates quickly, therefore it would be better if it were not totally mixed into this specific epileptic laudanum, but rather added proportionally to the dose when it is about to be administered. See the *Practice* pages 44 and 45.

Mix carefully and keep. <margin>e</margin> This observation is of no account.

<margin>f</margin> Opium and the juice of henbane only with difficulty lay aside their poisonous sulfur through spirit of wine <note>original: *spiritu vini*; high-proof alcohol or brandy</note>; rather, that same sulfur is rendered thinner by the spirit of wine, and afterwards becomes more effective <note>here meaning more potent in its harmful or "poisonous" narcotic effects</note>, and it makes the composition of the laudanum worse. Therefore, I cannot approve of this particular preparation. The best of all methods is that handed down above, which is done first by the slow evaporation of the opium (cut into very small pieces) and afterwards evaporated over a gentle fire, so that finally—the former foul odor having been extinguished—it smells most pleasant and sweet. Afterward, this same opium, freed from its excessive sulfur, should be extracted with distilled wine vinegar alone. Furthermore, I would not wish for opium to be extracted with spirit of wine, because, as was shown above regarding the <term>Vegetable Panchymagogon</term> <note>original: *Panchymagogon vegetabile*; a "universal" vegetable-based medicine intended to purge all four humors of the body</note>, it attacks the sulfur rather than the Mercury and Salt <note>According to Paracelsian chemistry, all matter is composed of the "Tria Prima": Sulfur (soul/flammability), Mercury (spirit/volatility), and Salt (body/solidity)</note>. Indeed, it is in the sulfur where that most powerful narcotic path exists which is hostile to human nature; however, vinegar—at least that which is purer—takes only what it needs from the sulfur and does not draw the remaining principles to itself. Therefore, vinegar is superior in this kind of work.

<margin>g</margin> Just as the essence of Henbane is deservedly excluded and omitted from the making of laudanum, so too are there other things that can be excluded: unicorn <note>original: *vnicornu*; usually narwhal tusk or rhinoceros horn, which were highly prized as panaceas</note>, Bezoar stone <note>original: *lapis Bezoardicus*; a stony mass found in the stomachs of goats or other animals, believed to be a powerful antidote to poison</note>, ambergris, musk, and various precious distilled oils, which increase not so much the virtue of the medicine as its price and the dose (which is abominable even in the smallest quantity). For altogether, in pharmaceutical <term>technurgemata</term> <note>works of chemical art or skilled craftsmanship</note>, the simpler they are, the more perfect they become.

## VIII.
# THE FRAGRANT MEDICINE.

*Human Nature is helped by odors, and the spirits are also helped: therefore Philagrius <note>a Greek physician whose works are primarily known through later citations</note>, according to Aëtius <note>Aëtius of Amida, a 6th-century Byzantine physician and medical compiler</note>, says not unskillfully: That Nature gladly embraces pleasant odors, and being refreshed by them and as if reviving, she recalls her strengths which had been oppressed by the ferocity of disease: For an odor drawn in through the nostrils is pulled to the heart and brain; it rouses the compressed and suffocated spirit, and retains the panting and fleeting spirit: Indeed, there are even hot regions where Pliny ^a <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> suggests the Astomi <note>literally "the mouthless ones," a legendary race said to survive solely on the scent of roots, flowers, and fruit</note> live on odors alone.*

*Air is of the greatest importance regarding health, for he who falls ill from a stench ^b is healed with difficulty, because the unpleasant odor permeates with the spirit to all parts of the body, and especially to the brain and chest. By the scent of the Elixir of Life composed of various spices, Giambattista ^c Porta <note>a famous Italian polymath and scientist known for his work on natural magic and alchemy</note> says that he, through multiple experiments, has retained the exhaling soul of many: Therefore, in many diseases, the spirits of life <term>Spiritus Vitalis: in early medicine, these were subtle vapors or fluids believed to flow through the body to sustain life and bridge the gap between the soul and the flesh</term> must be rectified and corrected: For the principal organs and the vital spirits (both of which are troubled and infected first of all by any poison) are wonderfully refreshed by fragrant things, and poisonous fumes are excluded: For it is necessary that the spirit be refreshed and restored by spirit ^d and odor:*

<header>THE ROYAL PHARMACY</header>

For sweet odors are analogous and communicable to our spirits alone, which are the very authors of our life. We see how we block our nostrils against unpleasant odors and hold our breath so that we do not perceive a stench, for when it is sensed, we are easily weakened by it. Moreover, when our spirits—enclosed by faintings or convulsions—are oppressed and cast down, as soon as we perceive fragrant things applied to us, we are raised up and recover our spirit and strength. We see the mouth of the womb <note>original: "matricis os." This refers to the historical medical belief in the "wandering womb," where the uterus was thought to move within the body in response to pleasant or foul smells</note> move downward or upward when a sweet odor breathes. In the same manner, not only in the Plague, but also in the Hungarian fever <note>original: "Vngarica febre." Likely a form of typhus that was common among troops in 16th-century Hungary</note> and similar poisonous diseases, the spirits—which are infected and contaminated by the drawing in of contagion—can and must be improved and restored by fumigations <term>suffitibus: the practice of inhaling medicinal smoke or incense</term>, as can be seen in the writings of Conradinus <note>Balthasar Conradinus, a physician who wrote specifically on the "Hungarian disease" in the late 16th century</note> in his booklet on the Hungarian Fever, in which he describes various fragrant candles and scented waters.

In preparing the fragrant Specific <note>A "Specific" is a medicine traditionally used to treat a particular disease or organ</note>, whose fragrant blaze wonderfully recalls the failing spirit, whoever wishes to follow the process of Paracelsus in the *Archidoxis* <note>Refers to the *Archidoxis* or *Archidoxa* of Paracelsus, a foundational text of alchemical medicine</note> will lose their labor and expense with me in preparing it through digestion <term>digestionem: in alchemy, this refers to the process of exposing a substance to gentle, consistent heat over a long period</term>. Civet <note>original: "Zibetta," a musky substance harvested from the civet cat</note>, gums, and Tragacanth <note>a natural gum obtained from dried sap</note> acquire an unpleasant odor during the digestion process.

human excrement or "human sulfur," <note>original: "stercus seu sulphur humanum." In alchemy, "sulfur" refers to the combustible or soulful essence of a substance.</note> when placed in digestion <note>The process of slow, gentle heating in a sealed vessel.</note> for some time, loses that most foul odor and, through its own long digestion, spontaneously acquires the highest fragrance. This is taught in the text of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and foundational figure in toxicology and medical chemistry.</note> at the location cited by him, and our author implies this both on this and the following page. He calls it **Western Civet** <note>original: "Zibetam occidentalem." True civet is a musky secretion from the civet cat, used in perfumes.</note> to distinguish it from that which is brought to us from the East Indies. It is well known that Civet is brought to us from the West Indies as well.

In a human, however, the "West" refers to the posterior parts <note>A euphemism for the buttocks or anus.</note>, just as the "East" is attributed to the front parts. Thus, by way of a metaphor, he understands **Western Civet** to mean human excrement that has been changed into a most sweet odor by long digestion. Paracelsus called this *carbos* in the book he wrote to **Garboantes Friesenden**, in which he placed all his secrets.

...build it up; likewise, let it turn back into stone in the cold. Afterward, using either the heat of the sun or a heating furnace <term>hypocaustum</term> <note>A heated room or stove used for drying substances at a controlled temperature.</note>, take 5 or 6 pounds of this dried vitriol <note>Vitriol refers to sulfate minerals; here, likely iron sulfate.</note> and distill it through a retort over an open fire, collecting both the phlegm <note>The watery, tasteless part of the distillate.</note> and all the spirits. Take the remaining dead head <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>The solid, useless residue left in the bottom of a flask after all volatile components have been driven off.</note>, grind it, and repeat this distillation eight times by pouring the liquid back over the residue <note>This process is called cohobation, intended to "open" the solid matter further.</note> just as before; do not conclude this work until the ninth distillation through the alembic <term>alembicum</term> <note>The cap of the still that leads the vapor to the cooling vessel.</note>. You will then possess a most penetrating spirit of vitriol, a supreme secret <term>arcanum</term> for epilepsy. Indeed, 5 grains or 1 scruple <note>A scruple (℈j) is about 1.3 grams.</note> of it, diluted in 1 dram <note>A dram (ʒj) is about 3.9 grams.</note> of peony root and lavender water and administered during a seizure, stops the fit. Furthermore, if the other requirements for food and drink are not neglected, and if it is administered daily—especially while the moon is waning—it most powerfully dissolves the disease.

*c* The best green, not blue.

*d* It is Sapphire.

*e* Predators there might snatch cloaks and other things from travelers. <note>This likely refers to a specific chemical reaction where "impurities" or "volatile components" are stripped away, or it may be an allegorical warning about the danger of the process.</note>

*f* Distilled, or at least filtered, because it is gathered from tainted herbs.

*g* Just like the foamy, foul-smelling sulfur at the bottom.

<margin>Sweet oil of vitriol</margin>
*h* Let it be distilled until a skin forms; let little stones grow again in the cold, which should be collected as often as possible. Let 6 or 7 pounds of this vitriol be distilled in a well-coated vessel <note>A glass vessel "luted" or coated with clay to protect it from the direct flame.</note> over an open fire.

*i* Keep pressing the heat until all the acidic spirits have come out.

*k* 1. 2. 3. in a hermetically sealed phial.

*l* It can hardly be believed, since it is not something floating on top.

*m* This sweet oil of vitriol can also be made in this way.

## SWEET OIL OF VITRIOL.

Let the oil be boiled in a new iron frying pan with common water for as long as it takes for the corrosive salt to collect at the bottom of the pan; the remaining oil will then be sweetened. Glowing iron, quenched several times in oil of vitriol <note>Concentrated sulfuric acid.</note>, achieves the same result. However, by these methods the extraordinary <note>original: "ἐξαιρετικαὶ"</note> virtues of the oil itself are greatly diminished, and medical effects are not to be hoped for from them.

<margin>Philosophical spirit of Vitriol.</margin>
The Philosophical spirit of vitriol is of better efficacy; it was described above under the butter of antimony <term>butyrum antimonij</term> <note>A thick, oily substance (antimony trichloride) used in various chemical preparations.</note>. It performs wonders in epilepsy, apoplexy, and all ailments of the head and stomach—especially the volatile kind, the preparation of which is known to very few. It is not corrosive, but pleasant in its bitterness <note>original: "austeritate"</note> alone, and its virtues are even more evident.

## Another description ᵃ of the Spirit of Vitriol.

♃ <note>The symbol for Jupiter, often used in these manuscripts to denote tin or a specific recipe marker.</note> *Take at least two pounds of raw vitriol which has been purified as described just before; distill it and drive it with a very strong fire so that the Spirit and the Oil come out. To the liquid that emerges, add two parts of distilled rainwater, and let a new distillation be set up in a <term>Balneum Mariae</term> <note>A "Mary’s Bath" or water bath, used for gentle heating to prevent the substance from burning.</note>. In this rectification <note>The process of refining a liquid through repeated distillation.</note>, the most subtle Spirit of Vitriol is raised with the rainwater and comes out, leaving the most acidic Oil at the bottom. That resulting Spirit, mixed with rainwater, is extremely penetrating and is typically used most effectively in Hungarian Fever <note>original: "Febri Vngarica"; a term used in the 16th and 17th centuries for typhus.</note> and other burning fevers.*

---

ᵃ By this description, our author had almost arrived at the description of the volatile spirit of vitriol.

Indeed, that volatile spirit alone, when mixed with rainwater, can hardly be removed; however, according to the method I provided above, it can be obtained separately immediately. To exterminate the epilepsy of children, my anti-epileptic spirit of vitriol for children is most effective, the description and use of which I faithfully share.

### ANTI-EPILEPTIC SPIRIT OF VITRIOL
### *for Children.*

Take 4 lbs. of the most purified Hungarian Vitriol <term>Vitriolum Ungaricum</term> <note>A high-quality sulfate, often iron or copper-based, sourced from Hungarian mines.</note>. Add 8 lbs. of recently collected urine from healthy children. Digest this in a closed vessel for some time in a Mary's Bath <term>Balneum Mariae</term> <note>A water bath used for gentle, consistent heating.</note>; afterwards, distill in the same vessel until dry, producing a double "phlegm" <note>A watery distillate.</note>. The first of these is an excellent soothing agent <term>parengoricum</term> to gently calm gouty pains <note>original: "dolores Podagricos"</note> and others; the second is an excellent eye medicine <term>ophthalmicum</term>, most useful for any defects of the eyes. Pulverize the "dead head" <term>Caput mortuum</term> <note>The solid residue remaining in the vessel after distillation.</note> and place it in a strong earthen retort. Using an open fire—though very slow at the beginning—drive the contents into a large receiver. As the spirits come forth in abundance, a most precious liquid flows out, having a sulfurous odor and a somewhat bitter <note>original: "austeriusculi"</note> taste. Once this has been rectified <note>Purified through re-distillation.</note> through a retort once or twice and properly stored in a sealed glass, it radically removes all epilepsy in children. Mix 1 scruple <note>A small measurement of weight, roughly 1.3 grams.</note> of this with 1 ounce each of peony root water and linden flower water. From this mixture, administer half a spoonful during a seizure <term>paroxysm</term>, after the contracted and convulsed limbs have first been straightened. A little while later, as their senses return, they will come to themselves; once this is observed, administer a little more, and so also a third time. If indeed the seizure should return, as often happens, repeat the same process three times, and do not...

## EPILEPTIC MEDICINE

<margin>
It is a wonder how the brain is moved according to the phases of the moon: becoming moister as the moon waxes and drier as it wanes, as can be seen in epileptics, who feel the harm of the waxing moon.
</margin>

First, it is proper to soak Vitriol <note>original: "Vitriolum"; a metallic sulfate.</note> that has been calcined <note>Heated to a high temperature to remove moisture and reduce it to a powder.</note> to a yellow color in Spirit of Wine <note>High-proof distilled alcohol.</note> until it becomes a paste.

Take 1 ½ lbs. of this.
Shavings of the skull of a man who died a violent death <note>original: "Cranij Hominis iustificati"; literally "a man brought to justice." Early modern medicine often used the remains of executed criminals, believing their sudden death preserved "vital spirits" in the bone.</note>.
Oak mistletoe.
Elk’s hoof.
Peony seeds—1 ounce of each.

Let all these be cut and pounded; then, once mixed, let them be distilled through a retort <note>A glass vessel with a downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids that require high heat.</note> in stages; finally, let them be driven out with a violent fire.

Of this resulting liquid, let 1 lb. be rectified <note>Purified through re-distillation.</note> in a Mary’s Bath <term>Balneum Mariae</term> <note>A gentle water bath.</note> over:
Castoreum <note>A yellowish secretion from the scent glands of a beaver.</note>.
Sweet *Diamoschus* species <note>A fragrant, musk-based medicinal compound.</note>—½ ounce of each.
Anacardium <note>The marking nut or cashew, used in various chemical oils.</note>—6 ounces.

Afterward, add 4 lbs. of spirit of wine.
Salt of Peony—1 ounce.

## ANTI-EPILEPTIC CONFECTION
->Of Paracelsus.<-

A liquor will distill into a capacious receiver; draw this out by distilling it over the same dregs <note>original: "fęces"</note> a third time, and finally rectify it through an alembic <note>A type of still-head used for refining liquids.</note>. ### Of Paracelsus.

### GALREDA OR GELATIN
->of the Human Skull.<-

℞ <note>The symbol ℞ (Recipe) is the traditional start of a medical prescription, meaning "Take."</note> Filings of a human skull that has never been buried and is free from any external moisture; <term>digest</term> <note>To soften or extract substances using gentle, consistent heat.</note> these for half a month with <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>original: "alcohole vini"; concentrated ethanol.</note> infused with sage, to a height of six fingers above the solids. # OIL OF AMBER.

*In preparing this, no ordinary diligence is required, for it demands a suitable and proper fire. From white <term>Amber</term> <note>original: "Succinum"; a fossilized resin often associated in this period with bitumen or mineral origins.</note> out of the purest and unmixed Bitumen...*

<header>CHEMISTRY</header>

...generated in the sea, we use in medicine, not the yellow kind <gloss>a</gloss>.

**Recipe:** Take, therefore, fragments of white Amber <term>Succinum</term> <note>original: "Succinum"; a fossilized tree resin highly valued in pharmacy for its "volatile salts."</note> (for example, 2 or 3 pounds) and pound them in a coarse manner; do not grind them into a fine powder. First, if necessary, let the impurities be washed away with common water; then let it be placed in a <term>Cucurbit</term> <note>A gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation.</note> or an <term>alembic</term> <note>A still-head or the entire distilling apparatus.</note> that is not too high. Pour in a good quantity of Rose and Betony water <gloss>b</gloss> (this is done so that the Oil is not burned, and so that it may begin to drip more easily by the "vehicle" or medium of these waters). A spacious <term>still-head</term> <note>original: "capitellum"; the cap of the distilling apparatus where vapors condense.</note> with a sufficiently wide beak should be put on, and the receiving vessel fitted to it. With the joints of the glassware closed up in the usual manner, and placed in a <term>sand bath</term> <note>original: "in arena"; a method of heating a vessel evenly by surrounding it with sand.</note>, the distillation should be completed—keeping the heat at an appropriate and continuous level so that it does not cool down (otherwise, it turns black like pitch and breaks the glass). Also, take care that the fire does not grow too strong, or else the receiver is put at risk.

First, there comes forth water and a white oil with spirits like a cloud; then the visible spirit no longer comes out, but streaks appear in the still-head, just as one can see in the distillation of <term>Spirit of Wine</term> <note>original: "Spiritus vini"; historical term for ethanol or high-proof alcohol.</note>. Finally, the yellow oil comes: at this point, one must stop the distillation, or, by changing the receiver, catch the reddish-black oil that will follow. Lastly, the Salt rises by <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process where a substance transitions directly from a solid to a gas and back to a solid, often depositing as crystals.</note>. The <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>Literally "dead head"; the useless solid residue remaining after all volatile components have been driven off.</note> remains at the bottom—crumbly, black, and light.

->B A S I L I C A<-

<margin>a</margin> But if white amber cannot be obtained—for it is rarer and more precious than the yellow variety—this yellow amber performs equally well, provided it is first reduced to whiteness by artistry; which you shall accomplish in this manner.

### *The Artificial PREPARATION OF WHITE AMBER.*

Take of Yellow Amber, for example 1 pound <note>original: "℔ j"; approximately 12 ounces in the apothecaries' system.</note>; place it in a strong earthen <term>cucurbit</term> <note>original: "cucurbitam terream"; a gourd-shaped flask used in distillation.</note>; add 2 pounds of sea salt, or if you lack that, 2 pounds of rock salt <note>original: "salis gemmæ"</note> or the best common salt. Pour over it enough rainwater to dissolve the salt. Once dissolved, pour fresh river water over it as well. Let these boil together after placing a <term>blind alembic</term> <note>original: "alembico cæco"; a still-head without a spout, designed to condense vapors and let them drip back into the pot, a process now called reflux.</note> on top, for 14 whole days with a continuous fire. Finally, remove and break a small piece of the amber to examine it. If it is sufficiently white, the boiling work should cease; if not, you must persist longer until it shows sufficient whiteness. During the boiling, care must be taken that the water does not run out; therefore, more boiling water should be added from time to time.

<margin>b</margin> Some distill simply through a <term>retort</term> <note>original: "retortam"; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids.</note> without using distilled waters as a medium, simply observing the different oils as they come forth, which they collect separately. First the white oil comes out, then the yellow, and finally the red. These oils are afterwards <term>rectified</term> <note>original: "rectificantur"; a process of re-distilling the oil to purify it and make it more potent.</note>. Others add to the fragments of amber either pure white sand, burnt bones, or even <term>calcined</term> <note>original: "calcinati"; heated to a high temperature to reduce to powder.</note> flints. All of these substances have the power to suppress the boiling amber, preventing it from swelling up and flowing or slipping through the neck of the retort into the receiver. This method is certainly more suitable and safer for distilling the oil of amber.

## Method of application.

*Let the sick person lie on their back in bed, and with the water injected into the open eyes like a tear, or let a drop be applied with a feather from a black hen; let the patient close and roll their eyes so that the water, forced into the cavities of the eyes, may be spread throughout the eye. Let this be done twice or thrice in a day, and he will be cured.*

*If there should be clouds <note>original: nebulæ; a historical term for cataracts or corneal opacities that obscure vision.</note> above or below the cornea, prepare a powder from sugar candy, burnt alum, and cuttlefish bone <note>original: sepiæ osse; the internal shell of a cuttlefish, used in historical medicine as a fine abrasive to "scrape" away film from the eye.</note>, <gloss>c</gloss> but let it be very finely ground and sifted through a fine sieve so that it cannot be felt by the touch. When the patient goes to bed, let a little of this powder be blown [into the eye] from the quill of a feather, and soon you shall drop in a drop of water <gloss>d</gloss>; let him close his eyes and sleep, for it will be dissolved very quickly.*

*Or if there be spots, let there be mixed with half an ounce of that Eye Medicine <note>Referring to the liquor described on page 244-245.</note>, four drops each of oil of bricks <note>original: Laterini olei; an alchemical oil produced by distilling bricks soaked in olive oil, believed to have powerful penetrative qualities.</note> four times rectified, and fennel oil once rectified; likewise two drops of rectified oil of amber. From this well-mixed liquor, let one or two drops be applied to the eye twice [daily], always in the morning and evening.*

*A wonderful and stupendous Eye Medicine is made from Crabs and Celandine <note>original: Chelidonia; a herb traditionally associated with eye health; its name derives from the Greek word for "swallow," based on the belief that swallows used the plant to heal their fledglings' eyes.</note>, which, if prepared with the proper skill and at the right time, most powerfully restores eyes damaged even to the point of despair, and knits together <gloss>f</gloss> all wounds <gloss>e</gloss> within the space of 24 hours.*

*Let a fourth part [of the vessel] be empty, which should stick out above the sand bath. Apply fire gradually so that it boils; let it be stirred diligently with a wooden spatula until almost all the Sulfur is dissolved in those boilings, which happens in the space of 5 or 6 hours. For then the liquor turns red, thickening at least moderately like a lye. If the water vanishes <gloss>d</gloss> while boiling, let more hot water be poured on. Finally, when almost all the Sulfur is dissolved and the red liquor remains to the height of three across-laid fingers, it is then filtered while hot through filter paper <note>original: chartam Emporeticam; literally "merchant's paper," a thick, unsized paper used by apothecaries for filtration.</note>. A small amount of the filtered hot solution is placed in another glass, and immediately, while it is still warm, wine is poured in (there are those who use distilled vinegar, but wine is better) slowly, yet with a swift and high fall <note>The author suggests pouring the wine from a height to ensure rapid mixing and aeration.</note>, for so long until it acquires the appearance <note>The Latin text reads "calorem" (heat), but in this context of "thick milk," it almost certainly intends "colorem" (color or appearance).</note> of thick milk. This is later kept in a special glass, and one proceeds in the same way with the remaining hot solution and the wine. Finally, mix all the milky liquor and place it in a warm spot until the whiteness of the Sulfur has separated itself from the blue and red wine by descending to the bottom. Then, draw off the wine by tilting the vessel <term>Decanting: A process of pouring off the top layer of liquid to leave the sediment behind.</term> and pour on distilled rainwater, mixing it. Let it stand for a day and a night, and let it be poured off again, adding new water. Let this be repeated so many times until no blackness or impurity appears in the water anymore,*

# CHEMISTRY

*I offer [this] to the eager reader—for whom it is available in its entirety—to be examined, though it is not yet proven by experience. Furthermore, the natural foundations of all arts and sciences are to be elicited and drawn forth from here first: But let us come to the communicated **Potable Gold** <term>Aurum Potabile: literally "drinkable gold," a legendary alchemical medicine believed to cure all diseases and grant longevity.</term>.

First, a most subtle **Lime of the Sun** <term>Calx Solis: gold that has been reduced to a fine, flour-like powder through chemical processes.</term> is required, which I have previously prepared in this way for other uses.

Take half a pound <note>original: "lb ss."</note> of common **Strong Water** <term>Aqua Fortis: Nitric acid, a powerful corrosive liquid.</term>, and dissolve in it one ounce <note>original: "℥ j."</note> of **Sal Ammoniac** <term>Sal Armoniaci: Ammonium chloride, used here to transform the nitric acid into a gold-dissolving solution.</term>, or as much as it can dissolve in gentle heat. In this way you will have **Royal Water** <term>Aqua Regis: A mixture of acids (nitro-hydrochloric acid) named for its unique ability to dissolve "the king of metals," gold.</term>, in which you shall dissolve as much **Gold** as you please <gloss>n</gloss>. Afterward, pour the solution into a large glass vessel, and at least drop by drop—because of the noise of the boiling and the danger—drip in some good **Oil of Tartar** <term>Oleum Tartari: A concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, which acts as a base to cause the gold to drop out of the acid solution.</term> <gloss>i</gloss> which has been resolved by itself in a cellar. In the absence of this, **Salt of Tartar** dissolved in common water may be used.

However, a good quantity of Oil of Tartar is required; then the **Gold** falls to the bottom by reaction. When the entire dissolved **Lime of Gold** seems to have sought the bottom—which you will notice by the color of the **Royal Water**, which ought to be white; for if it is still yellow, it is a sign that all the **Gold** has not yet been reacted, therefore more **Oil of Tartar** must be poured in drop by drop; be faithfully warned of this by my own loss <note>The author suggests he ruined a batch by not adding enough Oil of Tartar.</note>—then after it has settled for several hours in a warm place, pour off the upper liquid. *m* Which, if afterwards urged by the flame of a **reverberatory furnace** <term>reuerberij flama: a furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat onto a substance</term> in the usual manner, becomes brown in color, like the **Saffron of Mars** <term>crocus Martis: a reddish-brown powder made of iron oxide.</term>.
*n* The same explosive noise and volatility is immediately removed from this **solar calx** <term>calci solari: gold that has been reduced to a powder through chemical heating.</term> by a more copious pouring on of **Oil of Tartar** <term>olei Tartari: a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate.</term>, if indeed you pour it into a solution of gold made with **Aqua Regis** <term>aqua regis: "Royal Water," a mixture of acids capable of dissolving gold.</term> for as long as the whole compound turns black like printer's ink; yet you should not be certain that all the gold has been precipitated to the bottom, but also that it can never afterwards—even immediately after its first removal or collection—possess the power of exploding <gloss>fulminandi</gloss>. This is altogether marvelous: that one and the same cause can exist for two most diverse effects, which indeed otherwise does not seem possible by nature. For surely, the same thing, insofar as it is the same, produces nothing but the same. Therefore, the same thing cannot be the cause of opposites unless different principles concur within it, and concur in such a way that they sometimes impel one and the same thing to be the cause of opposites.

...for a **philosophical month** <note>original: "mensem Philosophicum," a period of 40 days often used in alchemical processes to signify a complete cycle of transformation.</note> of 40 days. Furthermore, the distillate should be rectified a third time from the **dead head** <term>caput mortuum: the "dead head" or solid, useless residue left in the flask after all volatile components have been driven off.</term> of the urine, so that the spirit can be properly raised from it (20, 30, or 40 measures of urine can be taken).

Therefore, using a long-necked flask with its alembic and receiver—with the joints well and properly secured on all sides—the distillation should be started using a boiling **hot bath** <term>Balneum: a water bath (marie-bath), used to provide steady, even heat.</term>. In this way, the **spirit of urine** <note>Essentially ammonia gas or a concentrated ammonium solution.</note> will rise like crystals and adhere to the joints of the alembic, with no watery moisture accompanying it, but only the **volatile spirit** coming forth. However, that which came forth above through **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process where a substance turns directly from a solid to a gas and back to a solid, used here to purify the crystals.</term> is dissolved with distilled rainwater and collected in the alembic. In the same manner as before, it is distilled from the flask through an oily sponge; this is repeated six times, always using fresh distilled water. Finally, this spirit of urine, having been brought to the highest purity and hidden away in a **hermetically sealed** <note>original: "Hermeticè reconditus," referring to a flask sealed airtight by melting the glass neck shut.</note> flask, is digested for fifteen days in the gentle heat of a **dew-bath** <term>Balneum roridi: a "vapor bath" or "moist bath" that mimics the gentle heat of morning dew.</term>, until it has been entirely resolved into a clear liquid.

To this is afterwards added an equal weight of **spirit or alcohol of wine** <note>Concentrated ethanol.</note>, made and refined from wine itself. When both are placed in a very cold place for an hour or two, they coagulate into a very white salt. This salt is once more converted into a liquid in a hermetically sealed flask by the gentle heat of a **vapor bath** over a period of 20 or 30 days...

For its medical use, only 10 or 11 drops are mixed with 2 pounds <note>original symbol: ℔</note> of the best wine; and from this mixture, 1 ounce, 1.5 drachms, or 2 drachms are drunk once or twice every month to preserve health, and in this way its power is **diaphoretic** <term>Diaphoretica: A substance that induces sweating, used to expel "humors" or toxins from the body.</term>. But in driving away the most dangerous diseases, its use must be tempered by the prudence of a skilled physician; it is accustomed to work in various ways, by expelling what is harmful through the individual **excretory organs** <term>Emunctoria: The organs or passages of the body through which waste is expelled, such as the skin, kidneys, or bowels.</term>.

# CHEMICAL MATTERS

The whole secret of the Art is that the metal<sup>a</sup> be thoroughly **calcined** <term>Calcinatio: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air or sulfur to change its physical state, often reducing it to a powder or oxide.</term> by means of **sulfur**.

[Tin/Jupiter symbol] <note>The symbol for Jupiter (Tin) appears here as a section marker, though the text describes the treatment of iron and copper.</note> Of **laminated iron** or of **Venus** <note>original: "Veneris," the alchemical name for Copper</note> (for the method for both is the same), take as much as you wish; cut it into pieces the size of a **half-thaler** <note>A large silver coin used throughout Europe.</note>. Create a **stratum super stratum** <term>Stratum super stratum: A technique of layering materials—in this case, metal plates and sulfur—to ensure an even chemical reaction.</term> with powdered sulfur in a **luted crucible** <term>Tigillo lutato: A ceramic melting pot sealed with "lute," a fire-resistant clay paste, to make it airtight.</term>. Place it in a **Wheel of Fire**<sup>b</sup> <term>Ignis Rota: A circular fire built around a vessel to provide a gradual, surrounding heat.</term>. At the beginning, the fire should not touch the crucible, but it must be increased by moving it closer bit by bit, and finally, you shall strengthen it. Thus, as the sulfur ignites, the aforementioned plates are calcined, a process which is completed within an hour. When everything has cooled, remove the blackish-gray material, which resembles **burnt copper** <note>original: "æris usti" or "aes ustum," a common alchemical term for copper oxide</note>; grind it and sift it. Place it in an open, un-glazed pot, positioned across the heat (just as is done in the preparation of **Glass of Antimony** <term>Vitrum Antimonij: A transparent, glassy substance made from antimony ore, used as a powerful emetic.</term>). Stir it diligently over a charcoal fire, taking care that it does not melt and the **Vitriol** <term>Vitriol: A historical term for metal sulfates, highly valued for their medicinal and chemical properties.</term> in the Copper does not vanish<sup>c</sup>. In this way, the sulfur is burned off or evaporates. Stir it from side to side with an **iron**<sup>d</sup> or **copper**<sup>e</sup> instrument—depending on which Vitriol you intend to make. When the material begins to stick to the iron, then it is sufficient, and it should be removed from the fire. Weigh this powdered **Calx of Venus** <note>The metallic ash or oxide remaining after calcination.</note>, and for every **pound** <note>original symbol: ℔</note> take three **lotones** <note>A "Lot" or "Loto" was a small unit of weight, roughly 15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of sulfur; mix them and place them in the pot on its side. Stir over a gentle fire for a **quarter of an hour**<sup>f</sup>; at the end, let the pot almost glow with heat. The Copper will soften like a paste and stick to the iron. Let it cool, then grind and sift it. Add again to one pound of the material three lotones of sulfur...

### Virtues, Use, and Dosage.

<header>CHEMICAL MATTERS.</header>

## FLOWERS OF SULPHUR.

No use of crude *sulphur* should be made in medicine, unless one has at hand that which is found in mines and is called *Scissile* <gloss>fissile or native sulphur</gloss> <note>original: "Scissile," referring to native sulfur found in a pure state that naturally breaks into layers or scales.</note>, purified by Nature. This type is in no way different from the "flowers of sulphur" prepared by art [alchemy]. For just as here [in the laboratory] the thinner part of the *sulphur* is raised to higher places by an artificial fire, so there [in the earth] it is raised by a Natural fire, and by that reasoning is more thoroughly cooked. Therefore, when *scissile* sulfur is available, it may be used in place of the Flowers. But because Nature rarely supplies us with an abundance of *scissile* sulfur, Chemical physicians began to devise an artifice by which they might be assisted in its scarcity.

<margin>The mountains of Campania.</margin>
In the territory of Krakow <gloss>in Poland</gloss> <note>original: "Cracoviensi."</note>, sulfur is seen purified by a wonderful artifice of Nature; I also saw it with great interest in the Kingdom of Naples near Puteoli <note>The modern Pozzuoli, a volcanic area famous for its sulfurous fumes.</note>, where Mount Vesuvius burns perpetually with *sulphur*. In that place, sulfur usually sweats out from the rocks like dew. That "flower" is most sweet, and if it were available in large quantities, a true Spagyric <term>Spagyric: An alchemical practitioner who uses the "solve et coagula" (dissolve and recombine) method to produce medicines.</term> could extract a singular remedy for himself from it through Chemical mastery.

Furthermore, sulfur is produced there after it is purified <gloss>cleansed</gloss> from stones and Earth by the power of fire.

Near Salzburg, in the copper mines where they boil *Vitriol* <term>Vitriol: A historical term for various metallic sulfates, highly valued in alchemy for their acidic properties.</term> from the ore by "roasting" <note>original: "assatione," a dry-heat metallurgical process.</note>, as they call it, the *sulphur* usually flies away from the ore, which...
