...phlegm <note>original: "phlegma." In early chemistry, this refers to the initial watery or tasteless distillate that comes off before the potent substances.</note> will begin to drip, and it will continue for 4 or 5 hours. The fire must be increased gradually with large coals, so that eventually the pan <gloss>e</gloss> <note>This likely refers to a label in a diagram in the original printed book.</note> in which the sand is placed glows red. If the fire is kept continuous, so that the Sulfur almost flows within the Alembic <term>Alembic: The top part of a still, where vapors condense and are collected.</term>, then it is sublimated <term>Sublimation: The process where a solid turns into a gas and then back into a solid without becoming a liquid first.</term> more quickly. However, the heat should not be excessive; otherwise, the sulfur would rise not as a yellow color, but black.

The "Flowers" <note>The fine, powdered form of a substance (in this case, sulfur) produced by sublimation.</note> raised into the Alembic should be removed quickly. Specifically, you should always hold a round, folded piece of paper underneath so that when the cap <note>original: "capitellum"</note> is lifted, the Flowers do not fall into the sand. Meanwhile, if the Cucurbit <term>Cucurbit: The bottom part of the distilling apparatus that holds the raw materials.</term> is extremely hot at that time, its opening must be covered without delay so that the Sulfur is not ignited by the incoming air—as often happens. Then, replace the Alembic and continue the fire for ten hours.

After the sublimation is finished, let everything be cooled. Once the Alembic is removed, the Flowers should be collected and mixed with the earlier ones. The **dead head** <term>Caput mortuum: The useless residue or "worthless remains" left in the vessel after the chemical process is complete.</term> in each sublimation should be porous and brittle; if sprinkled onto glowing coals, it should no longer burn. Indeed, this is the sign that all its "goodness" <note>original: "bonitatis," referring to the substance's medicinal or chemical potency</note> has been removed.

Mix these Flowers again with new salt and vitriol, maintaining the same proportions as before. Proceed in every way just as in the first instance. The more often this is done, the more fineness <note>original: "tenuitatis," referring to the subtlety or particle size</note> the Flowers acquire, becoming more and more pure. Do the same for a third time, though you will have fewer Flowers. From three pounds <note>original symbol: ℔</note> sublimated three times, you will have 20 ounces <note>original symbol: ℥</note> in this third repetition...

# THERIAC WATER.

*Take 5 ounces <note>symbol: ℥</note> of Venice Theriac <note>A famous ancient "cure-all" electuary containing dozens of ingredients including herbs, honey, and sometimes opium.</note>.*

Pour over this the best, carefully rectified spirit of wine <note>High-proof distilled alcohol</note>, or—if it is at hand—a spirit prepared from the seeds or roots of Angelica <note>A plant highly valued for its aromatic and medicinal properties</note>, which is more effective. The liquid should rise to a height of three or four fingers above the solids. Extract the tincture in a closed glass vessel using the gentle heat of ashes. Pour off the tinted spirit by decantation, and pour on fresh spirit until it is no longer colored. Afterward, distill off at least half of the tinted spirit of wine; let the remainder stay with the extracted essence. To this, you shall add 6 ounces of Spirit of Tartar <note>A chemical solution derived from the sediment of wine casks</note>; in this way, you shall circulate <note>A process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel</note> and digest the mixture for eight to fourteen days.

The *Zenexton* <note>term: Zenexton; a Paracelsian term for a specific type of defensive amulet or "physic" worn to ward off the plague</note> of Paracelsus is found in Book 2 of *On the Plague*, chapter 3. It is a "Pagoic" <note>original: *Pagoicum*; likely a corruption of "magical" or a specific Paracelsian term for protective arts</note> amulet; specifically, quicksilver—also known as mercury—enclosed in a hazelnut shell and hung around the neck. The power of this device is "magnetic-attractive"; it draws the pestilential poison to itself as a "homogeneous" <note>similar in nature</note> substance. Thus, the poison does not harm the human body (which possesses its own similar power of attraction), but is instead pulled away by its like—the Zenexton—and is dissipated within it. The same principle was later applied to arsenic, a type of amulet first discovered by Jacobus Garpensis <note>Berengario da Carpi, a famous 16th-century anatomist</note>. Later authors expanded upon and confirmed this; Fallopius, Montanus, Heurnius, and Crato <note>these were prominent European physicians of the Renaissance</note> all state that Pope Hadrian VI was delivered from a most severe plague by this very amulet.

### OTHER ZENEXTA

To the number of charms or <term>amulets|original: periaptorum; items worn on the body for protection</term> intended to be hung from the neck during a time of plague proposed by the author, others may be added. These indeed do not change in their type or material, yet they differ from the others in their preparation. Truly, there is great ingenuity in the human mind, which is ever busy with changing the same materials into different shapes and demonstrating its own nobility thereby. It was said from the beginning that <term>quicksilver|original: argentum vivum; mercury</term> placed in a hollowed-out hazelnut—which is afterward sealed tightly and hung from the neck—gave birth to the primary name of <term>Zenextum|a Paracelsian term for a protective plague amulet</term>. Later, arsenic was included in this same category. Both materials, while remaining the same in substance, can be reduced into a more suitable form. One must understand these preparations as follows, starting first with Mercury.

First, mix the Mercury with the sulfur in this manner: Melt the sulfur in a <term>crucible|original: tigillum; a ceramic or metal container used for melting substances at high temperatures</term> over a slow fire; afterward, mix the raw Mercury into the same, stirring constantly until it turns black and all the Mercury has been consumed within the sulfur. Then, grind this mass and mix it thoroughly with the remaining species. Sublime <note>The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifying it again on a cool surface</note> all these things from a <term>cucurbit|original: cucurbita; the gourd-shaped lower vessel of a still</term> with an <term>alembic|original: alembicum; the cooling cap or 'head' of a still</term> attached, in the usual manner. Through this sublimation, several parts will be reduced to very elegant red colors. Collect all of the sublimate, discarding the dregs, and then form the powder into small cakes using <term>tragacanth|original: Tragacantha; a natural gum used as a binder</term> dissolved in rose water. Wear these cakes, stamped with seals in the customary way, hanging from the neck in muslin or another silk, while observing those same precautions mentioned regarding the coagulated Mercury.

After everything has cooled, the material hardens like pitch; however, before this happens, with hands smeared with **oil of roses**, form the still-soft material into small cakes. These, when hung around the neck in a linen cloth, protect against infection in the same way. (NB. The smoke must be avoided, as it is poisonous due to the arsenic <note>original: "ex arsenico"; while only sulfur and antimony are listed above, these minerals were often found together in nature or previously combined in the "Zenexton" process</note>.) There is no need to fear, even though it is composed of deadly poisons. Indeed, sulfur mitigates the virulence of both antimony and arsenic, making them more suitable for good use.

From the same is made an excellent **attractive plaster** <term>attractive plaster|original: emplastrum attractivum; a medical dressing designed to "draw out" toxins, heat, or fluids from the body</term> for the **plague**, very quickly maturing and bursting **abscesses** <term>abscesses|original: apostemata; localized collections of pus or swellings</term> and **carbuncles**, and most powerfully drawing out poisons. ## FOR GOUT.

Incipient and mild **Gout** <note>original: "Podagra"</note>, according to **Severinus** <gloss>a</gloss> <note>Petrus Severinus (1542–1602), an influential Danish physician who harmonized Paracelsian chemistry with traditional medicine</note>, is cured by a single ointment or balsam; it permits a mixture of **Resolvents**, **Mitigators**, and **Corroborants** <term>Corroborantia|strengthening medicines intended to restore the "tone" or vigor of a body part</term>.

Confirmed Gout—which has established roots that are difficult to dissolve, whether in the blood, the flesh, or in the **synovia** <term>synovia|the lubricating fluid found in the joints; early physicians believed gout was caused by "corrupt" fluids settling here</term> itself—cannot be cured by external resolving, mitigating, and strengthening balsams alone...

# BASILICA

...gives, for removing all arthritic pains, page 187. In successfully curing Gout <term>Podagra|A painful form of inflammatory arthritis, historically associated with rich diets and often affecting the big toe</term>, this one thing must especially be provided for: that every year at the fixed time of the equinoxes or solstices—for it is precisely around these times that gouty fluxes <note>original: "fluxiones Podagricae"; the movement of "humors" or fluids thought to cause swelling and pain</note> usually flourish—the body should be well cleansed. Above all, a dietary regimen, which must never be neglected anywhere, should be skillfully and correctly established. After this cleansing, however, strengthening remedies and Diaphoretics <note>Medicines used to induce sweating to expel morbid humors</note> should be administered.

In this way, indeed, Gouty Paroxysms <note>Sudden attacks or fits of intense pain</note> rarely or never return; or, if attacks sometimes coincide due to some slight external error <note>Likely referring to lapses in diet or exposure to cold</note>, they are never severe, nor do they excite continuous or unusual pains, and they easily yield to external balms.

Furthermore, among the number of purgatives set down by the author, the most prominent are the secret remedy <term>arcanum|In Paracelsian medicine, a "secret" or highly purified essence of a substance that holds its curative power</term> of asarabacca <note>original: "asari"</note> or the essence of the roots of True Hellebore <note>original: "Hellebori veri"</note>. These, when extracted with spirit of wine in the common way, are often taken—either alone or mixed with the *arcanum* of asarabacca in a proper preparation—every morning for some time before the usual season of gouty attacks. This frees the whole body from the arthritic fluxes of that disease, especially if a temperate diet is added to this evacuation, and if lemon balm wine with avens root <note>original: "caryophyllata radice"</note> is drunk sparingly at the table as the primary beverage.

When these things have been successfully carried out, if any thicker impurities still remain, they are to be finally exterminated either by the coral-colored secret remedy <note>original: "arcano corallino"; a red mercurial preparation</note> or by the arthritic powder of Paracelsus <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541) whose chemical medicines revolutionized the era</note>, and one must immediately proceed to the strengthening Diaphoretics. # FOR DROPSY.
<term>Hydrops: an old medical term for dropsy or edema, the painful swelling of the body caused by the accumulation of excess watery fluid.</term>

Our nourishment, both Food and Drink, contains within itself three wastes: one is Water, another is Sulfur, and the third is Salt or **Tartar** <note>original: "Tartarus"; in the medical theory of Paracelsus, "tartar" refers to the stony or solid precipitates formed from food and drink that the body fails to expel, leading to various diseases.</note>. If this Salt—the intermediary of the other two—is damaged by the **Astral Fire** <note>The celestial or spiritual heat believed to govern the body's internal alchemy.</note> joined with its own elemental fire, then from that breakdown of Salt, Dropsy is created and generated.

That which is good brings no harm, but that which is evil does. There is no food that does not contain a foul and immature **sulfur** <term>Sulphur: in this alchemical context, sulfur refers to one of the three primary principles of matter (along with Mercury and Salt), representing the combustible or impure portion of a substance.</term>, and which is not of a laxative and elemental nature. But if it also strives for separation in the beginnings and spirits, it brings about the cause of diarrhea, and according as that separation is established, it becomes a disease of flux. 

If it moves those things which are not ingested, such as when it draws to itself the nourishment of the body's parts, or the coagulated sulfur in the blood, in the flesh, and in other members, it inflicts disease upon the body with that appetite; as soon as it withdraws nourishment from the body, and while it desires to absorb the body's own pure blood, it sinks down out of necessity and **dysentery** <note>original: "dysenteria"</note> occurs. Therefore, as often as the stomach is provoked by the desire of consuming immature sulfur, and as often as it is seized by the excessive pleasure of separation—and whether it separates one thing from another individually—a flux is stirred up by that excessive separation.

...[the discharge] of excrement through the bowels is called **diarrhea**.

This separated liquor should be saved for use by pouring it off; to this you shall add its own **Salt**,<sup>f</sup> some **Salt of Pearls**,<sup>g</sup> and even one or two drops of the oils of Cinnamon, Mace, and Nutmeg; in this way, the medicine will be more pleasant and effective. **Potable Gold**<sup>h</sup> <term>Potable Gold: "Aurum Potabile," a legendary alchemical elixir of dissolved gold believed to grant longevity and health.</term> could also be added, provided that a true and genuine version can be obtained, which has not been tainted or corrupted by corrosive substances.<sup>i</sup>

<header>CHEMISTRY</header>

This is brilliantly done when a **lye** <term>lye: A liquid solution made by leaching vegetable ashes, used here as a base for extracting salts.</term> is made from their ashes by the aid of common water; from this lye, once evaporated, a salt is produced. This salt is afterwards purified either by melting it in a fire—where, however, much of its potency is lost—or by many repetitions of dissolving and coagulating it. But this common manufacture of salts from vegetables is not entirely genuine; they easily liquefy and take on a smell and taste like urine or lye. Furthermore, they retain a certain quality of the **Salt of Tartar** <term>Salt of Tartar: Potassium carbonate, often used as a reference point for alkaline salts in early chemistry.</term>, which they closely resemble, making it difficult to distinguish them by either taste or smell. Therefore, our author rightly advises that a legitimate preparation of the **salt of satyrion** <note>original: "salis satyrionis." Salt derived from the orchid root discussed on the previous page.</note> be made, so that it tastes of none of these things.

### THE METHOD OF PREPARING CRYSTALLINE SALTS
->*of Vegetables, or those as transparent*<-
->*as Saltpeter.*<-

Take the ashes of any vegetable, with an equal part of elegant powder of **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphuris." Often called brimstone; used here to help purge "oily" impurities during burning.</note>; calcine or burn them with a fire that is not too gentle. In this way, all the lye-like oiliness is destroyed from the ashes by the sulfur. From these ashes, finally, draw out the salt with common water (or the plant's own distilled water), distilling the extractions until a **skin** <note>original: "cuticulam." A film that forms on the surface of a liquid, signaling it is concentrated enough to begin crystallizing.</note> forms, and afterwards placing it in a cold place to crystallize. Take as much sulfur as there are ashes. These salts are the best of all and work wonderfully; they do not taste like lye. Thus, **salt of wormwood** <note>original: "sal absinthij." Known for its extreme bitterness and use in digestive ailments.</note> prepared by this method purges the impurities of the stomach and chest through vomiting, if one **scruple** <term>scruple: A small unit of weight, roughly 1.3 grams.</term> or half a **drachm** <term>drachm: A unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams.</term> of it is administered in two **ounces** <term>ounce: A unit of weight, roughly 28 grams.</term> of water. Likewise, **salt of masterwort** <note>original: "sal imperatoriæ." An aromatic herb used as a "cure-all" in the Renaissance.</note> made from the roots according to this method, given in a dose of 4 to 8 **grains** <term>grain: The smallest unit of weight, roughly 0.06 grams.</term> in **elderberry rob** <term>rob: A thick, medicinal syrup made from the concentrated juice of fruit.</term>, removes all fevers.

℟ <note>The symbol for "Recipe" or "Take."</note> Take the ashes of any vegetable and dissolve them gradually in distilled vinegar, fortified with a small quantity of **aqua fortis** <term>aqua fortis: Literally "strong water," a historical term for nitric acid, used here to help dissolve the mineral components of the ash.</term>. These salts are pure, have a pleasant taste, and do not liquefy <note>Early chemists struggled with salts that absorbed moisture from the air (deliquescence); a salt that stayed dry was a sign of high purity.</note>.

## II. THE ARCANUM <term>Arcanum: a "secret" or "inner mystery"; in alchemy, a powerful medicine that acts directly on the life force</term> OF THEOPHRASTUS <note>referring to Theophrastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus</note>

such as **Sublimated Mercury**, **Arsenic**, **Monkshood**, **Diamond Dust**, <margin>a</margin> **Venom of Spiders and Toads**, **Wolfsbane** <note>original: "Thora," a highly toxic plant in the aconite family</note>, **Gall-brain**, <margin>b</margin> and **Menstrua** <note>menstrual blood, which was considered biologically potent or even toxic in early modern medicine</note>.

## STICTIC PLASTER. <gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: "Emplastrum Sticticum." A "stictic" plaster (from the Greek word for "pricked") was a specialized surgical dressing used primarily for puncture wounds, stabs, or deep cuts to prevent infection and promote closing.</note>

*In the composition of every wholesome Stictic Plaster, according to Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note>, four ingredients of different kinds must be considered.*

*1. Healing, which is achieved by means of Wax and Colophony <note>original: "Cera & Colophonia." Colophony is a brittle, amber-colored resin obtained from pine trees, often called rosin.</note>.*

*2. Accidents <note>In early medicine, "accidents" referred to secondary symptoms or complications that occur alongside the main injury, such as swelling or inflammation.</note>, which are removed and prevented by the benefit of gums, namely Opoponax, Galbanum, Sagapenum, Bdellium, Ammoniacum, and Elemi <note>These are all aromatic resins derived from various plants, valued in the Renaissance for their supposed ability to draw out toxins and soften hard swellings.</note>.*

*3. Rot <note>original: "Putredo."</note> (for any wound, even without complications, is liable to rot, producing worms and growths of bad flesh), which is removed and prevented by the help of great consolidatives <note>Medicines believed to "knit" or "consolidate" the edges of a wound together.</note>, namely Mastic, Myrrh, and the like.*

*4. To protect against mold, scabies, drying out, contraction, synovial fluid <note>original: "synouia." In this context, it refers to the loss or corruption of the lubricating fluid in the joints near a wound.</note>, and similar complications, which is achieved through minerals, namely Litharge, Minium, Antimony, Ceruse, Marcasite, Calamine, and the like <note>These are various mineral and metallic compounds, often lead or zinc-based, used as drying agents and preservatives in ointments.</note>.*

### ANOTHER DESCRIPTION OF PARACELSUS' OPODELDOCH

There is also another description of the great Opodeldoch plaster used by *Paracelsus*. Its formula is as follows:

Take:
Galbanum <note>A bitter, aromatic gum resin derived from Persian plants.</note>
Opopanax <note>A gum resin with a heavy odor, often used in ancient medicine.</note> — 3 ounces of each.
Ammoniacum <note>A medicinal gum resin obtained from a North African plant.</note>
Bdellium <note>A semi-transparent oleo-gum-resin similar to myrrh.</note> — 1 ounce of each.

Let them be macerated <note>Soaked to soften or extract components.</note> for eight days or more in distilled vinegar; strain, and then gently thicken to the consistency of honey; then

Take:
Litharge <term>litharge|original: "Lythargiri." A mineral form of lead oxide, traditionally used to help plasters harden and dry.</term>, very finely powdered — 1/2 pound.
Common oil — 1 1/2 pounds.

Cook over a slow fire and stir constantly with a spatula until it takes on a brown <note>original: "spadiceum." Referring to a chestnut or reddish-brown color.</note> color; add:
Wax — 1 pound.

Once melted, mix in the resins mentioned above, and shortly after:
Laurel oil — 3 ounces.

Stir very carefully until everything is mixed exactly. Remove from the fire, and at the end add these powders, very finely ground:

Take:
Saffron of Mars <note>original: "Croci Martis." A chemical term for iron oxide, used for its drying and strengthening properties.</note>.
Transmarine Mummy <note>original: "Mumiæ transmarinæ." Historically, this referred to powdered remains or bitumen, believed to have profound healing effects on wounds.</note>.
Prepared Magnet <note>original: "Magnetis præparati." Powdered lodestone or magnetite.</note>.

### Powers and Use.

*Its virtues are almost innumerable.*

1. On the external parts of the body, it suddenly removes all <margin>f</margin> ulcers <note>original: "ulcera"</note>: let them be washed morning and evening, and let a wet linen cloth be placed over them.
2. It removes all <margin>g</margin> discharges <note>original: "defluxiones." In historical medicine, this referred to the flow of "bad humors" or fluids to a specific part of the body.</note>, cleanses, and strengthens the affected part.
3. It dries wounds and old <margin>h</note> Aphrodisiac ulcers <note>original: "ulcera Aphrodisia," a historical term for sores caused by venereal diseases such as syphilis.</note>, if a soaked cloth is applied.
4. It strengthens the teeth and preserves the gums from rot.
5. It quenches tears of the eyes, removes redness and eye pains, and [clears] dimness of sight <note>original: "caliginem"</note>, if the outer corners of the eyes are moistened with a wet feather.

If we use it in Ophthalmia <term>Ophthalmia|A general historical term for severe inflammation of the eye or conjunctivitis.</term>, it can be dissolved in water of Roses, or of Eyebright <note>original: "Euphrasiæ," a plant traditionally used for eye ailments.</note> or of Vervain <note>original: "Verbenæ"</note>: Vervain should be gathered in June and July before sunrise, and after being digested with wine for a month, let it then be distilled.

6. It removes the "Sacred Fire" <note>original: "Ignem sacrum," a common name for various skin inflammations, often St. Anthony's Fire.</note> or Erysipelas <term>Erysipelas|A bacterial skin infection characterized by a bright red, swollen, and painful rash.</term>; a wet linen cloth should be applied, and when it becomes dry, let it be moistened again; within the space of 24 hours, it will depart; and if there are holes [sores], let them be washed out with this water.

<margin>a</margin> To **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who revolutionized medicine with chemical remedies</note>, *Sperniola* is **frog-spawn** <note>original: sperma ranarū</note>, which is found here and there around marshy lakes and ponds at the beginning of spring. From this, later, by the benefit of the Sun, frogs are hatched <note>original: excoquuntur, literally "cooked out" or "matured"</note> into living animals. However, for medicine, it must be collected in the month of March, specifically three or four days before the **New Moon** <note>original: Nouilunium</note>, and then put to use. Skilled surgeons soak strips of cloth <note>original: lacinias</note> in it while raw, and dry them in turn, repeating this often. They use these later to remove any inflammation of wounds; indeed, if plasters are spread over these same cloths, they retain those effects wonderfully. In **Erysipelas** <term>Erysipelas: a bacterial skin infection causing painful, red, and swollen patches; historically called "St. Anthony's Fire"</term> of the feet or hands, or of another external limb, which recurs often, nothing is more useful than if such a dry cloth, prepared with raw frog-spawn, is applied to the affected area and the limb wrapped. In the shins or legs, **Erysipelas** easily yields if skillfully made leggings <note>original: tibialia</note> are fashioned from linens. These should be soaked seven times or even more with the same frog-spawn, and as it were worked thoroughly <note>original: conquassentur</note> with it, and dried again. These can certainly last for many years, provided they are not wiped or cleaned with other water. From their use, **Erysipelas** does not return so easily, nor is it driven away with such difficulty, but rather from the very beginning of the application, both the pain and the swelling with redness depart.

### COSMETIC FROM THE GALLS
### Of Bulls.

Take the galls of bulls; let them be dried gently in the sun. Afterward, pour on **spirit of wine** <term>spiritum vini: high-proof distilled alcohol used as a solvent</term>, and let a tincture be drawn out which is somewhat red. Smear the face with this here and there, and leave it for three or four days, provided that they do not leave the house or expose themselves to the open air. When this time has passed, let the face be washed frequently with water made from **bean flowers**, or **water-lily**, or **Solomon's seal** <note>original: polyginati; a plant commonly used in early modern beauty waters to remove freckles</note>, or from **bran**, although the face can also be cleansed with these same waters before the application. In this way, it restores a most pleasing **whiteness** <gloss>albedo</gloss> to a miraculous degree, and makes the skin of the face and neck most tender and lovely. The noblewomen of Spain, as well as those of England, employ some cosmetics in the summer time, and others in the **winter** <note>original: hyberno; the catchword for the next page</note>.

After the cheeks have been tinted with a little bit of this according to one's desire, afterward smear other whitening cosmetics over it.

In the same way, certainly, the ebb and flow <note>original: *fluxum & refluxum*; the tides.</note> of the sea would have to be asserted as something magical, since its cause was and still is unknown to many. The same must be concluded about infinite other things. Surely many things lie hidden in the abysses of nature, and scarcely the smallest part is perceived by us; as for the rest, even a late posterity will hardly attend to it. Thus, because the "why" <note>original: *τὸ διότι* (*to dioti*); the underlying cause or reasoned explanation.</note> is unknown to us, the "fact that it is" <note>original: *τὸ ὅτι* (*to hoti*); the observable phenomenon.</note> should not therefore be rejected or proclaimed as magic. 4. ### A UNIQUE ANTIDOTE.
<note>original: *Alexipharmacum Singulare*. An "alexipharmic" is a medicinal herb or preparation used as an antidote against poison or infection.</note>

Take <term>℞</term> Camphor, for example, 1 and a half ounces <term>℥ j ß</term>. Oil of sweet almonds or spirit of Turpentine—or what is best and most precious of all, oil of Cloves—3 ounces <term>℥ iij</term>. Salt of wormwood <note>original: *Salis absinthij*; a salt derived from the ashes of the wormwood plant, often used in early chemistry as a purifying agent.</note> 2 and a half ounces <term>℥ ij ß</term>. First, grind the camphor as finely as possible, and then gradually grind it while soaking it with the oil until it becomes exactly like a pulp; finally, add the salt of wormwood and grind for some time longer, specifically until all the ingredients have been thoroughly mixed down to their smallest particles. 

Distill these in a retort <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids.</note> with a very short neck using a dry bath <note>original: *Balneo sicco*; likely a sand bath, which provides even, indirect heat.</note> enclosed within a reverberatory furnace <note>A furnace that reflects heat back onto the vessel.</note>. Distill into a receiver that is not too large, but short, using heat levels that are slow at first and then increased—though not entirely at full strength—until the oil itself comes forth. With it, the camphor will emerge in a thick and buttery form, accompanied by many white spirits coming out all at once. 

At the end, to ensure that it does not take on a burnt smell <note>original: *empyreuma*; the scorched taste or smell resulting from overheating organic matter.</note>—especially if almond oil was used (though this is less of a concern with the other oils)—the receiver must be removed with the oil that has already come over. Finally, the heat should be increased so that the salt of wormwood remaining in the retort may be thoroughly cleansed of its foul odor and calcined <note>Reduced to a powdery white ash by high heat.</note>, with the small retort eventually becoming red-hot in the intense fire. Afterward, grind that same salt of wormwood and, having poured over it all that oil which came forth in the first distillation, distill it again from another small retort in the same manner as before, until all the oil is drawn out clearer than it was at first. Calcine the salt again to remove the same foul odor...

## *Excellent DIAPHORETIC PRECIPITATE.*

First of all, let a spirit of nitre <note>original: "spiritus Nitri"; essentially nitric acid.</note> be made, as taught in the *Chemical Primer* <note>original: "Tyrocinium chymicum"; referring to Jean Beguin’s famous 1610 textbook.</note> Book 2, Chapter 4. Mix them, and immediately from a suitable retort <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation.</note>—which has already been joined to its receiver—let a very red water be distilled in a closed reverberatory furnace <term>reverberio</term>. Save this water. Then, take the reddest native Hungarian cinnabar <term>cinnabarim</term> <note>The bright red primary ore of mercury.</note>, which is the mineral of mercury or quicksilver <term>argenti vivi</term>, well-cleansed from mountain dross. Take as much as you wish and dissolve it little by little in the preceding water. Above all, see that you proceed cautiously: for they heat up violently together. Therefore, the ore must be cast in bit by bit; moreover, for its total dissolution—which turns a remarkable green—a sufficiently large quantity of the solvent <term>menstrui</term> <note>In alchemy, a "menstruum" is a solvent capable of dissolving a particular solid.</note> is required. Decant the clear solution (pouring it off from the combustible sulfur which either floats on the solution or resides at the bottom) and distill it from a gourd-shaped vessel <term>cucurbita</term> in a sand bath.

At first, the solvent comes forth, while the principles of the ore itself remain at the bottom—now indeed broken down because of this dissolution and the removal of the solvent, but needing to be separated hereafter. Therefore, after all the solvent has already been separated, increase the fire somewhat more strongly: and to the sides or neck <term>spondiola</term> of the vessel, a very white sublimated mercury will rise. At the bottom of the retort, however, the sulfur and the salt from the added substance will remain together. Therefore, break open the vessel—namely, the gourd—and [take] the mercury separately, nor...

->CHEMISTRY<-

...mixed with the other principles, so that you may have these same separated from it. Collect the common sublimate <term>sublimatum</term> <note>original: "Sublimatum"; likely mercuric chloride produced by the reaction described on the previous page.</note> carefully, and dissolve it with distilled vinegar in a cucurbit <note>A gourd-shaped glass or ceramic vessel used for heating and distillation.</note> by boiling over a sand bath <term>igne arenae</term> <note>Heating a vessel in a bed of sand ensures even, gentle temperature distribution, preventing the glass from cracking over a direct flame.</note>. Remove the dregs; draw off the clear vinegar to dryness, though it still contains the Mercury within it. Dissolve what remains again by boiling with rain water or May dew <term>rore majali</term> <note>Fresh dew collected in May was considered a particularly pure and potent solvent in early modern chemistry and alchemy.</note>. Discarding the dregs, distill the water until a somewhat blackish mass <term>magma</term> remains. Dissolve this same mass again by boiling with fresh distilled rain water, and after discarding the dregs, distill it. Repeat this a third and fourth time, until indeed the Mercury remains perfectly white after the fourth distillation. Finally, pour onto this excellent alcohol of wine <term>alcohol vini</term> <note>Highly rectified ethanol.</note> and digest it in a water bath <term>Balneo</term> with a blind alembic <term>alembico caeco</term> <note>A distillation head without a spout or "beak," used to circulate vapors back into the liquid (refluxing) rather than collecting them.</note> for several weeks, or even for an entire month.

In the meantime, separate and clarify the remaining principles that remained at the bottom of the cucurbit after the Mercury was removed, which you will obtain in this manner. Pour hot distilled rain water over them: immediately the salt <term>sal</term> will move into the water as it dissolves, while the yellowish sulfur <term>sulphur</term> <note>In this context, "Sulfur" refers to the oily or combustible principle of the mineral, not necessarily elemental sulfur.</note> remains alone. If any salt still adheres to it, it must be removed through several repeated washings with distilled rain water and mixed with the previous salt extraction. Both of these must then be purified, which is also to be accomplished solely by using the spirit of wine. Therefore, remove the distilled water from the salt—namely, the water you used to extract the salt—and dissolve the salt itself with the best spirit of wine. Once the dregs are removed, the resulting solution will be yellowish-green. Draw off the spirit of wine until a film <term>cuticulam</term> forms on the surface, and the salt itself, like transparent vitriol <term>Vitrioli</term> <note>original: "Vitrioli"; here referring to the glass-like crystalline appearance of the purified salt, resembling metal sulfates.</note>, [will be found] in the bottom...

...will be coagulated; collect this carefully and save it. But the **Sulfur** <term>Sulphur</term> <note>In the Paracelsian tradition, Sulfur represents the "soul" or the principle of inflammability and growth in a substance.</note>, having been previously washed several times with hot distilled water and dried, digest in the same way with **spirit of wine** <term>spiritu vini</term> <note>Highly concentrated ethanol.</note> for some time, and then remove the spirit. In this way, the two purified principles of **Salt** and **Sulfur** are ready; the **Mercury** <term>Mercurius</term> <note>The third principle, representing the "spirit" or the principle of fluidity and transformation.</note> must also be brought to the same purity. Leave everything after the distillation is finished, and after 24 hours, the crystallized spirit of Mercury will be dissolved in the spirit of wine that was first distilled; this must again be separated from the spirit of wine, which you should do by a gentle **water bath** <term>Balneum lene</term>. For the spirit of wine rises, and leaves the spirit of mercury at the bottom, ash-colored, which you should also save. Having obtained all these principles, you must finally proceed to their **equal conjunction** <term>coniunctionem anaticam</term> <note>original: "anaticam," from the Greek "ana," meaning "in equal parts." A balanced recombination of the separated elements.</note>; resolve it in this way. First, a "conjunctive water" of all things should be made from the same ore in this manner. Dissolve 6 ounces of **Hungarian mercury ore** <term>argenti viui Vngarici</term> <note>Cinnabar (mercury sulfide) from Hungarian mines, highly prized for its purity.</note> in a **solvent water** <term>aqua soluente</term> made primarily from **niter** <term>nitro</term> <note>Saltpeter or potassium nitrate.</note> and **rock salt** <term>sale gemmae</term>; after setting aside the dregs, distill the solution in a gentle bath until it reaches an oily thickness. Pour on fresh solvent water and distill again to oiliness; do this 5 or 6 times. Afterward, place it in a **Bain-Marie** <term>Balneo Mariae</term> in a closed vessel to putrefy for 14 days; finally, distill it over a gentle sand fire until any excess water is separated. # CHYMICA.

...[when they] have come forth, change the receiving vessel, and by attaching another and carefully sealing it with **lute** <term>lutando</term> <note>Lute was a paste, often made of clay, lime, or even dung, used to seal the joints of chemical apparatus to prevent the escape of vapors.</note>, capture them. Together with the water that comes out afterward, push the distillation until the vessel reaches **ignition** <note>The point at which the glass or ceramic vessel begins to glow red from the heat of the furnace.</note>; save this liquid. In 6 ounces of this, dissolve 2 ounces of the **salt** previously prepared and **circulate** <note>A process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel, intended to "ripen" or refine a substance through repeated cycles.</note> it for some time in a **water bath** <term>Balneo</term>. Afterward, pour 1.5 ounces of this water (in which the salt has been dissolved and digested) over half an ounce of **sulfur**. In turn, using a gentle water bath, separate the liquid until it reaches a certain thickness. Again, pour the previous quantity of the same water—namely 1.5 ounces—and draw it off by distilling in a water bath. Proceed in this way until one full ounce of the salt has been joined with the half-ounce of sulfur; you will know this by the weight, when a single viscous liquid has been formed from both. To half an ounce of this, add 2 ounces of the **spirit of Mercury** prepared above. In a vial closed with a **Hermetic seal** <note>An airtight seal made by melting the glass neck of a flask shut.</note>, cook it in an **Athanor** <term>Athanore</term> <note>A "painless" furnace designed to maintain a constant, steady heat over a long period without constant supervision.</note>, carefully applying the degrees of fire until everything has been turned into a **red powder** <term>pulverem rubicundum</term>. This will occur over the space of three or four months. Keep the powder prepared in this way, having finally been corrected with **alcohol of wine** <term>alcohole vini</term> <note>A highly rectified spirit or ethanol.</note>. This is a **universal medicine** <term>medicina universalis</term> <note>A "Panacea" or cure-all, believed in alchemy to be capable of healing any ailment by restoring the body's natural balance.</note>, of which one grain, or at most two, administered in suitable **vehicles** <note>A "vehicle" is a neutral substance (like wine, water, or broth) used to deliver the medicine to the patient.</note> for any disease, wonderfully assists the **internal balsam** <note>The body's innate healing power or life force, often called the "Archaeus" in Paracelsian medicine.</note> to expel the enemy dwelling within—whether through vomiting, through the bowels, or through sweat.

->*Blessed be the name of the Lord.*<-

# EPILOGUE.

Let the arrogant **boasters** <note>original: "Thrasones," a reference to Thraso, a stereotypical "braggart soldier" character from Roman comedy.</note> of the **Academies** now cease for the future; those revilers of **Chemical Medicines** who, decreeing from their high majesty with threats and violent rebukes, have until now foolishly mocked, condemned, and heaped a thousand insults upon the faithful **Truth** and divine science of our forefathers. Let them cease, I say, to brand the disciples of **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy and the "Hermetic" arts.</note> with the marks of infamy, envy, ignorance, and fraud. Let them no longer demand visible demonstrations and manifest methods of operations while using their own unusual and new ways of learning to imperiously demand **Spagyric** <term>Spagyrica</term> <note>The alchemical process of separating substances into their primary elements and then recombining them in a purified state.</note> secrets from the "**charcoal-burners**" <note>original: "Carbonariis," a derogatory nickname used by university-trained doctors for alchemists who spent their time laboring at soot-covered furnaces.</note>—as they call these physicians. These are the secrets which, through the inspiration of divine Virtue, I have on this occasion sincerely communicated from a full storehouse for the benefit of the **public** <term>Reipublicae</term>.

In the meantime, I ask this one thing with the most fervent prayers from the most sharp Avenger of all Falsehood and injustice: that all who—with an ardent invocation for the help of **Almighty GOD**, and with a grateful heart—shall use <note>The text here ends on the catchword "utentur" (they will use), which continues the sentence onto the next page.</note> these things rightly prepared for the praise and glory of the Creator, for the sincere benefit of their needy neighbor, and for the restoration of the due **Honor** of the **chemical art** which has been undeservedly cried out against—

But for those unworthy mockers, and those who secretly use these gifts of God while feigning contempt—as it is manifest that many idle **Galenists** <note>Traditional physicians who followed the ancient teachings of Galen and often opposed the "new" chemical medicines of Paracelsus and his followers.</note> have done until now, hunting for praise and esteem for themselves from the labors of others—and who, with internal treachery, will not cease to harass the Spagyric benefactors by word or deed, let all things turn out the opposite for them.

That this may be firm and established, may that Most Holy **TRINITY** grant it—the Trinity which gave me the will and ability to consecrate to the memory of perpetual posterity these **Chemical** labors, and these Spagyric grains winnowed from the chaff, which were examined most deeply and most frequently, and not without the greatest study. And let the whole **Spagyric Senate and People** <note>original: "Senatus Populuſq; Spagyricus," a play on the famous Roman "SPQR" (The Senate and People of Rome), suggesting that alchemists form their own noble civilization.</note> say with me from the bottom of their hearts: **Amen**.

# TO THE READER.

The following Series of Chemical Preparations <note>original: "Series Præparationum Chymicarum"</note> seemed so convenient to me—since from it whatever is notable in the preceding book can easily be extracted—that, along with the German editor, I did not hesitate to deliver to you the **Chemical Basilica** <note>original: "Basilica Chymica," the title of Oswald Croll's influential alchemical textbook, first published in 1609.</note> with its notes in this more convenient format, without need for a more extensive index. Farewell.

*P.C. The Printer.* <term>Typographus</term> <note>The Latin term for a printer or publisher.</note>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the dedication (Epistola Nuncupatoria) of the work. The author is addressing Peter Vok of Rosenberg, a major figure in Bohemian history.</meta>

A horizontal woodcut headpiece featuring scrolling foliage and two semi-nude seated human figures flanking a central decorative element. The figures are surrounded by floral motifs and vases of flowers.

# Dedicatory Epistle,

### TO

## The Most Illustrious Prince and Lord,

# PETER VOK ORSINI,
# OF ROSENBERG,

## LORD OF ROSENBERG,

### *Senior and last of the Renowned and Most Ancient House of Rosenberg, the foremost Magnate of the Bohemians, and a most Excellent Patron of all good studies.*

As I reflect, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE, Most Merciful Lord—you who, through your munificent and <term>Alexandrian<note>original: "ALEXANDRINA". A classical allusion to the legendary generosity of Alexander the Great, often used by Renaissance authors to flatter wealthy patrons.</note></term> liberality, have made me a debtor of perpetual gratitude to Your Highness—on what effort of my mind, or what mark of veneration toward Your Highness, along with my devo- <note>The text ends mid-word (deuoti-), likely continuing as "devotion" on the following page.</note>

<summary>This page is the formal opening of a dedication to Peter Vok of Rosenberg, the last male member of the powerful Bohemian Rosenberg family. The author praises the Prince's legendary generosity and patronage of the arts and sciences.</summary>

<keywords>Peter Vok of Rosenberg, House of Rosenberg, Bohemia, patronage, dedication, Orsini family, Alexandrian liberality</keywords>

--- Page 730 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Peter Vok of Rosenberg. The text completes the sentence from the previous page, shifting from the author's humility to a description of the book being offered as a "botanical garden."</meta>

->E P I S T O L A<-

—the most devoted respect of my soul, I might at least declare some attempt at gratitude as a testament to the beneficence you have shown toward me. It was my intention to adorn Your Highness (who is most worthy of the most beautiful and greatest things) with some beautiful and great gift. But things of gold or silver, radiant with gems and pearls (which Your Highness possesses in abundance by the good pleasure of God), have been denied to me and men of my station by Fortune.

I offer, therefore, another gift: a botanical one, namely a "Garden" furnished with the most beautiful <term>simples<note>original: "simplicibus". In early modern medicine, 'simples' were individual medicinal herbs or plants used as remedies in their natural state, as opposed to 'compounds' which were complex mixtures.</note></term>. This work is written and decorated to exhibit and represent, as a most delightful spectacle, the wonderful <term>Harmonic Correspondence<note>original: "Harmonicam Correspondentiam". This reflects the Renaissance belief that the universe (macrocosm) and the human body (microcosm) are perfectly synchronized through divine design.</note></term> between the <term>Innate Signatures<note>original: "Innata Signatura". This refers to the "Doctrine of Signatures," the historical theory that God marked plants with physical signs—like a shape resembling a human organ—to indicate their medicinal purpose.</note></term> of plants and the members of our own bodies.

For since among all the **GOODS** bestowed by **GOD**, the Best and Greatest, upon needy mortals—by the testimony of Orpheus himself, of Plato, and of all the Ancients—there is scarcely anything more noble than Medicine. ## epigrams on the chemical works

It is no small matter to know the powers and mysteries of things,

But you, Croll, provide something greater, while you offer chemical
Remedies, <term>Pharmaca</term> <note>original: "Pharmaca." In this context, it refers specifically to "chymical" or alchemical medicines prepared through distillation and purification, as opposed to raw herbal mixtures.</note> which certain Reason teaches are sufficient.

Proceed, glory of True medicine, proceed in your desire

### *Another by the same author.*

It is a work of great Art, if one knows the inner secrets of things,
And from there has applied healing hands.
But it is a work of greater Art to be able to teach the medicines
Which reason and Eye-witnessed Faith <note>original: "Fides... oculata." A common Renaissance expression meaning "the faith of one's own eyes," emphasizing empirical observation over mere hearsay or ancient authority.</note> themselves provide.
Since you have performed these things, Croll, your Glory is just.

# ON SIGNATURES, OR
# THE TRUE AND LIVING ANATOMY
### of the Macrocosm and the Microcosm,
<note>original: "maioris & minoris Mundi." These terms refer to the Great World (the universe) and the Small World (mankind), a central concept in Hermetic philosophy suggesting that the same patterns exist in both.</note>

## PREFACE TO THE READER BY 
## OSWALD CROLL, PHYSICIAN
## *and Hermetic Philosopher.*
<note>A "Hermetic Philosopher" was a scholar-practitioner who followed the teachings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, focusing on the spiritual and chemical links between nature, divinity, and humanity.</note>

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'V' decorated with intricate scrolling vines and floral patterns.</image-desc>

I wish that the Botanists of our time—who, being ignorant of the internal form, know only the matter, substance, and body of Herbs—would apply as much diligent care in recognizing the Signatures <term>Signaturis</term> <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" is the belief that God marked every plant with a physical sign—such as shape or color—that reveals its medicinal use. For example, a heart-shaped leaf might treat heart disease.</note> of Plants as they do in their accurate and often frivolous disputes over various names. If they did so, a far more abundant and fruitful benefit would overflow into the Medical Commonwealth. However, since most (as is usually the case in almost all arts) have abandoned the sweet and pitted kernel <note>original: "emedullato... nucleo," literally the "un-marrowed" or deseeded kernel; here meaning the inner essence.</note> of the Sciences, they are like commoners lacking "internal eyes." They consider only the external face of Things and are occupied only with the outer bitter husk. Thus it happens that many "Namers" of herbs are found, but they are merely like innkeepers who know only the dwellings, habitations, and external garments of Plants (in which the medicinal powers, as if in homes, are hosted...)

<meta>catchword: hosted</meta>

<summary>Oswald Croll begins his preface by critiquing contemporary botanists for focusing on naming plants rather than understanding their divine "Signatures." He argues that the true "anatomy" of nature requires looking past the physical exterior to find the hidden medicinal powers placed there by the Creator.</summary>

<header>ON SIGNATURES.</header>

<margin>
The place where God is said to have stood, and from the sign, God Himself or His essence is known: for all creatures demonstrate God as if present through their own properties.

## OF THE HEAD.

### I.

The **POPPY** with its crown <note>original: "cum corona"; likely referring to the disk-shaped stigma at the top of the seed pod</note> **represents the Head and Brain**; for this reason, its <term>decoction</term> <note>a medicinal liquid made by boiling down plant materials</note> is usefully administered for many ailments of the Head.

2. **Walnuts** possess the complete **signature** <note>original: "signaturam"; the theory that the physical appearance of a plant indicates its medicinal use</note> of the Head: The **outer husk**, or the green covering, represents the **Pericranium** <note>the membrane that covers the outer surface of the skull</note>; for this reason, the salt of the husks is extraordinary for wounds of the pericranium.

The **harder inner husk**, or the woody shell, represents the **Skull**.

The **thin skin** surrounding the kernel represents the **Meninges** <note>the three membranes that line the skull and enclose the brain</note> and the membranes of the brain.

### OF THE HEART.

1. *The* **Citron** <note>original: "Citrium"; likely the large, thick-skinned citrus fruit used in early medicine</note> *represents the* **Heart** <note>original: "Cor"</note> *by the likeness of its fruit.*
2. *The two roots of* **Yellow Monkshood** <note>original: "Anthoræ"</note> *show, as it were, little hearts.*
3. **Wood Sorrel** <note>original: "Alleluya"</note> *produces leaves in the shape of a Heart at the top of its little stalks.* <note>Wood sorrel was called "Alleluya" because it often flowers between Easter and Pentecost, the season of singing Alleluia.</note>
4. **Lemon Balm** <note>original: "Meliffophyllon"</note> *bears a leaf in the appearance of a Heart.*
5. **Motherwort** <note>original: "Cardiaca"</note> *or* **Molucca Balm** <note>original: "Molucca"</note> *produces leaves like those of lemon balm.*
6. **Nard** <note>original: "Nardus"</note>, **Myrobalan** <note>original: "Myrobalanum"</note>, **Quince** <note>original: "Mala Cydonia"</note>.
*The virtues of all these are exceptional for the Heart.*

### OF THE LUNGS.

1. **Lungwort** <note>original: "Pulmonaria"</note> *clings to both rocks and trees.* <note>This likely refers to the lichen Lobaria pulmonaria, which resembles lung tissue.</note>
2. *Certain species of* **Lungwort** *reflect the whitish spots of the* **Lung**: *therefore, a decoction of all of them is beneficial in various conditions of the Lungs.*

### OF THE BREASTS.

*The "eyes" of* **Peacock Feathers**: <note>original: "Specula Pennarum Pauonis"; the circular patterns on the feathers were thought to resemble the anatomy of the breast or nipple.</note>

## OF THE MATRIX AND THE WOMB.

1. The **True Round Birthwort** <note>original: *Aristolochia rotunda vera*</note> mimics the form of the female womb and provides the best help to women in childbirth <note>the name "Aristolochia" comes from the Greek for "excellent birth"</note>.

2. **Peas** <note>original: *Pisa*</note>.

3. The inner bark of the **Green Birch** <note>original: *Betula viridis*</note> has the signature of the womb with its small blood vessels; therefore, a decoction of it cleanses the womb.

4. **Savin Juniper** <note>original: *Sabina*</note> has the signature of the veins of the womb; therefore, it dissolves <term>Tartar</term> <note>in early modern medicine, "Tartar" referred to stony or inflammatory deposits caused by metabolic imbalances</note> within the female veins.

5. The **Pomegranate** <note>original: *Malum Granatum* or *Punicum*</note> is smooth and covered by a membrane called the <term>malicorium</term> <note>pomegranate rind</note>. The husk gapes open in the sun and is opened by even the slightest injury or breeze; in the same way, an infant at the time of maturity prepares its exit from the womb.

6. **Cyclamen** <note>original: *Cyclaminus*</note>, with its rounded root bulb, skillfully demonstrates the shape of the female uterus. Theophrastus stated that its bulb is effective for matters of love <note>often used as an aphrodisiac or to induce labor</note>.

7. **Lion’s Leaf** <note>original: *Leontopetalon*</note> has a root that, in its appearance and resemblance, skillfully demonstrates the female pubes with its downy and soft tuft. Dioscorides records that when worn as an amulet, it is effective for matters of love.

### ANAL PILES

*Greater and Lesser Figwort <note>original: *Scrofularia maior & minor*</note> possess the complete signature <note>The knobby roots of the figwort were thought to resemble hemorrhoids or "piles."</note>: therefore, a decoction is not only drunk effectively to wear away piles or tumors <note>original: *ficubus mariscisve*</note>, but it is also virtuously hung around the neck as an amulet, reaching down toward the orifice of the stomach.*

### FISTULAS

*Water Rushes <note>original: *Iunci Aquatici*</note> possess the signature <note>Being hollow and tube-like, these plants were seen as natural matches for fistulas—abnormal tube-like passages in the body.</note>: therefore, the salt skillfully extracted from them is offered as a helpful treatment both inside and outside the body.*

*The Rampion plant of Carrichter <note>original: *Rapunculus Herba Carrichteri*. Referring to Bartholomew Carrichter, a 16th-century physician and astrologer to Emperor Maximilian II.</note> with its blue flower has the same signature and efficacy.*

### THE FETUS IN THE WOMB

*The Eagle Stone <note>original: *Aetites Lapis*. This is a geode or hollow stone containing a smaller loose stone or pebble inside.</note> is as if pregnant, for when it is shaken, another stone rattles inside its "womb." It sustains the pregnancy for women when the womb is not secure enough <note>original: *parum tenax*</note>; it is bound to the woman's left arm until the hour of birth approaches. Then, it is placed upon the left hip so that she may give birth happily, without labor or danger. After the fetus is delivered, the stone must be removed immediately, lest the womb itself follow after <note>There was a historical medical fear of uterine prolapse, which people believed could be caused by the stone's "attractive" power if left in place too long.</note>.*

## FETUSES ATTACHED TO THE WOMB.

*The seeds of Linden blossoms <note>original: *Grana Florum Tiliae*</note> are beneficial because of their similarity, as they grow halfway attached to the leaf upon their stalk <note>This "attachment" of the seed to the leaf bract was seen as a signature for the placenta or a fetus attached to the uterine wall</note>. Five or six of these seeds are given at one time to infants born with physical attachments <note>Likely referring to birthmarks or remnants of the umbilical cord</note>, or even to a pregnant woman whose fetus is abnormally attached: They are collected on the feast of the Decapitation of St. John [August 29th], and the outer husk is discarded.*

## ENCHANTMENTS.

*Any herbs which grow through a crack or a hole in a rock, or through any stone, are beneficial <note>The plant’s ability to "break through" a hard constriction was believed to magically help a person "break" the binding power of a spell or the "evil eye"</note>.*

## ON HEMORRHOIDS.

All *shaggy plants* and *soft, woolly leaves* that are graying with a downy fluff are beneficial through <term>sympathy: the occult connection between things of a similar nature or appearance</term> for *Hemorrhoids*, which shrink from a rough touch.

1. Leaves of Mullein <note>original: *Verbascum*</note>, which are clothed in a white and dense down and a cottony padding; a decoction of this is beneficial.
2. The buds <note>original: *Oculi*, literally "eyes"</note> of the Poplar tree, soaked in olive oil and exposed to the sun, are wonderfully useful; the seed clearly represents the appearance of the buttocks <note>original: *nates*</note>.
3. The Hare’s Foot herb <note>original: *Pes Leporis*; likely *Trifolium arvense*</note> is also woolly, and its decoction is useful.
4. Figwort <note>original: *Scrophularia*</note>, which swarms with little nodules and nipple-like heads.
5. Small Arum <note>original: *Aron Minus*; also known as Cuckoo-pint or Lords-and-Ladies</note> soothes both the tonsils and hemorrhoids.
6. Among the names for Mullein is "Wolf’s Tail" <note>original: *Lupina Cauda*</note>, named for the soft, woolly hair which it mimics; its decoction is also profitable.

## ON DROPSY.

<note>original: *Hydropis*; a historical term for edema or the swelling of soft tissues due to the accumulation of excess water</note>

1. Bryony root <note>original: *Radix Bryoniæ*</note> possesses the signature of the feet of those suffering from dropsy; therefore, an extract of it draws out the waters.
2. Mechoacan root <note>original: *Radix Michoacæ*; a root from the New World (Mexico) known for its purgative effects</note>.
3. Toothwort <note>original: *Dentaria*</note> or the *Aneblattum* of Cordus <note>referring to a plant described by the botanist Valerius Cordus, likely the Toothwort *Lathraea squamaria*</note> also carries the signature of dropsical swelling.

## ON WITHERED LIMBS.

The **willow** <term>Salix: a tree known for its remarkable ability to grow from cuttings</term> does not bear seed, but a cut branch—even one that is almost withered—will grow simply by being thrust into the earth. For this reason, a bath made from a decoction of willow is most excellent for withered or wasting limbs <note>The willow's ability to "return to life" from a dead-looking stick was seen as a sign it could revitalize dying human tissue</note>.

## ON SPOTS.

1. **Garlic** <note>original: *Allium*</note>.
2. **Cuckoo-pint** and **Friar's Cowl** <note>original: *Arum* and *Arisarum*; plants often characterized by spotted leaves or stalks</note>.
3. **Dragon Arum** <note>original: *Dracontium*</note>.
4. **Smartweed** <note>original: *Persicaria*; specifically the species with dark spots on the leaves</note>.
5. **Lesser Celandine** <note>original: *Hirundinaria minor*</note>. *Likewise, all spotted plants clear away the spots and blemishes from our bodies.*

## ON NODES IN THE FLESH.

**Mercury herb** <note>original: *Mercurialis*</note> with its nodes <note>referring to the swollen joints of the plant's stem</note>: therefore, a decoction of it with **Mechoacan root** <term>Mechoica: a root from the New World, used similarly to jalap as a powerful cleanser</term> removes nodes and lumps from the skin.

## ON QUINSY.

1. **Sal ammoniac** <term>Sal Armoniacum: a salt used in alchemy and medicine, often associated with cooling and "cleansing" properties</term>: for this reason, its liquid, distilled with the juice of **houseleek** <note>original: *Aizoi*</note>, is an easily-prepared <term>Euporiston: a Greek term for a remedy made from readily available ingredients</term> medicine. It extracts the "tartaric" <note>Early modern medicine often attributed diseases to "tartar," a stony or crusty buildup in the body</note> sublimated **Realgar** <term>Realgar: typically an arsenic mineral; here used to describe the corrosive, toxic film or "crust" of a severe throat infection</term> that adheres to the throat or neck and turns the tongue black.
2. The flowers of **Self-heal** <term>Prunella: the Latin name for both the plant and the disease "quinsy" (a severe throat infection)</term>, which represent the throat by their very shape, are also highly recommended for this disease.

## SPASMS.
<note>original: *Spasmi*; referring to cramps, convulsions, or involuntary muscle contractions.</note>

1. **Slugs** <note>original: *Limaces*</note> contract themselves when barely disturbed: a tiny little bone found in **white slugs**, when they are cut through the middle, is kept in paper, and is most effectively administered for **Spasms**.

2. The **ham** <note>original: *Poples*; the back of the knee or hock</note> of a **Hare**, an animal most swift in running, is likewise beneficial.

## FOR SCROFULA.
<note>original: *Strumarum*; "Struma" refers to scrofula, a swelling of the lymph nodes (usually in the neck) caused by tuberculosis, or sometimes goiters. In the Doctrine of Signatures, plants with knobby or bulbous roots were believed to treat these swellings.</note>

1. The **Sword-lily** <note>original: *Gladiolus*</note> consists of a jointed root, sitting one above another in the manner of small bulbs—the lower one slender, the upper one more vigorous—it certainly heals **Scrofula**.

2. **Figwort** <note>original: *Scrophularia*</note> has a root roughened with tubercles and gifted with nipple-like heads, with a scrofulous-looking tuft stretching out beneath: it helps in softening **scrofulous ulcers** and tubercles hardened by cold humor.

3. **Figs** <note>original: *Ficus*</note> swell in the manner of a scrofulous tumor; they are effective for the same. <note>In medical Latin, "ficus" also referred to fig-shaped tumors or hemorrhoids.</note>

4. Likewise **Sea Sponges**.

5. The scrofulous root of the **Iris** destroys scrofulous swellings.

6. There is also a small herb called **Lesser Figwort** <note>original: *Scrophularia minor*; likely Lesser Celandine (*Ficaria verna*)</note> with leaves like ivy; it has many small roots hanging by a certain callous skin, gathered together like grains of wheat in a heap, three or four of which stretch out longer. More recent physicians use this with great force and practical experience in removing **scrofulous swellings**, **fig-like tumors**, and **hemorrhoids** <note>original: *mariscis*; fleshy swellings or piles</note>.

# MEDICINES,
## WHICH HELP THROUGH
### SIMILARITY.

*It should also be noted that we have discovered certain medicines benefit through similarity <note>original: "à similitudine"; referring to the principle that "like cures like."</note> and free one from diseases in a marvelous way, because one possesses the "anatomy" <note>In this context, "anatomy" refers to a shared essence or structural correspondence between the remedy and the ailment.</note> of the other: for to what should a thing be more rightly compared than to its own likeness?*

* **Arsenic** <term>Arsenicus</term> relieves **Arsenical ulcers**; among all the "fruits of the water," <note>A Paracelsian term for minerals or substances categorized under the elemental property of water.</note> there is no greater poison than that found in the matter of **Resins**, and all the poisonous nature of **Resins**, as **Paracelsus** confirms, has flowed together into **Arsenic**, as if into a single body.*

* **Monkshood** <term>Aconitum</term> given in warm wine to those bitten by a **Viper** <term>Vipera</term> or **Scorpion** <term>Scorpio</term> has been found to be life-saving by many highly skilled physicians; indeed, poisons are very often "poisons to poisonous things." <note>A reference to the concept that a toxic substance can neutralize the effects of another toxin.</note>*

* The **Deer Truffle** <term>Boletus Cervinus</term> is a fungus which they use for **sexual matters**; <note>Referring to its use as an aphrodisiac or fertility aid.</note> it arises from the genital seed of that animal. <note>Refers to the ancient folklore that these fungi grew where the semen of rutting deer fell to the earth.</note>*

The **skin of a wolf's stomach** <term>Stomachi Lupi Corium</term>, when worn [against the body], aids the digestion of the stomach. In the same way, the skins of the **vulture and the swan** <note>original: "Vulturis & Oloris"; birds known for their strong digestive powers or hardy nature.</note>, when prepared by a tanner, are beneficial.

The foul odor of the **Spirit of Tartar** <term>Spiritus Tartari</term> expels the stench of putrid humors from the human body during the **Plague** <term>Peste</term>.

**Tartar**, or the salt of human urine, is an exceptional remedy against tartar [deposits in the body] and the **stone** <term>Calculum</term>. <note>Like curing like: the "tartar" or crystalline buildup in a vessel was thought to treat similar stone-like buildups in the kidneys or bladder.</note>

The **knotty root of Tormentil** <term>Tormentillæ Radix Nodosa</term>, when crushed and applied, removes knots [lumps or growths] on the skin.

For the **twisting of the intestines** <note>likely referring to "volvulus" or severe cramping.</note> in colic, a dried belt made from a **wolf's intestine** is helpful, as are its excrements when worn.

A decoction of **turnip seeds and lentils** cures **smallpox** <term>Variolis</term> in infants by virtue of similarity. <note>The small, round seeds were thought to resemble the pustules of smallpox.</note>

**Deer and snakes** are not seized by **vertigo** [dizziness] when they navigate trackless and precipitous places; therefore, their fat, if a little of it is smeared on the temples, is a great help against vertigo. So too is the **Fifth Essence of Storks** <term>Ciconiarum Essentia Quinta</term>, since storks are accustomed to circling in the air for a long time [without becoming dizzy].

## POISONOUS DISEASES

* **Aconite** <note>original: "Aconitum"; also known as Monkshood or Wolfsbane, which was previously mentioned as "health-giving" on the prior page in a specific context despite its toxicity.</note>, as has been said, heals the bites of **Vipers and Scorpions**.*

*If the **shrew-mouse** <term>Araneus mus</term> <note>In antiquity and the early modern period, the shrew was often erroneously believed to be a venomous animal whose bite caused paralysis or death in livestock.</note> that inflicted a bite is dissected and applied to the wound, it atones for the harm of its own strike.*

***Honey** heals the embedded **stings of bees**.*

*With the **Toad-stone** <term>Bufonio Lapide</term> found in the head of a toad, the diseases caused by that animal are cured.* <note>The Toad-stone was a mythical gemstone believed to grow inside a toad's skull; it was highly prized as an antidote that would heat up or change color in the presence of poison.</note>

***Toad-powder**, when placed upon a venomous bite, draws out the poison.*

*Those urinated upon by a **toad** soothe themselves with the aid of a **dried toad**.*

*For the bite of a **mad dog** <term>Canis Rabidus</term>, the hairs of that same dog are first applied externally to the wound, since they indeed draw out the venom; likewise, the hairs are burned and given to the patient to drink. Furthermore, the **roasted liver** of the mad dog, if eaten by the person bitten, frees and protects them so that they are not afflicted by the **fear of water** <term>Hydrophobia</term> <note>original: "Aquae metu"; a defining symptom of rabies where the victim cannot swallow liquids.</note>. For this reason, they also bind a **tooth** taken from that same dog—placed in a small piece of skin as an **amulet**—to the person's arm.*

***Crocodile fat** heals its own bites.*

*The burnt **powder of mice** heals the bites of mice.*

*Those who have been urinated upon by **mice** sprinkle on the ashes of those same mice before the discharge eats away at the flesh.*

*The **bone of a stag’s heart** <term>Os Cordis Cerui</term> <note>A bony growth or calcified cartilage often found in the hearts of older stags, historically used as a heart tonic and antidote.</note>... the venomous tail of a stag...*

*Just as the cold is drawn out of an **egg frozen by frost** and restored to its original state by placing it in very cold water for a time—where the cold is pulled out like ice—so too are **limbs damaged by cold** healed by the application of cold **snowy water**: Thus, cold draws out cold.*

*In a similar way, limbs that are heated beyond measure—*

# ON THE INTERNAL NATURE OF THINGS

## Powerful Men Impatient of Partners, struggling for Dominance:

## The Mutual Love of Praiseworthy Marriage:

Compared to **Wood-pigeons**, which are the most chaste among birds. Male and female, as if bound by the bonds of marriage, remain attached to one another by such a stable and mutual consent, and in a certain union through the highest purity, that neither ever touches the bed <note>original: *cubile*, referring here to the nest as a "marital bed."</note> of another. If, captured by a shameless love, they cast their eyes upon another's spouse, the remaining birds sitting around them tear them to pieces—and the females likewise tear apart the females, as Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus (c. 175 – c. 235 AD), a Roman author whose natural history writings were frequently used to provide moral examples for human behavior.</note> testifies. 

In a similar way, the same author relates that **Doves** do not permit themselves to mate with the wives of others, nor do they desert a marriage entered into from their very first youth, unless they are unmated or widowed. They are most chaste regarding adultery; for never is the male separated from the partnership established between them, unless by death itself, nor is the female dissociated, unless she has been widowed. At the birth <note>original: *partu*, here referring to the laying and hatching of eggs.</note> the male is present, and performs every duty and care. 

If the female goes too slowly to the nest, the male strikes her with his wings and forces her to enter. When she has laid the eggs, he compels her to sit upon them, and both sit in turn—the male by day, and the female by night. If the husband should die, the female, abstaining from all food and drink, mourns for a long time and [herself...] <note>The sentence ends abruptly at the bottom of the page.</note>

# ON INTERNAL MATTERS
<note>original: *INTERNIS RERVM*</note>

...they brood over [the eggs] and hatch chicks, and during that time they maintain silence, for they are truly conscious that they are performing a woman's duty. Furthermore, they fight for females just as stags do, and they destroy one another with mutual wounds and the danger of death.

| **The Human Art** | **Learned From...** |
|---|---|

They keep watch during the night, holding a small stone in their foot... <note>According to ancient natural history (like Pliny the Elder), a crane acting as a sentry would hold a stone in its raised claw; if the bird fell asleep, the stone would drop and wake it up.</note>

# ON SIGNATURES
<note>original: *DE SIGNATURIS* — In this context, "signatures" refers to the theory that the outward appearance or behavior of a living thing reveals its inner purpose or medicinal use.</note>

*...who, if loosened by sleep and falling, would prove their negligence:* <note>This refers to the ancient belief that a crane acting as a sentry would hold a stone in one claw; if it fell asleep, the stone would drop and wake it up.</note> *They choose a **Leader**, who cries out while the flocks sleep; when they fly, they have others positioned in turn at the rear of the line to call out and keep the flock together with their voice. When they descend to the earth, the Leader cries out loudly so that all may gather and feed together; but if he grows hoarse from too much shouting, another is substituted. When they travel, because of the sharpness of their senses, they form a **Triangle** so that they may more easily cut through the air ahead; then, gradually on each side, they lift the course of their wings like oars. If the sky rages and the wind arises, they do not fly head-on (whereas they fly in a crescent-shaped formation when it is calm), but instantly shift into a wedge. If they see themselves attacked by an **Eagle**, they stand in a circle, and curved as if drawn up in a battle line, they show the appearance of a fight, so the Eagle retreats. In flight, by resting their necks on the backs of those flying ahead (which even **Stags** do when swimming across rivers), they make the work easy, and the one who tires in the front moves to become the last. When they stop, the others sleep; the Leader, staying awake, signals with his voice whatever he has sensed. In a similar way, the **Goose** performs nightly **Sentry-duty**, and continually testifies to its watchfulness with its song.*

Furthermore, consider what signature of our first Parent <note>Referring to Adam, often linked to the cultivation of wheat in medieval lore</note> is found in **Wheat**; what mysteries of the **Virgin Mother of God** <note>original: *DEiparæ Virginis*</note> are in the artificial grafting of the **Vine**; the signature of the **double-headed Eagle** and other mysteries found in the **Fern**, if it is cut with artful skill <note>It was a common folklore belief that cutting a fern root or stalk transversely would reveal a pattern resembling an eagle</note>; and what signatures exist in the **Sword Lily** <note>original: *Gladiolus*</note>, the **Thunder-stones** <note>original: *Tonitru Cunei*; prehistoric stone tools like axe heads were historically believed to be "ceraunia" or stones that fell from the sky during lightning strikes</note>, and both types of the **Root of Victory** <note>original: *Victorialis Radix*; likely *Allium victorialis*, a mountain leek whose layered bulb was worn by miners and soldiers as a protective amulet</note>—which is entangled in many layers and must be gathered at a time aligned with the stars—as well as the **Cross-wort** <note>original: *Herbæ Cruciatæ*</note>. These are natural magical signs against the force of striking weapons, to be revealed only to the students and initiates of true Magic.

Let it suffice for this time to have given these hints, lest by chance we provide material for scorn to argumentative **Sophists** <note>In this context, "Sophists" refers to academic critics who use clever but fallacious reasoning to dismiss new or "hermetic" ideas</note>, or give an opening to wicked men for devising evil deeds; otherwise, we might have served those minds very eager to learn of wondrous things with a fuller offering. When I have first observed with what attitude these things are received, it may incite me toward further publication:

**First**, regarding **Magnetic**, **Magical**, and **Character-based Cures** <note>Medicinal practices involving the hidden "sympathy" between objects, or the use of written symbols/characters believed to hold spiritual power</note>.

**Second**, at what proper time of the **Constellation** the majority of medicinal plants ought to be collected.

**Third**, concerning the diagnosis and cure of **Incantations** and **Sorceries** <note>original: *Veneficiis maleficiatis* - specifically referring to harm caused by poisoning or witchcraft</note>.

**Fourth**, concerning the <term>diagnostics <note>original Greek: δοκιμασίας (*dokimasias*)—critical tests or examinations used to evaluate the state of a patient</note></term> of many diseases, which are the truest harbingers of recovery or death.

<header>ON THE INTERNAL PROPERTIES OF THINGS.</header>

<image-desc>A horizontal decorative woodcut border featuring two rabbits facing outward, surrounded by ornate floral scrolls and leaf patterns.</image-desc>

# COROLLARY.

<margin>See the *Hieroglyphic Monad* <note>original: *Monadem Hieroglyphicam*. A famous 1564 work by John Dee explaining a complex symbol representing the unity of the cosmos.</note> of John Dee of London.</margin>

**T**he most ancient *wise men, whom we call Philosophers in the Greek tongue, if they had discovered any Secrets of either Nature or Art, would hide them in various ways and figures lest they fall into the knowledge of the wicked. In the same way, the Hermetic Philosophers <note>Followers of the legendary Hermes Trismegistus, associated with alchemy and secret wisdom.</note> were accustomed to mark the Earthly Planets <note>In alchemy, the seven metals were believed to be terrestrial counterparts to the seven celestial planets.</note> with certain Hieroglyphic signs, by which they might set before the eyes of the "Sons of Art" <note>A traditional term for dedicated students or practitioners of alchemy.</note> who are intelligent and observant, their hidden powers or virtues to be contemplated. However, so that such signs might be rescued from destruction or burial, I have judged that I would be doing something worthwhile if—together with the Characters of other Minerals devised by a Provident Antiquity to keep the Profane and unworthy Common Folk away from this study—I were now to communicate them at once to the Chemical Republic <note>The early modern "Republic of Letters" or community of scholars, specifically those focused on chemistry.</note> for the sake of Hermetic disciples.*

# THE FIRST INDEX.

**PHYSICIANS** and **SURGEONS** were taught many remedies for diseases and the medicinal virtues of things by irrational animals <note>original: *à brutis*. This refers to the ancient and medieval belief that humans learned medicine by observing animals—for example, watching a wounded deer seek out specific herbs.</note> 101

From which animals these same men learned the use of emetics <note>medicines used to induce vomiting.</note> and purgatives 103

**LEGAL EXPERTS** saw in storks a council of judgments <note>original: *Iudiciorum consessum*. This likely refers to the "Lex Ciconiaria" or "Stork Law," an ancient Roman concept of reciprocal obligation, inspired by the belief that storks cared for their elderly parents.</note> 104

**HERMETIC PHILOSOPHERS**, the **ADEPTS**, <note>Hermeticism is a philosophical and alchemical tradition; "Adepts" were those believed to have mastered the secrets of alchemy, such as the Philosopher's Stone.</note> from which animals they learned the method of renewing youth 105

Notable examples of our **RESURRECTION** and **TRANSFORMATION** found in the Ant and the Silkworm <note>original: *Formica & Bombyce*. The metamorphosis of the silkworm was a common early modern metaphor for the soul leaving the body and the Christian resurrection.</note> 107

The entries reflect the "Doctrine of Signatures," where the physical properties of animals (like crabs and toads) or plants (like capillary ferns) are believed to indicate their medicinal uses. There is also a strong focus on "sympathetic medicine," such as using parts of a rabid dog to cure its own bite.</meta>
